chapters.title: Chapter 1901 Screaming Mountain
paragraphs: "I know. I'll just massacre a couple million dissidents at most. I consider the dwarven people mine already, so I won't destroy them."
"...Good."

Quinlan moved to the window, thoroughly pleased with the new mission, and collected his second-in-command on the way, one arm scooping Ayame off the window seat and folding her under it like a sack of very expensive potatoes.
"Wha... Quin!" The samurai's legs kicked once at the indignity. "I can walk!"
"I'm excited."
"And?!"
"I felt like picking you up."
"..." Ayame went still under his arm, chin propped on one hand, ears faintly pink.
She sighed. "Carry on, then."
The window swung shut behind the Primordial Villain, his dangling samurai, and the sound of a governor pretending very hard that her hands weren't still shaking over the tax rolls.

Serika was pouring the last of the moonwine into Kitsara's cupped hands, the foxkin having lost cup privileges an hour earlier, when Quinlan came up the royal roofline with a samurai folded under one arm.
His boot never finished landing.
A streak of blonde and lightning crossed the entire rooftop between two heartbeats, and Blossom hit his chest with her arms already locked around him, tail going like a war banner.
"Master!"
The rooftop laughed, started composing its usual greetings, and then actually looked at him.
The words died where they stood.
His eyes had gone bright and ominous, lit from somewhere far beneath the warmth he'd carried when it was time to laze around.
Every woman on that roofline had seen those eyes before.
It was time to fight.
The change swept the rooftop in a single breath. Serika set the bottle down, and when she straightened, her eyes were burning emerald and her ponytail had begun its slow molten pulse.
Kitsara's five tails lifted and sharpened, the drink gone from her face between one blink and the next. Vex spun her pentagrams up bright, and her crimson tattoos woke with them.
Friends who had spent the evening rating nobles now stood the roofline as warrioresses, and the night turned colder around them.
Blossom dropped off his chest to his heel, and Ayame put herself back on her own feet with what dignity remained.
Quinlan tore space open along the roofline, a dimensional seam widening into a gate.
He walked through first, and his family followed him in, one by one, each delicate face wearing the look of a trained killer on the prowl.
The sound arrived before the mountain did.
It came up through their boots the moment they stepped through, tens of thousands of dwarven voices dragging one melody through solid stone until the floor itself sang along.
The royal smithy of the dwarven capital was filled past overflowing, every tier packed, dwarves on the stairs, dwarves on the rails, dwarves standing on cold quench-troughs for the view.

And every last one of them was geared. Mail over work-leathers, axes across backs, war-braids bound in iron rings, hammers resting on shoulders that had swung them since childhood. They sang like drunks and stood like an army.
On a bench in the middle tiers, an elven royal guard in full armor screamed the chorus, sword raised high, having the time of her life.
At the heart of it all, on the great anvil, a helmet was being born.
Brokk struck it with Everwright to the song's own beat, and the hall sang to her hammer. Every fall of the water-grained head threw sparks the color of a fresh pour.
*CLANG!*
"That's thirty!" a smith bellowed from the second tier, and the whole tier roared the number back at him.
The rune-script down the haft burned steady, an elf's hammer drinking a dwarf's mana and giving it back in the strike.
The gate's light touched the far wall, and the song stumbled.
For one held breath, the royal smithy stared at the Primordial Villain and the women arrayed behind him.
Then the mountain went berserk.
"THE VILLAIN!"
"Don't call him that! He's a master smith!"
"HE CAME! HE ACTUALLY CAME!"
"LORD ELYSIAR STANDS WITH THE MOUNTAIN!"

The name three hundred smiths had refused to speak in this hall now came off every wall of it at once. Hafts hammered shield-rims and boots hammered the tiers. The war song came back twice the size it had died at, rolling over the newcomers in a wall of heat and voices.
On her bench in the middle tiers, the elven royal guard's sword came down very slowly.
"...Oh," Elowen said. "Oh, no. No, no, I was... I was singing. That was a cultural exchange. That was diplomacy."
Brokk never broke her rhythm.
She struck Everwright down one final time, and the helmet on the anvil went quiet, finished. She lifted it in both hands, pushed her braid back, and set it on her head.
Then the First Hammer of the Royal Smithy looked across her overflowing hall, found Quinlan, and nodded to him, once.
Quinlan nodded back to her.
Everwright went up over her head, and the hall's thunder cut itself off to hear her.
"SONS AND DAUGHTERS OF THE MOUNTAIN!"
Her voice came off the tiers like a hammer off hot steel.
"Kings wrote our lives in their books! Councilors wrote our deaths! We wrote nothing!" The haft's runes flared with her grip.

"Tonight, that ends! Tonight we go up, drag every corrupt son of a bitch off his council seat, and murder our way to the mountain's heart! And when the last of them falls, we build the golden era of the dwarven race with our own hands!"
"AYE!!"
The answer came from tens of thousands of chests at once.
Brokk brought Everwright down on the bare anvil with everything her arm and her titles were worth.
Quinlan's mana was waiting for it.
It slid beneath the strike, obedient to nothing but his intent, and the gong that should have filled a hall filled the mountain instead.
The note went through the mountain's bones as though they were air, down into the roots and up through every tier, rattling lamps in their brackets and shivering dust off ceilings a mile away.
In the farthest galleries, dwarves who had never seen the royal smithy felt the First Hammer's anvil arrive in their chests, and understood.
And just like that, the dwarven rebellion began.

The hall emptied upward, roaring, a river of mail and axes pouring through every gallery mouth toward the lords' tiers. The first screams came back down the shafts within seconds, and the smell of blood followed them.
Quinlan watched the rushing dwarves from beside the great anvil, and the light coming off his eyes had nothing to do with the forges.
"Oh, how I've missed this," Serika said beside him, watching the axes pour past.
Then, in the heart of a war being born, the Primordial Villain called upon a window he hadn't opened in a long time.
[Name: Quinlan Elysiar]
[Race: Primordial]
[Health Points: 3300 ➣ 3469]
[Mana Points: 3919 ➣ 4200]
[Vitality: 220 ➣ 231]
[Strength: 164 ➣ 183]
[Agility: 174 ➣ 193]
"It's time to resume the grind," he said to no one in particular.
"Finally," his girls spoke in perfect sync, drawing their weapons.

chapters.title: Chapter 1902 Song of the Rebellion
paragraphs: The high council of the dwarven capital was in session.

It was always in session these days. The throne had sat empty since Ragnar's fall, four claims had been filed against it, and the high clans had spent every night since shouting at each other across the council table at the crown of the city.
Lord Harrek of the Copper Vaults never got to finish his argument.
*CLANG!*

One anvil strike came up through miles of solid rock without losing an ounce of itself. Crystal rattled in the chandeliers, wine jumped in the lords' cups, and every beard in the hall turned toward the floor.
"What in the deep was that?" a lord whispered.
"An anvil," said another, barely louder. "That was an anvil."
Nobody argued. Every dwarf in the hall had been born over that sound, and dread crawled up through Harrek's boots along with the echo, because an anvil was exactly the problem.
Stone ate sound. A hammer strike died within three floors of its own anvil.

Whatever had just driven a smith's note through the bones of the whole world was mana beyond anything the mountain had ever held. And this very council had named the one creature with mana like that an enemy of the mountain only hours ago.

The council hall sat at the heart of it all, the highest chamber of a city carved in rings around a great central shaft. Beneath it hung the lords' terraces, then the trade halls, then the crowded districts of the under-tier, gallery after gallery.
At the very bottom burned the royal smithy, whose forges lit the shaft from below like a sunrise kept in a well.
The lords had always found the glow beautiful. It was, after all, theirs.
Tonight the glow was climbing.
The war hymn rose with it, tens of thousands of voices dragging one melody up the great shaft until the council hall's floor buzzed under Harrek's boots.
"A tantrum," Lord Mogrun declared across the council table, though he had to raise his voice to do it. "Cut the coal to the low districts. They'll remember their place by breakfast."
"You cut their coal last week," Harrek snapped. "That's half of why they're singing."
The great doors banged open, and a captain of the terrace watch stumbled through with a dent the size of a fist in his breastplate.
"My lords! The third gallery is gone!"
"Gone where?"

"Up, my lord! They're coming up!" The captain's voice broke in front of the most powerful dwarves alive. "The tunnel-wardens joined them at the second landing! The lift crews cut their own chains and rode the counterweights down to join the mob! And the... the household companies are requesting orders!"
"Requesting orders." Mogrun's beard bristled. "Against porters. How many rats can one stair hold?"

"All of them, my lord." The captain had gone grey around his own beard. "The under-tier is empty. Every district, every warren, every mine, empty! The watchers counted forty thousand on the processional stair and gave up counting when the royal smithy's geomancers began widening it for them."
The council hall took a moment to digest the number.

A third voice slid in from the side, oiled and reasonable, from a cousin of a cousin who held the thinnest claim to the empty throne and wore the strongest perfume in the room. His household soldiers guarded half the passes above the trade halls, and he never let the council forget it.
"Perhaps a gesture first, my lords. An amnesty. Rebellions are expensive, and dead laborers pay no levy."
"They aren't asking for amnesty," Harrek said. He was watching the floor. The song had gotten louder. "They want our blood. Wake the anchors."
The order reached back past every clan at the table.

Sunk into the lintels and thresholds of the lords' tiers sat anchor-stones of ancient dwarven master craft, ward-cores older than the council itself, laid by smiths whose names were etched into legend.
Their promise had held for all of recorded history: within a warded threshold, magic died. No spell had ever crossed one, from the meanest candle-spark to a king's grand working.
The dwarves who owned everything had slept soundly behind that promise.

Around the hall and down every approach to the high terraces, the anchors woke. Ancient blacksteel drank mana for the first time in living memory, and rune-light crawled the doorframes and settled into a steady burn.
Harrek let out a long breath at the sight. "Haaah... Magnificent. If only modern craftsmen were half this proficient."
Around the table, lords who had been sweating into their collars began to remember how important they were.

"Our professional soldiers hold the lords' tiers," Mogrun said, loud enough to convince himself. "And the old stones hold the halls. Let the long-ears' pet monster come. In here he'll be one man with a saber, and rabble is still rabble. Grind them on the processional stair and be done with it!"
Far below, beneath the war hymn, a new sound came up through the stone. Lord Harrek needed a moment to place it, because it was coming from the household companies' positions.
It was screaming.
Three tiers below the council hall, on the great terrace of the processional stair, the household army of the high clans had chosen its ground well.

The processional stair was the capital's one grand road, forty dwarves wide, climbing from the trade halls to the lords' tiers past the statues of dead kings. Anything that wanted to reach the high clans had to come up it, and the terrace at its head was built to make sure nothing ever did.

Fifty thousand soldiers held it tonight. Shield-walls of steel and tower plate stood in ranks twenty deep across the terrace, crossbow lines packed every balcony above, and the entire rebellion was funneling toward all of it up one stair.
Every officer present had run the numbers and liked them. Their enemy was brave, furious, and made of smiths, porters, and miners. The companies were made of soldiers.
"First rank! ADVANCE!"
The shield-wall took one step down the stair.
The stair moved first.

Hidden in the rebellion's front ranks, the royal smithy's geomancers pressed their palms to the steps, and the stone answered the men who had shaped it their entire lives. The stairs beneath the descending shield-wall melted flat, steepened, and froze again as one polished chute.

Three hundred soldiers in full plate lost their footing at once. They rode their own shields down the length of the stair, a screaming avalanche of steel, and the rebellion's front line stood waiting at the bottom with hammers raised.
The under-tier fell on them roaring. Hammers rose and fell, and what they left on the steps no longer looked like soldiers.
"GEOMANCERS!" an officer howled from the balcony rail. "Find their geomancers! Counter-"
The rail turned to magma under his hands, and his howl chased it down into the shaft.
Below, at the foot of the stair, the crowd was parting around a man walking up.
He came unhurried, arms loose at his sides, dark armor breathing around him, two red eyes burning behind the visor.

A tide of molten rock climbed the stair with him, step over step, parting around every rebel boot and spreading wide around his own. Wind that had no business existing indoors screamed along the balconies, and frost webbed the statues of dead kings as he passed them.
The rebellion's roar found its shape.
"THE VILLAIN!"
"LORD ELYSIAR IS WITH THE DWARVEN REBELLION!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1903: Anchor Stones
paragraphs: "LORD ELYSIAR IS WITH THE DWARVEN REBELLION!"
The Primordial Villain climbed the processional stair of the dwarven capital one step at a time, and the mountain rearranged itself around his mood.

A hundred crossbow bolts dove at him from the balconies. A crosswind swatted the entire volley sideways into the shaft. Then the balconies themselves leaned outward, politely, like servants pouring wine, and emptied their crossbow lines off into the dark after it.
The screaming on the terrace changed register.
"The stone threw them off! The stone itself!"
"The mountain’s helping him! The mountain wants us dead!"
"Hold the line! HOLD, DAMN YOU!"
A sergeant with a two-handed maul broke ranks and charged down the stair, bellowing his clan at the thing in dark armor. "KORVASH! CLAN KORVASH FIGHTS TO THE END!"
Frost took him mid-swing. The Primordial Villain walked past without turning his head, and the statue stayed exactly where its courage had carried it, maul raised forever.

The soldiers nearest the new statue stopped fighting to stare at it. One of them, a veteran with twenty border clashes in his beard, put down his axe and sat on the steps, done with the entire fight already.

Along the terrace’s flank, the garrison’s sally-doors glowed orange at the hinges and slumped shut, welding the reserve companies into their own barracks. Fists hammered the cooling metal from inside, and the hammering turned to howling.

Lightning entered the front rank of the eastern shield-wall through their tower shields and left through the back rank’s boots. Two hundred soldiers dropped where they stood with smoke crawling off their pauldrons, and the smell of cooked meat rolled across the terrace.
"That’s no man!" someone wailed from the collapsing line. "RUN! RUN!"
"Trials. Coronations. Signatures." The man in dark armor rolled his neck as he climbed, red eyes shining. "I almost forgot what pure joy feels like."
This was war again, honest war, with nobody in front of him worth sparing.
He was humming.
"Monster!" dwarves screamed and wailed as he approached them at his own pace.
The Villain’s family spread across the terrace behind him, each woman picking her hunting ground on sight.

"Everyone!" Kitsara’s voice sang over the battlefield from a balcony rail, twin daggers already dark with poison. "This noble lady proposes a game! We’ll count our kills until the mountain runs out of idiots! Loser draws the winner’s bath for a week~!"
"Deal!" answered the deadliest women alive, from every corner of the terrace at once.
The household soldiers who heard the exchange needed a heartbeat to understand that these delicate-looking, tall women were dividing up their deaths like party favors.
Serika helped them understand.

She landed on the western shield-wall fist-first, and the wall stopped being one. Solar force erupted from the impact and folded the formation against the terrace wall in a single wave of heat. "[Solar Eruption]!" arrived a heartbeat late, announced mostly for fun.

"Eight," Vex corrected from inside a crumbling crossbow line. Her pentagram eyes tracked a soldier crawling for the stairwell, and her hex closed around his heart like a fist. "The one by the brazier was mine. My hex reached his heart before your blade did."
"Finders keepers~"

"Split him," Aurora offered. She was walking the stair’s edge below, staff in hand and untouched, [Dreamveil] running like a second skin over the rebel wounded being dragged clear. Every bolt aimed at the wounded sparked off thin air and quit.
"Split?!" both women scoffed together, equally offended.
"Since when do you make the rules?!" Kitsara demanded.
"...Behave, foxy."
"Or?"
"Or I’ll add frog slime to your potions."
"On second thought, splitting sounds good!"

"Good girl," Quinlan called without looking.
The tail nearly achieved flight.

"Not that I know of. Only from the inside."

"Well, you’ve not given them much of a reason to doubt~" Lucille purred.
"Ego checked. Quin must show off now." Serika grinned, already knowing her lover more than well enough to see where this was going.
Quinlan flexed his fingers, and the Soul Reaper began brimming in his fist.
"Time to show them the error of their ways."
Quinlan stepped over the ward line and kept walking, followed by a handful of deadly women grinning from ear to ear, watching their man pave the way into the heart of dwarven power.

chapters.title: Chapter 1904 Careless Blunder
paragraphs: Beyond the arch, in a colonnaded gallery built as a killing ground, waited the honor guard of the high clans: three thousand veterans in rune-dense blacksteel, tower shields interlocked rank behind rank into the dark, twin ballista platforms flanking the far end.
Their commander had watched the tide of magma die at the threshold, and his voice rang out in triumph.
"You see that, lads?! The old stones hold! He can't cast in here!" A blade swept the length of the gallery. "He's one man with a saber! Loose! Cut him down!"
Quinlan, two steps past the threshold, had stopped.
"Ah," said the Primordial Villain. "I forgot."
He had not called Kaelira and Black Fang.
The first ballista bolt caught him square in the chest while his mouth was still open.
The crew had been laying that shot since his boot crossed the line, and it arrived as the whole argument of dwarven siegecraft in one length of blacksteel.

Synchra surged to meet it, living plates stacking at the point of impact, shrieking with the effort of the catch, and the effort was not enough. The blow went through armor and ribs alike, and the Primordial Villain left the floor.

The bolt's force carried him back down the gallery, back through the arch, past his women still on the safe side of the line - just about to step through after him - and out across the landing beyond, where the mountain's masons had thoughtfully provided forty feet of polished stone for him to land on.
"Quin?!" Kitsara's ears shot straight up.
"What are you doing?!" Ayame hissed.
Quinlan, for his part, spent the flight productively.
'I'm a terrible husband. How could I step into the no magic barrier before inviting them?'
He hit the landing on his back, skipped once, and slid the rest of the way in a long scream of sparks, coming to rest with one boot hanging over the top step of the processional stair.
Behind the arch, the gallery went insane.
"He's down!" the commander was roaring, hoarse with joy. "Did you see it, lads?! The stones hold! Ancestors bless the old stones, the stones hold!"
And the rebellion, cresting the processional stair at exactly that moment, did not wait to see whether he would get up.

The war hymn broke over the landing, and the under-tier's first wedge came boiling past the crash site: tunnel-wardens with mining picks, smiths with forge-hammers, porters in scavenged plate, thousands more on the stairs behind them.
They had fought up through their whole city for this door, and they went through the arch first, straight onto the shield-wall of the finest soldiers their mountain had forged.
His girls did not charge anywhere.
They gathered around the crash site instead, settling into a loose circle around their man, arms crossed, eyes narrowed.
Serika watched him raise one hand and wave it vaguely: the universal signal of a man requesting not to be perceived for a moment.
"You're too tanky for your own good. Synchra pampers you so much you've become careless."
"You forgot to invite Kaelira and Black Fang, didn't you~" Lucille's purr carried zero surprise. "I was wondering when you'd notice~"

Blossom said nothing at all. Her tail hung limp behind her, and she was fighting the hardest battle on the landing: refusing to meet his gaze. Her eyes kept sliding toward him anyway, and kept being hauled back, and what finally escaped her was barely a mutter.
"Master... bad...! Careless!!"
It landed harder than the ballista had.
Synchra's plates were still rippling over his chest in agitated waves, examining a dent the size of a shield boss. Cracks ran through three of them. Something deeper creaked when he breathed.
Quinlan reached along the link. Out here it was alive, and it was already occupied.
<Quin.>
He blinked at the ring of faces above him.
<Kaelira. Perfect timing.>
<Where are you?> Flat. Suspicious.
<Hm? Why do you ask?>
<The Reservoir has been running hot for some time. That only happens when the girls are on a battlefield.> A pause that had weight behind it. <So. Where. Are. You.>
<Damn.> The furious girlfriend tone alone told him he was in deep trouble.
<Quin.>
<I may be exterminating the dwarven resistance at the moment.>
The link fell silent. It did not close. It simply sat there against his mind and sulked, loudly.
Quinlan chuckled out loud, and his ribs made him pay for it.
<I might have gotten ahead of myself,> he admitted. <In my defense, the rebellion started abruptly and I rushed here to escape paperwork.>
<Mhm.>
<I was just about to invite you over. There's a door here with your name on it.>
<Mhm.>
<I mean it.>
<Mhm.>
He sat up inside the semicircle, wincing, and opened the warp gate.
<Voilà.>

Kaelira stepped through it four seconds later in full armor, hammer already in hand, violet eyes finding him instantly: sitting on the ground, dented, at the crime scene. Black Fang came a silent half-step behind her, blade in its sheath.
Then both of them just looked at him.

A glare, he could have weathered. What he got instead was the stare of two kittens who had just learned that dinner had happened without them. Kaelira's version came with wounded violet eyes and long ears quivering with grievance. Black Fang's version was no expression at all, held on him one full second longer than no expression requires.
"What happened doesn't mean you can ignore me now..." Black Fang muttered under her breath.
He'd armed her with a bunch of pills, effectively ending their wager. Now she no longer needed to be around him.
"I'm sorry, I didn't mean it like that at all," Quinlan managed, hand arriving on his dented chestplate.

"Hmph." Kaelira swept past him without another word, chin high, straight through the arch and into the war, waiting for nobody. Black Fang followed her in, and the sounds of the battle promptly gained two new instruments: a hammer, and a silent katana that killed things.
The semicircle filed every second of it away for later.

Quinlan, still sitting in his crater, began opening more warp gates. They spun open across the landing one after another, cut to places scattered across half of Iskaris, and his old guard came through them ready.
Lyra arrived in full tower-shield harness, pink braid bound for war, Ria at her heels already laughing at the dent in his chest. Sylvaris followed in moonlit glory.
Cedric and Selene came through sword-first, and Abudha took one measuring look at the arch and cracked his knuckles.

Blackjack ducked out of the next gate wearing the grin that had emptied border towns, and Raika came through scoffing, furious that the fight had started without her. Orianna walked out of the last one, read the anchor-stones, the arch, and the battle beyond in a single unhurried look, and said nothing at all.
Two gates stayed shut. Sera was still tending Iris's wounds tonight, and not even a war got to interrupt that.
"Fair warning," Quinlan called over the din. "No casting past the line."
Ignis arrived overhead on a pillar of flame at exactly the wrong moment to hear it.
"You're joking. You called me?" He landed grinning, fire still crawling on his shoulders. "I thought you'd forgotten about me."
"I kinda did, to be honest."
"...You're only honest at the worst of times."
Quinlan elected to ignore that. "Also, would I summon you for a joke?"
"Yes."
"...True." Quinlan gestured grandly at the arch from the ground. "Regardless. In there, you're a tall man with good shoulders."
"No problem." Ignis seemed full of confidence.

Two more gates opened at the back of the landing, well clear of the arch, and this time nobody came through armed for a charge. Liora stepped out with light already pooling at her fingertips. Shallan followed, and took in the landing like a quartermaster claiming ground. Adventurer Kai's ex slaves, Kaelira's teammates.

"Past the arch, nothing heals. Could you two build me a station? Anyone who comes back through that line bleeding is yours." Quinlan told them, nodding at the first wounded rebels already being dragged back over the line.
"Leave it to us," Liora said, already moving toward the nearest stretcher.
Shallan was already redirecting rebels with a voice that expected obedience: walking wounded to the left, dying men to Liora first.
All gates were opened with clear purpose.
The last, he opened on a whim.
Morgana Ravenshade stepped through it with her staff in hand, crimson eyes sweeping the landing, the arch, and the mountain in one cold inventory.
"Where," she said.
"Through the arch," Quinlan said pleasantly. "One detail. The hall beyond is a null-domain."
A silence arrived and settled in.

Kaelira stepped through it four seconds later in full armor, hammer already in hand, violet eyes finding him instantly: sitting on the ground, dented, at the crime scene.
Black Fang came a silent half-step behind her, blade in its sheath.
Then both of them just looked at him.
A glare, he could have weathered.
What he got instead was the stare of two kittens who had just learned that dinner had happened without them.
Kaelira's version came with wounded violet eyes and long ears quivering with grievance.
Black Fang's version was no expression at all, held on him one full second longer than no expression requires.
"What happened doesn't mean you can ignore me now..." Black Fang muttered under her breath.
He'd armed her with a bunch of pills, effectively ending their wager.
Now she no longer needed to be around him.
"I'm sorry, I didn't mean it like that at all," Quinlan managed, hand arriving on his dented chestplate.
"Hmph." Kaelira swept past him without another word, chin high, straight through the arch and into the war, waiting for nobody.
Black Fang followed her in, and the sounds of the battle promptly gained two new instruments: a hammer, and a silent katana that killed things.
The semicircle filed every second of it away for later.
Quinlan, still sitting in his crater, began opening more warp gates.
They spun open across the landing one after another, cut to places scattered across half of Iskaris, and his old guard came through them ready.
Lyra arrived in full tower-shield harness, pink braid bound for war, Ria at her heels already laughing at the dent in his chest.
Sylvaris followed in moonlit glory.
Cedric and Selene came through sword-first, and Abudha took one measuring look at the arch and cracked his knuckles.
Blackjack ducked out of the next gate wearing the grin that had emptied border towns, and Raika came through scoffing, furious that the fight had started without her.
Orianna walked out of the last one, read the anchor-stones, the arch, and the battle beyond in a single unhurried look, and said nothing at all.
Two gates stayed shut.
Sera was still tending Iris's wounds tonight, and not even a war got to interrupt that.
"Fair warning," Quinlan called over the din.
"No casting past the line."
Ignis arrived overhead on a pillar of flame at exactly the wrong moment to hear it.
"You're joking.
You called me?" He landed grinning, fire still crawling on his shoulders.
"I thought you'd forgotten about me."
"I kinda did, to be honest."
"...You're only honest at the worst of times."
Quinlan elected to ignore that.
"Also, would I summon you for a joke?"
"Yes."
"...True." Quinlan gestured grandly at the arch from the ground.
"Regardless.
In there, you're a tall man with good shoulders."
"No problem." Ignis seemed full of confidence.
Two more gates opened at the back of the landing, well clear of the arch, and this time nobody came through armed for a charge.
Liora stepped out with light already pooling at her fingertips.
Shallan followed, and took in the landing like a quartermaster claiming ground.
Adventurer Kai's ex slaves, Kaelira's teammates.
"Past the arch, nothing heals.
Could you two build me a station?
Anyone who comes back through that line bleeding is yours." Quinlan told them, nodding at the first wounded rebels already being dragged back over the line.
"Leave it to us," Liora said, already moving toward the nearest stretcher.
Shallan was already redirecting rebels with a voice that expected obedience: walking wounded to the left, dying men to Liora first.
All gates were opened with clear purpose.
The last, he opened on a whim.
Morgana Ravenshade stepped through it with her staff in hand, crimson eyes sweeping the landing, the arch, and the mountain in one cold inventory.
"Where," she said.
"Through the arch," Quinlan said pleasantly.
"One detail.
The hall beyond is a null-domain."
A silence arrived and settled in.

chapters.title: Chapter 1905 Into the Null-Magic Barrier
paragraphs: "You summoned me," said the Witch Queen of Vraven, the strongest elemental mage on Iskaris, five hundred years of mastery across seven elements, "to a place where magic does not exist."
"I did."
"Why."
"Why not. Aren't you my strongest slave?" Quinlan shrugged, quoting her earlier claim.
Morgana's left eye twitched.
"You gate-hopping, primordial son of a-"
"Silence," Vex demanded with a tone of pure menace.
The eruption strangled itself at the halfway point, and the rest of the sentence stayed in Morgana's eyes, at length.

Then her gaze snagged on the lintel. On the anchor-stones, quietly drinking a discipline she had spent five centuries perfecting, as if it were spilled water. The fury stayed exactly where it was. Underneath it, against her will, a research problem began unpacking its instruments.

"Move." The strongest elemental mage alive shouldered her staff and marched toward the one hall in the world where she was a woman with a stick, because the alternative was letting him watch the curiosity arrive.
The Primordial Villain surveyed the army he had just pulled out of thin air, and gravity entered his bearing.
"Avengers," he declared, from the floor, "assembled."
"Now is not the time for silly Earth references, baby~" Lucille chided him with a tender smile.
"I was worried when you flew," Aurora admitted. "But if you're saying things like that, you're fine."
And just like that they went, his girls and his old guard together, through the arch and into the mountain, leaving him sitting in the crater they had all declined to mention.
"Dibs on the ballista crews!" Kitsara was already through.
"Avengers," Quinlan noted to the empty landing, "dispersed."
... Not quite. A tower shield planted itself beside his crater, and a gauntleted hand came down into his field of view.
His valiant pink-haired tanker hauled him to his feet with one pull.
"Thank you, Lyra. Always so reliable."
She smiled at him, bright and brief, then shouldered her shield and jogged after the girls.
Despite Quinlan's complaints, he was grinning from ear to ear because of what his girls had just done. Namely, not waiting for him.

Nobody had asked him where to stand or what to hit. They were not his soldiers, and they had never for one day been his minions: they were his partners, monsters with their own scores to settle and their own styles of settling them.
Just like how he preferred his perfect warrior wives.
Quinlan pulled a healing potion off his belt and drank it in one long pull. The creak in his chest faded. The dent in Synchra's plates did not.
"Sorry, partner," he murmured, laying two fingers flat on the wounded plate. "That one was on me."
Synchra rippled under his fingers and flared, once, in unmistakable disapproval.
"Fair," he agreed. "I won't take you for granted."
Then the Primordial Villain rolled his neck, and his eyes gained a terrible glint.
'Might as well do that, then.'
One more warp gate spun open beside him.
The gallery filled with everything a war is supposed to sound like.

The honor guard of the high clans were three thousand of the finest heavy infantry the mountain had ever produced, in interlocked formation deep enough to swallow a charge whole, on ground built for them, with the two best ballista crews alive working the platforms. They had no sorcery, and on this floor, neither did anyone else.
"For the high clans!"
"Bury them!"

The under-tier's first charge broke against the shield-wall in front of everyone. So did the second. Tunnel-wardens died on blacksteel with their picks still raised, the wall gave back not one inch of floor, and the ballistae worked the packed stair-mouth in turns, every bolt going through three people before it stopped.
Serika hit the wall next, and the wall held.

Her opening blow, the kind that folded siege doors, landed square on the interlock, and the interlock drank it: runes flared down the linked shields, the force ran away along the whole formation and bled into the stone, and thirty dwarves grunted, took one collective half-step, and closed up again.
The Solar Fist stood in front of an unbroken shield-wall for the first time in years, and her grin came up slow and wide.
"Oh," she said. "You lovely little bastards."

She went to work, and it was tough work. The wall rotated fresh shields into every breach she made. A war maul she never saw came around a shield rim and caught her across the ribs, and the sound of it echoed off the colonnade. She put its owner into the third rank, spat a worrying amount of blood, and kept swinging.

Kaelira's opening detonation should have taken six of them. Her hammer met a tower shield, the rune-channel behind the blow fired, and the shield drank that too: grounding-lattices, worked into the blacksteel by smiths who had spent generations learning to break other people's runework, pulled her detonation apart and fed it into the floor.
The sulk on the Runeweaver Titan's face turned, slowly, into something with far more respect and far more violence in it. "I'm starting to understand the mechanism."
She began recutting her channels between swings, testing, adjusting, her craft against the mountain's, and every blow landed a little deeper than the last.
"Uh oh~" Kitsara giggled, ducking a halberd.

Kitsara herself had lasted eight seconds on the ballista platform before its guard detail arrived, and her tails were just tails in here. A slit-bolt tore through the space she had just vacated, close enough to trim fox fur.
"Grr!! Mountains are bad news for graceful ladies such as I! Cavemen girls, I'll leave this to you."
"Watch out!"
Lyra planted her tower shield over the foxgirl and took the follow-up bolt full-on, and even braced, the tanker went three steps sideways with her boots carving grooves in the stone.
"Uhh, thanks!!"
Black Fang walked, and soldiers died where her walk had been. This time, the dead did not get to rise.
"Your best...?" she spoke calmly, looking straight at the dead.
Her expression did not change. "Lacking."
"Shut it, serpent bitch!" A dwarf woman screamed. "My husband died in your invasion. Don't presume this is the full dwarven glory!"
Indeed. What remained of the dwarven nobility and their retainers was a crippled force of the once glorious military their race sported.
But...
"And?"
It wasn't Black Fang's problem.
Her katana's blade flashed and came down again.

"Big siiis~" Ayame called from the west colonnade, where a gray-bearded captain with a lifetime of blade-drill was somehow still alive in front of her, giving ground one perfect parry at a time. "Were you lonely? Did you two rehearse the sulking together?"
Black Fang treated the gallery as empty of little sisters.
"You're really powerful, by the way," Ayame told the captain sincerely, and their blades met four more times before either of them breathed.

Raika's punches came off the flank with shockwaves that scattered helmets three ranks deep, and the wall bent around her and did not break. Blackjack waded into the press grinning, came back out bleeding from four places, and went back in grinning wider.
"Zehahaha! More, more! Come at me!"

Cedric and Selene worked as one blade in two hands along the colonnade, Abudha's open palms turned halberds aside with a monk's economy, and Ria ghosted the murder-line where the platforms couldn't crank down far enough to track her. Blossom was a rumor in the dark between the pillars that both ballista crews had already learned to fear.

Orianna, robbed of every trick that made her Orianna, had taken over the rebel wedge at the stair-mouth instead, and under her flat, unhurried orders, the under-tier's charges stopped being suicide and started being a siege.
Ignis punched someone very hard. It helped less than advertised.
"Hold!" the commander called down the line, hoarse and exact. "The stones hold and so do you! Nothing is coming that you weren't forged for! Hold and bleed them!"
And they did. The wall reformed over its own dead, rank stepping into rank, and the gallery floor grew crowded with bodies from both sides.
Then the fighting nearest the arch stuttered, because the Primordial Villain had come back through it at a stroll, carrying something upright in his left hand.
"VILLAIN! YOU DARE?!"
Quinlan's eyes flashed a brilliant crimson. Beneath his helmet, a terrible expression sat on his face.
"Yes."

chapters.title: Chapter 1906 Royal Shield
paragraphs: "VILLAIN! YOU DARE?!"
The Primordial Villain's eyes flashed a brilliant crimson. Beneath his helmet, a terrible expression sat on his face.
"Yes."
A limbless torso in crumbling fused plate. One socket empty, one eye burning with a hatred the ice had not cooled by a single degree.
"It's the king." The whisper ran the shield-wall end to end, and the fighting died where it passed. "Stone have mercy, it's the king."
An axe hit the tiles somewhere in the second rank, and nobody bent to pick it up.
"He's alive," a guardsman said, hushed. "Stone above, what did he do to him?"
"Eyes front!" an officer barked down the line, and his own eyes never moved from the king.
Ragnar. The last king of the dwarves.
The king who had fed his own body to a forbidden ritual to become his people's unkillable shield, aimed the result at the wrong man, and lost his limbs, his war, and his mountain for it.
Quinlan had frozen what remained, and kept it.
He was gray where the frost had burned him, grayer where it hadn't, and sinking inside his own fused plate.

The ice had died at the gallery arch, drunk out of the air by the old stones the moment the Villain carried him across. Only the ritual held the last king of the dwarves together now, and the ritual had never once let him go.
Ragnar's eye had found Black Fang before the whisper finished traveling, and it never left her.
She passed within arm's reach of the king who had tormented her with his own royal hands, hour after hour, and then handed her to dozens of renowned torturers with orders to do their worst.
"You." Ragnar's rasp climbed out of the ruin of his chest on royal habit alone, a king summoning his prisoner. "You will look at-"
Her eyes never once arrived on him. To the Venomborne Terror, the last king of the dwarves was an empty stretch of gallery.
The far platform loosed.
"HOLD! THE KING-!" The scream went up from half the gallery at once, a heartbeat too late.
The Primordial Villain brought the royal torso up to meet the bolt without breaking stride.
"What a great shot," he chuckled ominously, the sound reverberating across the hall.
"Ng!" Ragnar made a wet sound.

The king took it below the collarbone, the shaft burying to half its length. The ritual's black threads came crawling for the wound, sluggish as cold tar, hauling it closed around the shaft while the honor guard watched their king pay for it out of what little king was left.
Stinking ooze welled up around the shaft as the threads worked, ran off the fused plate, and spattered the tiles.
"HRRAAGH!"
"YOU SHOT THE KING!" A guardsman's voice cracked somewhere along the shield-wall.
On the far platform, the loader backed away from his own weapon with both hands raised, as if it had fired itself.
The Villain drew [Soul Reaper], and the black saber drank the gallery's light along its edge.
Then the hush ran out.
"WALL EAST!" an officer screamed. "THE WALL, EAST!"
Serika had not spent the hush mourning anybody, and the interlock in front of her was one rune-flare from failure.
*Clang!*

The gallery came back to killing all at once. Kaelira's hammer took up its rhythm against the grounding-lattices again, each strike biting deeper than the mountain wanted to admit. Blackjack's laughter rolled up from the southern press. At the stair-mouth, Orianna's level voice was still turning charges into a siege.
Chaos owned the floor from colonnade to colonnade.
The commander had asked for a man with a saber.
What came up the center now had a saber in one hand and the last king of the dwarves in the other, moving at a working pace.

The first guardsman to reach him took two cuts to put down. The black edge skated off his breastplate, runes flaring where it scraped, and found him on the return instead, through the seam under his sword arm, where rune-plate had to end so a dwarf could swing.
"You people truly have amazing armor," he noted, hunting the next seam. "Can't wait to fit my armies in your best gear."
"Shut your foul mouth, monster!"
*GONG!*
A war maul came down at his spine, full swing, honest force, and rang off the last king of the dwarves instead.
Quinlan had brought the royal torso around behind his shoulder without turning his head, and the maul's owner stood frozen over the finest swing of his life, spent on his own king's plate.
"Even now, you're so sturdy. Truly admirable," Quinlan mused.
"Damn... you, Villain." The rasp shook its way out of the king in pieces, and each word cost a wet wheeze and a string of dark filth off the royal chin.
Synchra was still knitting herself together from the ballista, and he gave her nothing new to pay for.
The next axe met empty air as he slid inside its arc, a spear got turned wide on the flat of the black saber, and everything heavier found the king waiting for it.
The wall was dying at both ends while its center spent itself on him.
Serika had a shield rim in each hand and was folding a tower shield in half, fighting next to Vex, who, without her Hexes, was working overtime to keep up with her more brutish fellow harem elder.
On the west colonnade, Ayame's masterful cuts were exploiting the smallest of gaps in dwarven craftsmanship, cutting her enemies down with frightening accuracy.
Then the commander spent his masterpiece.
"PRESS!" His arm dropped. "CHAIN!"
The first wall of shields came in low and fast, lives spent to buy half-beats, and Quinlan met it with the last king of the dwarves.

The lead shield-bearer had his thrust lined up for Quinlan's visor, and the king's face swung into its path. The thrust died half-launched, checked by a reverence no parry could have bought, and the black saber came over the royal shoulder and took him through the throat.

It was cruelty with nothing wasted in it. Every man in that press had sworn his line to the body on the Villain's arm, and the Villain wore their king like a buckler, and turned their love into gaps in their guard.
"He's using the king as a shield!" a guardsman screamed from the second rank, his axe frozen at the top of its arc. "I can't swing! Stone forgive us, I can't swing!"
"He is dead!" the commander bellowed. "That thing is a shield! Cut through it!"
The cuts pulled anyway.
Almost every arc that met the king's glare bent soft at the last inch, and every softened arc fed the saber another opening.
Quinlan worked through them at a butcher's pace, two fingers rolling the saber's hilt through its angles, presenting the king's ruined glare to one dwarf while the black edge finished another.
"Not... my men." Ragnar's rasp shook against his own plate, air whistling through some new hole the ritual had not bothered to close. "Villain! Not with me! DON'T DO THIS TO ME!"
"Shh. Only Anima-grade shields talk, and you're nothing but deteriorating Junk." Quinlan angled him into a descending hammer. The hammer swerved wide, and the saber repaid its owner for the kindness.
"Curse your wretched..." The wail broke into a wet, hacking cough that sprayed the royal plate black. "...existence!"

The black edge skated off his breastplate, runes flaring where it scraped, and found him on the return instead, through the seam under his sword arm, where rune-plate had to end so a dwarf could swing.
"You people truly have amazing armor," he noted, hunting the next seam.
"Can't wait to fit my armies in your best gear."
"Shut your foul mouth, monster!"
*GONG!*
A war maul came down at his spine, full swing, honest force, and rang off the last king of the dwarves instead.
Quinlan had brought the royal torso around behind his shoulder without turning his head, and the maul's owner stood frozen over the finest swing of his life, spent on his own king's plate.
"Even now, you're so sturdy.
Truly admirable," Quinlan mused.
"Damn... you, Villain." The rasp shook its way out of the king in pieces, and each word cost a wet wheeze and a string of dark filth off the royal chin.
Synchra was still knitting herself together from the ballista, and he gave her nothing new to pay for.
The next axe met empty air as he slid inside its arc, a spear got turned wide on the flat of the black saber, and everything heavier found the king waiting for it.
The wall was dying at both ends while its center spent itself on him.
Serika had a shield rim in each hand and was folding a tower shield in half, fighting next to Vex, who, without her Hexes, was working overtime to keep up with her more brutish fellow harem elder.
On the west colonnade, Ayame's masterful cuts were exploiting the smallest of gaps in dwarven craftsmanship, cutting her enemies down with frightening accuracy.
Then the commander spent his masterpiece.
"PRESS!" His arm dropped.
"CHAIN!"
The first wall of shields came in low and fast, lives spent to buy half-beats, and Quinlan met it with the last king of the dwarves.
The lead shield-bearer had his thrust lined up for Quinlan's visor, and the king's face swung into its path.
The thrust died half-launched, checked by a reverence no parry could have bought, and the black saber came over the royal shoulder and took him through the throat.
It was cruelty with nothing wasted in it.
Every man in that press had sworn his line to the body on the Villain's arm, and the Villain wore their king like a buckler, and turned their love into gaps in their guard.
"He's using the king as a shield!" a guardsman screamed from the second rank, his axe frozen at the top of its arc.
"I can't swing!
Stone forgive us, I can't swing!"
"He is dead!" the commander bellowed.
"That thing is a shield!
Cut through it!"
The cuts pulled anyway.
Almost every arc that met the king's glare bent soft at the last inch, and every softened arc fed the saber another opening.
Quinlan worked through them at a butcher's pace, two fingers rolling the saber's hilt through its angles, presenting the king's ruined glare to one dwarf while the black edge finished another.
"Not... my men." Ragnar's rasp shook against his own plate, air whistling through some new hole the ritual had not bothered to close.
"Villain!
Not with me!
DON'T DO THIS TO ME!"
"Shh.
Only Anima-grade shields talk, and you're nothing but deteriorating Junk." Quinlan angled him into a descending hammer.
The hammer swerved wide, and the saber repaid its owner for the kindness.
"Curse your wretched..." The wail broke into a wet, hacking cough that sprayed the royal plate black.
"...existence!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1907 Cruel Monster
paragraphs: The chain came in the half-beat when the king's weight tied up his shield arm, out of the shield-wall's blind side, runes burning down every link. Steel could not reach the Villain past their king, so the commander had stopped asking steel to.
Quinlan saw it late, and met it in the air anyway. The black saber struck blacksteel with a *CRACK!* that stung his palm to the elbow. The blow left a pale scratch on one link.
Blacksteel forged under the mountain did not open to a single strike, even his, and there was no time for a second: the weighted end wrapped his sword-side shoulder, cinched, and bit.
Synchra's plates dimmed wherever the grounded links touched, her light draining into the floor.
"Now!" the commander roared. "Kill him now!"
Axes came down from every side, and he fought inside the chain the whole time, wrenching the king up to block high, the saber deflecting low on a pinned arm's worth of reach.

A halberdier came in through the one line the royal body did not cover, found the seam under Quinlan's raised arm, and opened it deep. The seam went wide, cold first, then a deep spreading burn. The blood ran fast and dark down his ribs.
Somewhere in the press, an old veteran began laughing with desperate hope.
"WE HAVE HIM!" he howled through his own laughter. "LADS, WE HAVE HIM!"
Quinlan pinned the king against his chest with one forearm and closed his free gauntlet around the blacksteel links.
Under Synchra's cracked plates, the muscles of his back and shoulders swelled against the armor from inside.
He exhaled, set his feet in his own blood, and pulled.
The links held. The men holding the other end did not. The first heave dragged the anchor-team forward a full step, boots plowing tile dust, and the second tore the floor-pin out entirely.
"What in the Goddess is this Strength stat?!"
"Impossible! A mage is overpowering us?!"
Four dwarves arrived airborne into their own shield-press, screaming.
Quinlan stood in the wreck of the finest maneuver the mountain had left and unwrapped the dead chain from his shoulder.
"Much better," he sighed contently.
"Just what are your stats, you damned... creature?!" the commander cursed.
"They're getting pretty high, right?" Quinlan laughed.
"STOP BRAGGING!"
Down the gallery's flank, Orianna's wedge had forced the servants' gate, and the under-tier was squeezing through a doorway four dwarves wide, packed shoulder to shoulder with nowhere to scatter.
"Forget the Villain!" an officer shrieked by the far platform. "Kill the rats in the gate! Make him watch! He's powerful without magic but not overwhelming!"
The ballista came around toward the doorway.
Quinlan's helmet turned toward it, and the amusement went out of him mid-breath.
'Damn.'
They were aiming at a cluster of rebels, enthusiastic but severely lacking in speed or durability.
He didn't want to see them all dead.
'Time to put some work in, legs of mine.'
The last king of the dwarves hit the tiles, dropped without a glance.
Then the floor detonated where the Villain's heels had been.

Wind cracked down the length of the gallery, slapping banners flat against their poles, and a straight line of shattered tile ran from where he had stood to the far platform before a single dwarf could turn his head.
"LOOSE! LOOSE, LOO-!" the crew chief screamed at his own weapon.
The crew's trigger-hand never finished tightening.
The black saber went through the ballista's frame, the loaded bolt, and the man behind, all three in one savage, brutal slash. The great weapon folded off its mount in halves.
The officer who had given the order got one step.
"Wrong target," the Villain said, and cut him down where he stood.
The bolt meant for forty rebels never flew.
"Why do you care so much about some weak rebel scum?!" the commander screamed in utter outrage. At this point, it seemed some of the opposition just wanted to understand what nonsense was going on.
The big bad Primordial Villain was all over the place, bragging, sword fighting with great proficiency, and now saving nobodies?
Incomprehensible.
The reason was simple.
"I consider the dwarven people mine already."
For a breath, nobody in the servants' gate made a sound.
"He dropped the king," a veteran said somewhere in the wreckage, hollow. "He... the shield he took a war to win, he just... for porters. For porters."
Then a young smith's voice tore out of the crowd.
"HE CAME FOR US!"
"LORD ELYSIAR STANDS WITH THE MOUNTAIN!"
The under-tier came through the gate roaring, and the weight of a risen city landed on the honor guard's flank.
Across the gallery, the last king of the dwarves still lay where the Villain had dropped him.
"THE KING!" a sergeant bellowed, peeling off with four shields behind him. "Recover the king! Get him behind the wall!"
Five of the honor guard's fastest broke for the royal torso, and the first outstretched gauntlet got within a foot of the fused plate.
*Swish!*
A blonde blur beat him there.
Blossom came out of the pillar-dark at a dead sprint, hit the tiles in a one-handed cartwheel that was mostly bare thigh and straining leather straps, and came up spinning.
"Master!! Catch!!"
Her flying kick took the royal torso off the floor, and the last king of the dwarves crossed half the gallery in a flat, screaming arc, trailing a thin ribbon of dark spray.
"FUUUUUUUUUU!"
Quinlan received him into his already-waiting arm.
"Thanks."
"Ehehe!" Blossom beamed across the gallery, ears up, tail wagging hard. "Master saved the weak ones!! Master is no longer bad!!"
She dropped the five empty-handed dwarves a small curtsy, and was gone back into the dark between the pillars.
The Villain looked down at the cursing king in his arm, and his chuckle rolled out over the battlefield.
Even then, the honor guard did not run.
The end came from every direction at once.
The gallery fell rank by rank, backward, in order, and the commander died somewhere in the last knot of shields with his voice still level. It took nearly all of them, and it took time.

The final approach to the council hall was a hundred paces of killing corridor, and it held everything the high clans had left: the remnant of the honor guard, the lords' personal guard in blackened ancestral plate, murder-slits down both walls, and the last two ballistae in the mountain, laid directly on the entrance.
The null ran oldest here, from anchor-stones sunk beneath the peak itself, and in the corridor's dark, only bolts flew.
The whisper had outrun the Villain, passing from murder-slit to murder-slit, fraying as it went. Behind one slit, a guardsman began to pray, and stopped halfway through.
At another, Captain Torvek of the personal guard refused to believe it. Then he looked, and could not stop looking.

Quinlan walked into the killing ground with the last king of the dwarves held before chest and face. The royal flesh had gone from gray to a wet, sunken slate, sagging against the fused plate that held it, and the wound the gallery had paid for wept tarry filth in slow threads down the royal chest.
His girls followed him in, bloodied and smiling, fanning into the murder-dark along both walls. Behind the barricades, the lords' finest stilled.
Through the slit, Torvek watched the Villain come up the center at a stroll. The Villain's voice filled the length of the killing ground, warm and reasonable.
"Every man and woman who kneels shall be spared. Surrender and end this farce-"
"Loose!" someone barked from the barricade, and nobody loosed.

chapters.title: Chapter 1908 Final Resistance
paragraphs: From behind the great doors at the far end came the muffled fury of the council's last lords.
"WHAT ARE YOU WAITING FOR?!" That was Mogrun, pitched high with terror. "THAT THING IS ALREADY DEAD! THE COUNCIL COMMANDS YOU! LOOSE! LOOSE!"
And then their king used what the ritual had left of his lungs.

"SHOOT!" The roar came out ruined and enormous, dead air forced through a broken instrument, and every soldier in the corridor flinched as it hit them. "FORGET WHAT I AM NOW! SHOOT HIM THROUGH ME! THAT IS YOUR KING'S LAST COMMAND!"
Something tore in what remained of his chest. His last word frayed at its edges, and black ran freely from the corner of the royal mouth.
On the right, the ballista crew obeyed their king.
The great bolt crossed the corridor, and the Villain met it with their king.
Ragnar took it a hand's width from the first shaft, burying to half its length. The black threads came for the wound slower this time, slow enough that the whole corridor watched them labor.
The ooze crawling down the shaft ran thin and dark. The smell of it reached both barricades, old rot and older iron. The stones were still drinking. The king was still paying.
The scream that left him had gone threadbare. The approval underneath it had not.
Quinlan's voice rolled down the corridor, not sounding one bit pleased. "Okay. Bloodbath it is then."
Every dwarven spine at once felt a terrible shudder rush through it.

Their king's own order closed over the killing ground, and every dwarf in it now owned an impossible choice. Shoot, and the bolt landed in the body of the king they had sworn their lines to. Hesitate, and they were still armed soldiers holding weapons on the Villain's path, in a dark his family had already dissolved into.

Their king's own order closed over the killing ground, and every dwarf in it now owned an impossible choice. Shoot, and the bolt landed in the body of the king they had sworn their lines to. Hesitate, and they were still armed soldiers holding weapons on the Villain's path, in a dark his family had already dissolved into.
The choices came due one at a time.

A sergeant on the left barricade leveled his crossbow, hunting a clean angle past the king that did not exist, and his prayer got as far as "Stone keep-". Blossom was through him and elsewhere before the trigger finished its travel.
On the right wall, a slit-crew got their second weapon cranked halfway back to tension. Ayame's blade came in through the slit itself, and the cranking stopped.
A barricade tried to rally around its standard. Serika's fist arrived, and the standard went down with everyone still holding it.
Twice, a slit-crew caught Black Fang's outline and tracked her instead of him, then died before they could react.
"Mercy!! I don't want to die! I have children-"
Then a crying guardsman threw his crossbow over the barricade and sat down with his hands on his helmet.
"Huh?"
Nobody touched him, and no one was more shocked than the man himself.
Two more shots came from the right, brave and quick. Both landed in their king, and the men who had fired lowered their weapons afterward and could not look at what they had done.
"Mercy..."
Steel began hitting the floor.

It went down the barricades in both directions, axes, crossbows, ancestral blades, ringing off the flagstones one after another, and the lords' finest knelt where they stood. Captain Torvek laid his axe down last, unbuckled his helm, and knelt to his king.

"STAND UP!" Ragnar screamed at them, thrashing in the Villain's grip, all four stumps jerking against nothing, black spraying off his lips with every word. "COWARDS! TRAITORS! PICK THEM UP! SHOOT! SHOOOOT!"
They knelt, and kept kneeling, and the last command of the last dwarf king landed on soldiers who loved him too much to obey it.
The roar cracked, then failed altogether. The ruin of Ragnar hung in the silence he had ordered them to break, a bolt still working its way out of his mending chest.
"See that?" The murmur arrived warm against the side of the royal skull. "They love you."
A beat passed.
"You must've done something well."
"Damn you..." Black, filthy tears began welling up in Ragnar's eyes. "Damn you... Just kill me already... Stop this torture..."

The great doors of the council hall stood at the corridor's end, blacksteel from sill to crown, built to drink force, sorcery, and time. The oldest null-lattice under the peak burned across them in unbroken lines.
Quinlan set the king down against a pillar beside the doors, upright, facing back down the corridor, where the eye could miss nothing.

Kaelira came up the killing ground between the kneeling soldiers, hammer over her shoulder, the sulk still officially in force. Then her eyes found what burned across the great doors, and the sulk fell off her between one breath and the next. What burned there was the finest ward-lattice she had ever touched.
"This is a null-lattice." Her gauntleted finger traced the lintel, feather-light, and her voice had gone fluent and sure, the forge register, the one that had never once stammered.
"Six anchors, cross-braced, and they share their load with every ward on this tier. The whole ring hangs off this door. Whoever laid it was a genius."
Along both walls, the kneeling soldiers listened to an elf read the mountain's oldest secret off the stone like a shopping list.
The royal smiths had maintained that lattice for generations by copying it, because no living dwarf could read the original work.
"She can see the anchor points," Torvek heard himself say. "She just... looked at it."
The hammer came up. Six taps followed, unhurried, each one landing on a point nobody else in the corridor could see, and on the sixth, the rune-light across the great doors guttered and went out.
Down every approach and around the council hall itself, the old anchors died with it. The absolute promise every lord in the city had gone to sleep behind died of six hammer taps.
"It's open," Kaelira informed the corridor at large, still not looking at him, and stepped aside. Her long ears had turned red anyway.
"A true prodigy to the end," Quinlan grinned.
The not-looking became ferocious.
"I'm still mad at you. Praise will get you nowhere. Hmph..."

Behind them, the war hymn arrived at the lords' tiers. It came up out of every gallery mouth at once, tens of thousands strong, the rebellion cresting the last stairs of a city it had climbed one tier at a time. Brokk walked at the head of it, new helmet on her brow, Everwright in her fist.
Quinlan collected the king from his pillar, pushed the great doors of the council hall open with one hand, and let the mountain in.

The last lords of the high clans stood at the far end of their hall, and there was nowhere above them left to go. Their eyes went to the lintel first, where the oldest ward under the peak had died without a sound.
Then their eyes found what the Villain was carrying, and the room's courage went out.
Quinlan set their king down on the council table, upright among the maps of a mountain he no longer owned, facing his lords.
"Greetings," the Villain told the room.
Lord Mogrun looked at what remained of his king and sat down on the floor without deciding to.
"Elysiar!" Harrek's voice went to syrup on the first syllable. "My lord! The Copper Vaults recognized your quality from the very first-"
"They're yours," Quinlan said, to the First Hammer, and stepped aside.
Nobody recorded the order in which the lords died, though Lord Mogrun went down still bellowing about quotas, and Lord Harrek died mid-offer.
The perfumed cousin made it four steps toward the servants' stair before the tunnel-wardens took him back down the galleries he had bled dry. His screaming lasted three full tiers.

Through it all, Brokk walked to the council table and laid Everwright down on its surface, beside her king's ruin. Her hand stayed on the haft a moment longer than setting a thing down requires, and then she made it let go.
The smiths nearest the table saw where she had put it, and stopped moving.
"There's never been a hammer at that council table," one of them whispered, the oldest grievance of the smithy arriving at its own funeral.
One rested on it now.
Then it was done, and the hall filled, and kept filling: dwarves on the stairs, dwarves on the rails, dwarves packed shoulder to shoulder between the pillars.

Quinlan set the king down against a pillar beside the doors, upright, facing back down the corridor, where the eye could miss nothing.
Kaelira came up the killing ground between the kneeling soldiers, hammer over her shoulder, the sulk still officially in force.
Then her eyes found what burned across the great doors, and the sulk fell off her between one breath and the next.
What burned there was the finest ward-lattice she had ever touched.
"This is a null-lattice." Her gauntleted finger traced the lintel, feather-light, and her voice had gone fluent and sure, the forge register, the one that had never once stammered.
"Six anchors, cross-braced, and they share their load with every ward on this tier.
The whole ring hangs off this door.
Whoever laid it was a genius."
Along both walls, the kneeling soldiers listened to an elf read the mountain's oldest secret off the stone like a shopping list.
The royal smiths had maintained that lattice for generations by copying it, because no living dwarf could read the original work.
"She can see the anchor points," Torvek heard himself say.
"She just... looked at it."
The hammer came up.
Six taps followed, unhurried, each one landing on a point nobody else in the corridor could see, and on the sixth, the rune-light across the great doors guttered and went out.
Down every approach and around the council hall itself, the old anchors died with it.
The absolute promise every lord in the city had gone to sleep behind died of six hammer taps.
"It's open," Kaelira informed the corridor at large, still not looking at him, and stepped aside.
Her long ears had turned red anyway.
"A true prodigy to the end," Quinlan grinned.
The not-looking became ferocious.
"I'm still mad at you.
Praise will get you nowhere.
Hmph..."
Behind them, the war hymn arrived at the lords' tiers.
It came up out of every gallery mouth at once, tens of thousands strong, the rebellion cresting the last stairs of a city it had climbed one tier at a time.
Brokk walked at the head of it, new helmet on her brow, Everwright in her fist.
Quinlan collected the king from his pillar, pushed the great doors of the council hall open with one hand, and let the mountain in.
The last lords of the high clans stood at the far end of their hall, and there was nowhere above them left to go.
Their eyes went to the lintel first, where the oldest ward under the peak had died without a sound.
Then their eyes found what the Villain was carrying, and the room's courage went out.
Quinlan set their king down on the council table, upright among the maps of a mountain he no longer owned, facing his lords.
"Greetings," the Villain told the room.
Lord Mogrun looked at what remained of his king and sat down on the floor without deciding to.
"Elysiar!" Harrek's voice went to syrup on the first syllable.
"My lord!
The Copper Vaults recognized your quality from the very first-"
"They're yours," Quinlan said, to the First Hammer, and stepped aside.
Nobody recorded the order in which the lords died, though Lord Mogrun went down still bellowing about quotas, and Lord Harrek died mid-offer.
The perfumed cousin made it four steps toward the servants' stair before the tunnel-wardens took him back down the galleries he had bled dry.
His screaming lasted three full tiers.
Through it all, Brokk walked to the council table and laid Everwright down on its surface, beside her king's ruin.
Her hand stayed on the haft a moment longer than setting a thing down requires, and then she made it let go.
The smiths nearest the table saw where she had put it, and stopped moving.
"There's never been a hammer at that council table," one of them whispered, the oldest grievance of the smithy arriving at its own funeral.
One rested on it now.
Then it was done, and the hall filled, and kept filling: dwarves on the stairs, dwarves on the rails, dwarves packed shoulder to shoulder between the pillars.

chapters.title: Chapter 1909 No Longer Tortured
paragraphs: The under-tier carried its wounded in so they would miss nothing. The kneeling soldiers of the personal guard were herded in too, disarmed and dazed, because tonight belonged to them as well, whether they understood that yet or not.
The First Hammer of the royal smithy lifted Everwright back off the table, walked the length of the hall, and stopped in front of the Primordial Villain.

The noise of the packed hall died on its own, tens of thousands of dwarves falling still at once, and the hush ran out the open doors and down every gallery until the whole vertical city held its breath.
"Unworthy kings ordered us," Brokk said. Her voice came off the walls flat and exact. "Corrupt councils demanded of us. That ends tonight."
Her eyes, under the helmet she had forged while her people rose, measured the man in front of her.

"You came to my hall a villain and worked like a smith. You fought a battle that wasn't yours." She paused, and the next words came out as a verdict. "The mountain chooses its own hands now. And its hands choose you."
She did not bow.
The First Hammer raised Everwright and brought it down on the stone at the Villain's feet.
*CLANG!*
For one heartbeat, the strike hung alone in the hush, and the whole hall listened to it fade.
Then the hall answered her.

Every dwarf holding a hammer struck stone with it. Axes reversed and came down haft-first. Fists came down, then boot-heels, then the flats of surrendered blades, one strike apiece, tens of thousands arriving as one.
*CLANG!*
*CLANG!*
*CLANG!*

The rhythm caught, and the mountain became the drum. The strikes rolled out the open doors and down the galleries, tier taking it from tier, until the beat came back up through the floor of the hall from a city striking in time. Dust sifted from the vault with every pulse.

At the edge of it, the disarmed soldiers of the personal guard looked at one another. Then Captain Torvek brought his bare fist down on the flagstones, and his kneeling guardsmen followed him, knuckles splitting on the stone, striking with everything they had left to swear with.
"All hail the new sovereign of the dwarven race!" an old smith bellowed over the thunder.
"ALL HAIL! ALL HAIL!"
The answer came out of a hundred thousand chests at once, an oath taken in the only language the mountain had ever fully trusted.
Light rose at the corner of Quinlan's vision.
[The dwarven people of Iskaris have acknowledged your dominion.]
[Peoples of Iskaris conquered: 3/4]
[Conquer the beastkin people to claim rulership of Iskaris.]
[Reward: ???]
Through all of it, upright on the council table of his own hall, the last king of the mountain had watched.

He had watched his personal guard kneel in the corridor. He had watched the council die to porters and smiths. He had watched his people choose, with one voice made of stone, and no part of any of it had been addressed to him.
The hall's thunder was still rolling when Quinlan crossed to the table.

What sat among the maps scarcely held the shape of a dwarf. The flesh had sunk to the bone, the fused plate ran slick with the night's leavings, and a dark pool was widening beneath him on the council table.
Ragnar looked up at him. The hatred was still there. It had simply run out of things to stand on.
"Finish it, Villain. I've watched enough."
Quinlan considered him for a moment.

He could've tried healing Ragnar, he could've tortured him more for what he'd done. But frankly, Quinlan no longer cared. All of it was in the past. Ragnar taught him a good lesson, paid for the treachery many times over, and that was that.
Quinlan wanted to look toward the future, toward becoming the ruler of the Iskaris Continent, toward venturing out into the grand world of Thalorind.
Keeping this grudge no longer interested the Primordial Villain.
"Greet her for me."
He turned and walked back toward his family.
He closed his hand without looking back, and the ritual's black threads came apart around a heart they had cinched shut all night.
His wind gathered the royal torso up and bore it out through the hall's shaft-side arches, out into the open dark at the center of the mountain, the only sky the deep city had ever owned.
"Finally..."
The orange glow of the ritual woke in the ruined chest, and this time no black threads came crawling to strangle it.

Ragnar did not scream. The glow spread through what remained of him, brighter and brighter, veins of fire mapping a body the ritual had spent a war devouring, and for one stretched heartbeat the last king of the dwarves hung burning in the middle of his mountain's sky.
"Goddess... I'm coming..."
Then he became light.
The cascade filled the great shaft from wall to wall.

A sun bloomed at the heart of the mountain, and its glare poured through every tier, every gallery, every doorway of the vertical city at once, throwing the shadows of a hundred thousand watching dwarves against their own walls.
The boom that followed went through the mountain's bones, the last sound of the old era, and faded.
Miles below, the light reached even the royal smithy, and the smiths looked up from their anvils into it, and did not sing.

At the shaft-side arches, Captain Torvek watched his king become light, helm under one arm, fist against his chest in a soldier's last salute to his ruler. Down the rail from him, his kneeling guardsmen did the same, one after another.
Brokk pulled her helmet off, let it hang at her side, and did not look away until the glare died.
And just like that, the age of dwarven kings was over.

The hymn came back slowly, from far below first, climbing tier by tier, and this time there was celebration in it. The forges burned brighter, and somewhere down the corridor, dwarves were already singing.
"Three down," Serika said, rolling her shoulder, thoroughly satisfied with the night.
"One more to go~" Kitsara chirped, five tails swaying.
The tails stopped mid-sway.
"Wait." The Slutty Foxy's ears went flat. "We have to conquer my people!!"
"Yeah," Quinlan hummed. "I have something quite special in mind."
"Quinnie!! Not my dad!!" Kitsara yelped.
