chapters.title: Chapter 1910 The Villain's Vision
paragraphs: The thunder of a hundred thousand dwarves took a long time to die, and Quinlan Elysiar stood in the middle of it with a foxgirl attached to his arm.
"Quinnie, promise me!! My dad-"
"I can't possibly lie to my beloved woman."
"!!" Kitsara's eyes widened, her cheeks going a soft pink. "N-no, I won't be bought with a few words spoken with such charming macho confidence..."
"Foxy, use your brain for a moment. He doesn't need to kill your father," Serika placed an arm around the worried foxkin's neck, laughing.
"I-I know!! But father... He isn't the type to kneel..."
"I'm sure he can be reasoned with," Vex smiled, tender. Then her red eyes flared and she licked her blade, long and sadistic. "And if not..."
"Noo! Bad Vexie!!"
"If you get aids like this, Sera will die of laughter," Lucille snickered.
"!! My class prevents it!" Vex stomped. Getting a sexual disease from a random dwarf corpse sounded plain wrong to the yandere witch's brain, as if she was unfaithful.
Past their little knot of chaos, the council hall of the dwarven capital was still learning how to be something other than a battlefield.

The hymn had risen again through the open doors with the war gone out of it, tens of thousands of voices settling into a slower, warmer register that rolled up the great shaft like the mountain humming to itself.
Smiths embraced strangers. Tunnel-wardens sat down right there on the bloody tiles, laughing at nothing, too spent to stand and too happy to care.
And along the walls, disarmed and dazed, knelt the personal guard of the high clans.
The tunnel-wardens had herded them up out of the killing corridor and left them there, helms off, watching the celebration of the people they had been killing an hour ago.
Captain Torvek knelt at their head, bare knuckles still split from the oath he had hammered into the flagstones for the Villain.
His eyes had not left the shaft-side arches since the light died.
"He let King Ragnar go to the Goddess." Torvek said it to nobody in particular.
The guardsman beside him wiped at his beard with the back of a shaking hand. "I was at the war, Captain. I saw what the king did to earn that monster's..."
He stopped, tried again. "If anyone alive had cause to feed Ragnar to his own ritual an inch at a time..."
Torvek nodded slowly at the dark arches. "He had cause. He had cause for... for anything he wanted, and nothing in this mountain could have stopped him taking it."
The Villain had fought the whole night with their king held in front of him as a shield.
Every man kneeling on that wall had watched it, had wept through it, and had braced for the ending such a night deserved: the last king of the dwarves kept as a trophy, or worse, kept as a toy.
Torture measured in years.
That was what villains did with allies who betrayed them.
Instead, the monster had said greet the Goddess for me, and let their king depart without any added mockery.
"A merciful death," an old guardsman managed.
Torvek kept his eyes on the dark where the light had been, and the truth of the life ahead of him settled into place piece by piece.
'Did he...' the thought arrived. 'Did he do this on purpose?'
Because of how Quinlan showed mercy after victory, the loyalist dwarves could at least end the era knowing their final king had been granted the honor of death.
There would be no years of swallowed bile for any of them, no sons raised on whispered revenge, no shame in wearing his conqueror's colors.
'I don't know if it was on purpose. But if yes...' he gulped. 'You're a truly frightening creature, Villain.'
His thought process was interrupted,
"Captain." The young guardsman's whisper wobbled. "What... what happens to us now?"
"..." Torvek exhaled, long and hard. "We'll enter the new era with our heads held high. If our conqueror permits."
"Captain..."
Across the hall, wind gathered under Quinlan's boots, lifted him off the flagstones, and set him down on the council table.

He stood among the maps of a mountain that was now his, dark armor drinking the forge-light. The same wind ran out ahead of him through the hall's open doors and down the galleries, tier by tier, bending banners and forge-smoke outward as it went.
Every face it passed turned up to find out what had moved.
The hymn thinned and died as the word went down the tiers ahead of him, mouth to mouth: the Villain was going to speak.
A hundred thousand dwarves leaned in toward the hall, and the mountain gave its whole attention to the man it had just crowned with stone and fists.
Then he put wind under his voice, so that the whole city got him at once.

"Dwarves of the mountain!" The words filled the hall to the vault and landed in the lowest warren in the same breath, warm and enormous. "Before we speak of tomorrow, let me tell you what I already know about your people."
"Hah? Tomorrow? Our people?" came a ripple of shock. This was not how they expected him to open.

"In my lands sits a settlement called Miri Town, the first city I ever built. Humans founded it, but while I assisted the Elvardian Alliance's invasion of Ravenshade, I liberated and relocated many dwarves, beastkin, and elves into it."
"By now the dwarves who settled there have built half of everything in it worth looking at. Humans, elves, dwarves and beastkin all live on the same streets."
He let the impossible picture hang for a breath.

"But it is the dwarven industrial spots that are the loudest and warmest parts of the town. They're where everyone carries anything broken, because it comes back better than it was bought. Nobody planned any of that. I believe it's simply what happens when dwarves are allowed to work."
Murmurs rolled through the galleries. The mountain had never heard of Miri Town, yet all of it understood the last sentence.
"So believe me when I say I value your craft. Your engines, your stonework, your runework, and..." The Villain paused, savoring it. "...your liquor. Now that is craftsmanship."
"He just said that?!"
"What?!"
"Haha!"
Startled laughter cracked along the tiers, and somewhere below a miner bellowed that he'd drink to that.

"You crowned me just now, and I know what's sitting underneath the cheering." The warmth in his voice stayed, but the play went out of it. "You've traded a council of lords for the Villain, and nobody has told you what your future will look like."
"My dream for Iskaris is a simple one: every race doing what it was born to do best."
His gauntlet swept across the lit shaft below.
"Your dead lords treated those forges of yours as their properties to tax, and when their resources ran short, the mountain itself went cold. That ends tonight."
"In my domain, a smith's furnace will be the last light to go out. We will rebuild this mountain properly, gallery by gallery, and then begin work on the whole of Iskaris!"
"The whole of Iskaris?!"
The roar that answered him shook dust from the vault.
He raised one hand, and a coil of his wind went down into the crowd and came back up with a passenger.
Kaelira arrived on the council table with a startled "Wha-!", set down beside him as gently as a finished piece. His arm hooked around her waist before she could plan an escape.
"Q-Quin!" The scarlet reached the tips of her long ears instantly. "A hundred thousand people are watching!"
"I noticed."
Her eyes narrowed.
He faced the hall with his flustered smith reeled in against his side.

"But let me make one thing very clear. Just because you're born a dwarf doesn't mean you must be a craftsman. Forcing the races into a few jobs would be a pure disservice to what you all are. Just take a look at this wonderful woman," he grinned, pulling her closer.
"The elves punished my Kaelira for the crime of crafting. Their law decided what an elf was allowed to be, and it nearly killed the finest crafting partner I've ever had."
"Punished?! For crafting?!"
"Stone above, they outlawed making things?!"
The growl that went up the tiers had nothing to do with the Villain at all.

"Our new nation is in the business of tearing down cages, not of building new ones. A dwarf can be more than a smith, a brewer, or an architect, just as an elf can be more than a forest-dwelling ranger."
"I desire to give all my people the opportunity to become the version of themselves they were meant to be."
The crime she had been exiled for had just become the founding principle of a nation, announced to a hundred thousand people by the man holding her.
Kaelira, scarlet to the shoulders, stared at the map table with tremendous focus and made not one attempt to leave the arm around her waist.
The cheering was still building when a blonde streak came up the processional stair, through the great doors, and landed on the council table in a three-point crouch, tail high.
"Master!!" Blossom's ears stood at full alert. "Blossom found the treasury!!"
The noise died mid-throat.

"It's this deep-" her arms stretched their widest, which was not a unit of measurement anyone could use, "-and it's full!! Gold to the ceiling!! And liquor, whole rooms of just liquor!!" Her nose scrunched into a full accordion. "Blossom sniffed one barrel to check for poison and her nose is still recovering. Too strong!!"
For one heartbeat, the hall did the sum in silence.
"The treasury," a smith near the table said slowly. "The lords swore to us the vaults were empty."
"Empty!" A tunnel-warden's voice cracked off the colonnade. "They cut our coal over empty vaults!"
"We froze all winter while they sat on a lake of gold?!"

Murmurs rolled through the galleries.
The mountain had never heard of Miri Town, yet all of it understood the last sentence.
"So believe me when I say I value your craft.
Your engines, your stonework, your runework, and..." The Villain paused, savoring it.
"...your liquor.
Now that is craftsmanship."
"He just said that?!"
"What?!"
"Haha!"
Startled laughter cracked along the tiers, and somewhere below a miner bellowed that he'd drink to that.
"You crowned me just now, and I know what's sitting underneath the cheering." The warmth in his voice stayed, but the play went out of it.
"You've traded a council of lords for the Villain, and nobody has told you what your future will look like."
"My dream for Iskaris is a simple one: every race doing what it was born to do best."
His gauntlet swept across the lit shaft below.
"Your dead lords treated those forges of yours as their properties to tax, and when their resources ran short, the mountain itself went cold.
That ends tonight."
"In my domain, a smith's furnace will be the last light to go out.
We will rebuild this mountain properly, gallery by gallery, and then begin work on the whole of Iskaris!"
"The whole of Iskaris?!"
The roar that answered him shook dust from the vault.
He raised one hand, and a coil of his wind went down into the crowd and came back up with a passenger.
Kaelira arrived on the council table with a startled "Wha-!", set down beside him as gently as a finished piece.
His arm hooked around her waist before she could plan an escape.
"Q-Quin!" The scarlet reached the tips of her long ears instantly.
"A hundred thousand people are watching!"
"I noticed."
Her eyes narrowed.
He faced the hall with his flustered smith reeled in against his side.
"But let me make one thing very clear.
Just because you're born a dwarf doesn't mean you must be a craftsman.
Forcing the races into a few jobs would be a pure disservice to what you all are.
Just take a look at this wonderful woman," he grinned, pulling her closer.
"The elves punished my Kaelira for the crime of crafting.
Their law decided what an elf was allowed to be, and it nearly killed the finest crafting partner I've ever had."
"Punished?!
For crafting?!"
"Stone above, they outlawed making things?!"
The growl that went up the tiers had nothing to do with the Villain at all.
"Our new nation is in the business of tearing down cages, not of building new ones.
A dwarf can be more than a smith, a brewer, or an architect, just as an elf can be more than a forest-dwelling ranger."
"I desire to give all my people the opportunity to become the version of themselves they were meant to be."
The crime she had been exiled for had just become the founding principle of a nation, announced to a hundred thousand people by the man holding her.
Kaelira, scarlet to the shoulders, stared at the map table with tremendous focus and made not one attempt to leave the arm around her waist.
The cheering was still building when a blonde streak came up the processional stair, through the great doors, and landed on the council table in a three-point crouch, tail high.
"Master!!" Blossom's ears stood at full alert.
"Blossom found the treasury!!"
The noise died mid-throat.
"It's this deep-" her arms stretched their widest, which was not a unit of measurement anyone could use, "-and it's full!!
Gold to the ceiling!!
And liquor, whole rooms of just liquor!!" Her nose scrunched into a full accordion.
"Blossom sniffed one barrel to check for poison and her nose is still recovering.
Too strong!!"
For one heartbeat, the hall did the sum in silence.
"The treasury," a smith near the table said slowly.
"The lords swore to us the vaults were empty."
"Empty!" A tunnel-warden's voice cracked off the colonnade.
"They cut our coal over empty vaults!"
"We froze all winter while they sat on a lake of gold?!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1911 Council of Hammers
paragraphs: The anger came up the galleries like a wave. Quinlan's laughter rolled out over it, loud and genuinely delighted, and broke it apart.
"Let the greedy ones rest now. Every one of them is dead, and every coin they hoarded is going back into the mountain they starved."
Then he let the grin fade, and the hall quieted with it.
"We have long work ahead of us, and tomorrow we begin. But tonight..." His voice reached the deepest gallery without rising at all. "...tonight, we honor our dead, and we celebrate our living."
Torvek heard it from the wall, and his split knuckles closed hard against the flagstones.

Our dead. Some of tonight's dead had fallen to the Villain's own saber, guardsmen who had held their posts to the last order. Their killer had just claimed all of them, rebel and loyalist alike, as his own loss.
Their new sovereign would cut down anyone who stood against him, then mourn the fallen as his own people in the same night, and he saw no contradiction in any of it.

"So take the rest of this night off." The energy came back into the Villain's voice. "Tend to your wounded. Mourn your fallen. And, naturally, we open the liquor stores and we drink to a better tomorrow!"
And just like that, the mountain came apart.

The hymn crashed back up the shaft, tens of thousands of voices colliding with tens of thousands more. Somewhere in the surge, the first barrel was already rolling toward the hall with religious purpose.
"He's getting frighteningly good at motivating the masses," Aurora remarked from the foot of the table. "He just finished killing their brethren and they're singing his praise."
"He promised alcohol to a race of alcoholics," Serika chuckled, watching a hundred thousand dwarves lose their minds over it.
"Shh. Let him have this." Lucille had her chin propped on her knuckles, watching her man win a mountain, deeply and hopelessly fond of him.
The hours after midnight belonged to smaller things.

The wounded came down the galleries in relays, rebel and guardsman side by side on the same stretchers. The healers refused to sort them, and after the third attempt the veterans who could still stand stopped asking them to.

Liora's station by the processional stair burned through vials and mana at a rate that made both apprentice alchemists and mages cry, and Shallan's voice had gone hoarse redirecting traffic somewhere around the thousandth patient.
Between Liora's station and Shallan's, a blonde tail moved through the stretcher rows at a steady trot.

"This one's bleeding faster than he smells like he should be!" Blossom announced, depositing a protesting tunnel-warden in front of Liora. "Blossom sniffed out four hidden bleeders and carried sixteen grumpy dwarves!"
"Thanks. Your nose is truly amazing," Liora smiled. "I could use your help more often."
The tail achieved blur. "Whenever Blossom is free!!"
Two guardsmen on the nearest stretcher line followed the little dogkin assassin as she wagged her way in among the wounded again, and quietly decided not to understand their conquerors all at once.
"Four," the old bone-setter told the tunnel-warden's wrist, still holding it. "Four bleeders my own people walked straight past."
He looked after the dog ears bobbing away between the rows.
"We've had healers under this mountain since there was a mountain, and it took a girl with dog ears to smell out those four."
"Perhaps the Villain has a point," the old bone-setter said, half to the wrist he was still holding. "Different races, different advantages... When working together..."
He didn't finish the sentence.

Quinlan felt the last knot of the night loosen in his chest at the adorable sight of his dogkin lover rushing off to help more of his newly gained people. He set off after the one meeting that couldn't wait for morning.
He found Brokk alone in the royal smithy, standing over her own anvil with the hammer Everwright laid flat across it and the helmet she had forged during the rising set aside.
The First Hammer did not turn when the most powerful being on the continent walked into her hall.
"Back down at the bottom, huh?" Quinlan grinned. "You could've stayed with your companions. They're busy getting drunk."
"These few hours might be the last quiet I get for a very long time."
Quinlan leaned a shoulder against the door-post. "You probably got that one right."
Brokk turned. "...You didn't come down here to chat."
"True," Quinlan nodded.
He strolled along her racks of tools with his hands clasped behind him, browsing everything and touching nothing.
"I'm not seating another council of lords. I want a Council of Hammers. Every hall that works raises its own master. Smiths, artificers, brewers, masons, miners, the tunnel-wardens."
He stopped at the end of the rack and turned to face her.
"They run the mountain's affairs in the mountain's interest and answer to me and mine for the rest."
Brokk's face did not move for a long moment.
"Every hall raises its own master..." Her voice had gone quiet and very exact, the forge register. "The hall picks its own master."

"I'll never once vote in it," Quinlan confirmed cheerfully. "Though I'll be having my own requests. I'm the Primordial Villain, not the God of Charity. I have expectations in exchange for the freedom and protection I provide."
"...That's only natural. We never asked for a free handout, just the opportunity to work properly."
"That you'll have. You have my word."

Brokk's thumbs came out of her belt. "So who sits at the head of it? If you put all these different craftsman masters at a table and don't have a voice that is above theirs, the arguments will never end."
Quinlan's smile had teeth in it.
"Take a wild guess."
It took a moment to land, because there had never been a hammer at that council table.
Hammers made the mountain. Lords decided what the mountain was for.
And the man who had ended those lords was now offering her the head seat with a straight face.
Her mouth opened. Nothing came out.

It closed, and tried again. The First Hammer of the royal smithy, who had stared down war-notices and lords without blinking, stood in her own hall looking like she'd bitten into a mouthful of quench-water.
Refuse, and the lords had been right about hammers all along. Accept, and she would rot in a chair three tiers above her anvil, running meetings until somebody buried her in one.
"I." The word came out like a nail being pulled. "It would be. An honor."
Quinlan burst out laughing.
It bent him sideways against her tool rack, loud and delighted, rolling around the royal smithy wall to wall while Brokk's glare climbed toward working temperature.
"That's a wonderful face you're making, First Hammer," he managed at last.
"You were joking." Her voice promised violence. "You offered me the mountain as a joke."

"The offer was real. But I knew you would hate it." He straightened, entirely unrepentant. "I'm not hauling a smith in her prime off her anvil to argue seating orders, unless she's happy to be there. Here's the shape I actually propose."
"Why didn't you start with this...?" Brokk grumbled under her breath, and was ignored.

"Every hall has its old masters. The retired ones, the ones whose backs gave out before their craft did, who carry the whole trade in their heads and have nothing left to do all day but argue about it."
"The halls raise them to the seats. Retirement suddenly becomes a promotion. You're allowed to pursue the craft you love even after your body can't."
"And beside them, a few competent administrators, [Subjugated] for efficient communication..."
"Efficient communication..." Brokk repeated with a wry tone, though the violence had left her. By now, she, too, was grinning.
"Yes, of course. I wouldn't enslave anyone just to hold more power in my hands. What am I, a tyrant?"
Brokk's eyes were drier than a desert.

"So the elders keep the council honest about what the mountain needs. The administrators keep it running. The workers stay at their forges. And when I want something from this mountain, I don't even need to lift a finger. Doesn't it sound wonderful?"
"As for the head seat, it stays empty. Deadlocks come to my administrators, and my administrators come to me."

Every hall would be governed by the hands that built it, and the seats would go to the old masters who had been discarded for growing old. Brokk had spent her whole life being told the world did not come in that shape.
She looked at him for a long moment, then exhaled.
"You're one hell of a smug bastard, if I may."
It turned into laughter.
"But I agree! That's a good shape. My people will love it."
"Good," the Villain smiled.
Dawn didn't exist under the mountain, but the shift-bells did, and when they rang, the mountain went back to work.
It went back to work strangely.

The trade halls opened to queues of dwarves holding a winter's worth of the old council's paper, and they left weeping over fistfuls of honest coin. In the galleries, masons argued over which dead lord's terrace to strip for the under-tier's rebuilding, an argument conducted at a volume that suggested profound happiness.
High above all of it, Quinlan leaned on the terrace rail with Ayame at his shoulder, the shaft glowing under them like a lit forge the size of a city.
"You've gone and built an empire and you haven't even given it a name. Honestly. All that primordial ambition and not one drop of follow-through."
"It's not finished yet," Quinlan said simply. "It doesn't get its name until it is."

His eyes drifted past the shaft's glow, past the mountain's bones, toward the lands of the Beastman Confederation, the last stretch of the continent that was not yet his. His grin sharpened at its edges.
'One left.'

chapters.title: Chapter 1912 Overlord, Not Administrator
paragraphs: The shift-bells were still ringing when Quinlan Elysiar rode his own wind back up the great shaft from the deep tiers, and set down on the high terrace beside the council hall, where his girls lounged and chatted with each other.
Below them, the vertical city glowed tier upon tier, and its people were answering the new era on their feet.

Cart teams hauled battle debris along the tier roads. Masons walked the galleries with chalk, marking what the war had cracked. A column of miners tramped down toward the deep seams, singing, still in last night's bloodstained clothes.

"They fought a war all night," Lucille mused, watching them go. "Drank through the aftermath, and lined up for the morning shift anyway." A small frown followed the miners down the tiers. "It's like their bellies convert booze to nourishing food."
"Sturdy people." Serika's grin kept widening. "I know we're a family that went the elf route but they're growing on me with every hour."
"If only they produced women that could get Quinlan Junior to stand at attention, maybe their fate would've been different," Kitsara snickered.
The foxy received quite a few dry glances, but no one corrected her.

Word of the new Council of Hammers had gone out with the shift-bells too, and the arguing had started before the hangovers ended. The broad concourse outside the council hall still held half of last night's celebration, beards crusted with ale. All of them had opinions.
"It has to be Old Thargrim!" a mason bellowed at his crew. "The man rebuilt the second tier three times!"
"Thargrim's deaf as his own bricks!"
"You'll be deaf too when he hears you said that!"

Farther along the concourse, two brewers had each other by the aprons. "Mother Bruna! She has to be the one. Her stock is legendary and she has the finest beard in the under-tier! Who else speaks for the vats?!"
"She drank half that stock herself!"
"That's called quality control, you ignorant pup!"
Vex watched the shoving matches multiply along the concourse, delight all over her face. "A brawl is about to start~"
"Why am I not surprised?" Ayame sighed.
Then Quinlan raised one hand, and a warp gate opened.

Through it came dwarves in town clothes. They wore aprons and tool belts instead of armor, carried road dust instead of weapons, and their wide eyes climbed the lit tiers of the mountain of their birth.
The dwarves of Miri Town, the ones he had liberated out of Ravenshade and given a home in his own lands, stood on home stone once more.
For one breath, the two crowds just looked at each other.
"...Brannek?" A tunnel-warden shoved out of the crowd with his axe forgotten. "BRANNEK?! YOU'RE ALIVE?!"

The concourse dissolved. Brothers found brothers. A gray smith crushed a daughter he had mourned for dead against his chest, weeping into her shoulder with his whole body. Somewhere in the crush, two old women were screaming happily at each other in a dialect nobody under eighty still spoke.
Lucille had gone still beside him, watching that smith, and she did not look away.
She had spent months walking into her own daughter's life under a borrowed name, wary of being herself.
What sat in her while she watched him was envy, plain and honest. He had gotten his reunion out loud and in front of everyone, with nothing to explain and nothing owed.
Hers had needed a borrowed name, months of pretending, and a husband stubborn enough to drag the truth out for her. She kept her face aimed at the crowd.
Quinlan then resummoned his dwarven Elite Souls, letting them meet their families as well.
He let the reunions run their course around him, watching people find their loved ones while he was surrounded by his family, each woman wearing a soft expression.
When the liberated slaves turned back his way, he spoke warmly.
"Help your friends and family find their feet in the new era. Afterward, you may decide to stay here, bring your loved ones to Miri Town, or go wherever you prefer."
"Thank you, Lord Elysiar!" a forewoman called back. Many echoed the statement.

Orianna stood by the side, took in the concourse, the reunions, and the shoving brewers in one unhurried look, and set off toward the quartermasters' stations. By afternoon, the mountain's enthusiasm would have schedules.
As the city began to move again, Quinlan was ready to do the same.
"Well, then-"
Ayame read that perfectly.
"You keep running from rulership," the petite samurai observed at his shoulder, dry as chalk.
Quinlan reached over and pinched her cheek, pulling with great love.
"Mmgh?!"
"I run from nothing. I'm an overlord, not an administrator."
He meant it.
Quinlan knew his own limits as a person: he could plant himself in that council hall and bark orders until the pillars cracked, and the mountain would not move a single day faster for it.
The dwarves knew stone, Brokk knew the halls she had spent her whole life in, Jasmine knew her ledgers. What the Primordial Villain knew was how to break the things standing in his people's way.
Nothing on this mountain needed breaking anymore.
Besides, he had somewhere better to be this morning.
"My work here is done."
The girls giggled. Ayame tried to scoff at him with her cheek stretched between his fingers, and what came out was, "Thath ith not-"

He looked around at the rest of them while his second-in-command kept yapping on and on. "We begin in a few hours. The morning is yours until then. There are beds waiting at home, if resting is what any of you want."

"And leave a hundred thousand drunk dwarves unsupervised?" Serika stretched until her shoulders popped. "We'll stay. Someone has to make sure your new mountain doesn't rebuild the wrong wall out of pure enthusiasm."
"A hundred thousand dwarves who drank the night on empty stomachs," Lucille added, already rolling up her sleeves. "I'm opening a kitchen."

Blossom's ears shot straight up. "Blossom will help Miss Liora with the wounded! Blossom can sniff out all the ones who are pretending to be fine out of pride!" She was accelerating down the processional stair before anyone could bless the mission. "Dwarves are terrible patients!!"

Serika was already a tier down by then, cracking her knuckles at a crew of masons wrestling rubble twice their size. Lucille went the other way, hunting down the mountain's kitchens with a trail of hungry dwarves falling in behind her on pure instinct.
That left Ayame. Cheek still captive, arms crossed, dignity holding at roughly sixty percent.
"When will you let go?" she demanded.
"I don't know." Quinlan considered her with deep scholarly attention. "My petite samurai is way too cute when she's pouting."
Ayame stomped.

"My, my." Vex arrived at her other side, and slender fingers claimed the free cheek. "Come, scowling miss. Let's pick up hubby's slack. I want to make sure the dwarves seat 'reasonable' people on this new council of theirs."

The Hexwitch's definition of reasonable was simple. Any dwarf who thought her hubby could be crossed would never sit on that council, and she intended to be standing in the hall in person to make sure of it.
He finally released Ayame's cheek. The two of them walked off toward the council hall's great doors, Ayame hissing and rubbing her face, Vex grinning and steering her by the elbow.
Quinlan watched his girls go, warmth sitting openly on his face.
'Truly the most amazing women in the world.'
Still smiling about it, he opened a warp gate and stepped out of the mountain entirely.
In the royal palace of Vraven, Queen Felicity Valorian stood before her study's desk with her hands on her hips, glaring at the paperwork as if it had insulted her ancestors.

"Look at it, Feng. Just look at it." She gestured at the stacks with both arms. "There's more this morning. It's like being handed homework for the rest of my life!! So terrible!! I want to be like Quinlan and ditch all the work-"

"You're just a figurehead. No one is forcing you to do anything. In fact, I'm pretty sure things would work smoother if you stopped trying," Feng Jiai grinned from the windowsill, flipping a grape and catching it in her mouth, entirely without sympathy. "Ask your father to take over all your duties. He can be your Jasmine."
"I can't!! Father finally gets to relax a little, I want to see him work less!"
"And you think his teenage daughter doing statecraft in his stead lets him relax? He's a workaholic."
Felicity puffed her cheeks at her best friend.

Then her gaze drifted to the tall doors that joined her study to her father's. Behind them the old man was already awake and already grumbling at somebody about something, loud enough to carry through solid oak, and she found herself smiling at the wood instead of glaring at her desk.

"Iskaris would feel awfully dull without that old bastard's incessant grumbling."

sentences.text: The shift-bells were still ringing when Quinlan Elysiar rode his own wind back up the great shaft from the deep tiers, and set down on the high terrace beside the council hall, where his girls lounged and chatted with each other.
Below them, the vertical city glowed tier upon tier, and its people were answering the new era on their feet.
Cart teams hauled battle debris along the tier roads.
Masons walked the galleries with chalk, marking what the war had cracked.
A column of miners tramped down toward the deep seams, singing, still in last night's bloodstained clothes.
"They fought a war all night," Lucille mused, watching them go.
"Drank through the aftermath, and lined up for the morning shift anyway." A small frown followed the miners down the tiers.
"It's like their bellies convert booze to nourishing food."
"Sturdy people." Serika's grin kept widening.
"I know we're a family that went the elf route but they're growing on me with every hour."
"If only they produced women that could get Quinlan Junior to stand at attention, maybe their fate would've been different," Kitsara snickered.
The foxy received quite a few dry glances, but no one corrected her.
Word of the new Council of Hammers had gone out with the shift-bells too, and the arguing had started before the hangovers ended.
The broad concourse outside the council hall still held half of last night's celebration, beards crusted with ale.
All of them had opinions.
"It has to be Old Thargrim!" a mason bellowed at his crew.
"The man rebuilt the second tier three times!"
"Thargrim's deaf as his own bricks!"
"You'll be deaf too when he hears you said that!"
Farther along the concourse, two brewers had each other by the aprons.
"Mother Bruna!
She has to be the one.
Her stock is legendary and she has the finest beard in the under-tier!
Who else speaks for the vats?!"
"She drank half that stock herself!"
"That's called quality control, you ignorant pup!"
Vex watched the shoving matches multiply along the concourse, delight all over her face.
"A brawl is about to start~"
"Why am I not surprised?" Ayame sighed.
Then Quinlan raised one hand, and a warp gate opened.
Through it came dwarves in town clothes.
They wore aprons and tool belts instead of armor, carried road dust instead of weapons, and their wide eyes climbed the lit tiers of the mountain of their birth.
The dwarves of Miri Town, the ones he had liberated out of Ravenshade and given a home in his own lands, stood on home stone once more.
For one breath, the two crowds just looked at each other.
"...Brannek?" A tunnel-warden shoved out of the crowd with his axe forgotten.
"BRANNEK?!
YOU'RE ALIVE?!"
The concourse dissolved.
Brothers found brothers.
A gray smith crushed a daughter he had mourned for dead against his chest, weeping into her shoulder with his whole body.
Somewhere in the crush, two old women were screaming happily at each other in a dialect nobody under eighty still spoke.
Lucille had gone still beside him, watching that smith, and she did not look away.
She had spent months walking into her own daughter's life under a borrowed name, wary of being herself.
What sat in her while she watched him was envy, plain and honest.
He had gotten his reunion out loud and in front of everyone, with nothing to explain and nothing owed.
Hers had needed a borrowed name, months of pretending, and a husband stubborn enough to drag the truth out for her.
She kept her face aimed at the crowd.
Quinlan then resummoned his dwarven Elite Souls, letting them meet their families as well.
He let the reunions run their course around him, watching people find their loved ones while he was surrounded by his family, each woman wearing a soft expression.
When the liberated slaves turned back his way, he spoke warmly.
"Help your friends and family find their feet in the new era.
Afterward, you may decide to stay here, bring your loved ones to Miri Town, or go wherever you prefer."
"Thank you, Lord Elysiar!" a forewoman called back.
Many echoed the statement.
Orianna stood by the side, took in the concourse, the reunions, and the shoving brewers in one unhurried look, and set off toward the quartermasters' stations.
By afternoon, the mountain's enthusiasm would have schedules.
As the city began to move again, Quinlan was ready to do the same.
"Well, then-"
Ayame read that perfectly.
"You keep running from rulership," the petite samurai observed at his shoulder, dry as chalk.
Quinlan reached over and pinched her cheek, pulling with great love.
"Mmgh?!"
"I run from nothing.
I'm an overlord, not an administrator."
He meant it.
Quinlan knew his own limits as a person: he could plant himself in that council hall and bark orders until the pillars cracked, and the mountain would not move a single day faster for it.
The dwarves knew stone, Brokk knew the halls she had spent her whole life in, Jasmine knew her ledgers.
What the Primordial Villain knew was how to break the things standing in his people's way.
Nothing on this mountain needed breaking anymore.
Besides, he had somewhere better to be this morning.
"My work here is done."
The girls giggled.
Ayame tried to scoff at him with her cheek stretched between his fingers, and what came out was, "Thath ith not-"
He looked around at the rest of them while his second-in-command kept yapping on and on.
"We begin in a few hours.
The morning is yours until then.
There are beds waiting at home, if resting is what any of you want."
"And leave a hundred thousand drunk dwarves unsupervised?" Serika stretched until her shoulders popped.
"We'll stay.
Someone has to make sure your new mountain doesn't rebuild the wrong wall out of pure enthusiasm."
"A hundred thousand dwarves who drank the night on empty stomachs," Lucille added, already rolling up her sleeves.
"I'm opening a kitchen."
Blossom's ears shot straight up.
"Blossom will help Miss Liora with the wounded!
Blossom can sniff out all the ones who are pretending to be fine out of pride!" She was accelerating down the processional stair before anyone could bless the mission.
"Dwarves are terrible patients!!"
Serika was already a tier down by then, cracking her knuckles at a crew of masons wrestling rubble twice their size.
Lucille went the other way, hunting down the mountain's kitchens with a trail of hungry dwarves falling in behind her on pure instinct.
That left Ayame.
Cheek still captive, arms crossed, dignity holding at roughly sixty percent.
"When will you let go?" she demanded.
"I don't know." Quinlan considered her with deep scholarly attention.
"My petite samurai is way too cute when she's pouting."
Ayame stomped.
"My, my." Vex arrived at her other side, and slender fingers claimed the free cheek.
"Come, scowling miss.
Let's pick up hubby's slack.
I want to make sure the dwarves seat 'reasonable' people on this new council of theirs."
The Hexwitch's definition of reasonable was simple.
Any dwarf who thought her hubby could be crossed would never sit on that council, and she intended to be standing in the hall in person to make sure of it.
He finally released Ayame's cheek.
The two of them walked off toward the council hall's great doors, Ayame hissing and rubbing her face, Vex grinning and steering her by the elbow.
Quinlan watched his girls go, warmth sitting openly on his face.
'Truly the most amazing women in the world.'
Still smiling about it, he opened a warp gate and stepped out of the mountain entirely.
In the royal palace of Vraven, Queen Felicity Valorian stood before her study's desk with her hands on her hips, glaring at the paperwork as if it had insulted her ancestors.
"Look at it, Feng.
Just look at it." She gestured at the stacks with both arms.
"There's more this morning.
It's like being handed homework for the rest of my life!!
So terrible!!
I want to be like Quinlan and ditch all the work-"
"You're just a figurehead.
No one is forcing you to do anything.

"Ask your father to take over all your duties.
He can be your Jasmine."
"I can't!!
Father finally gets to relax a little, I want to see him work less!"
"And you think his teenage daughter doing statecraft in his stead lets him relax?
He's a workaholic."
Felicity puffed her cheeks at her best friend.
Then her gaze drifted to the tall doors that joined her study to her father's.

Behind them the old man was already awake and already grumbling at somebody about something, loud enough to carry through solid oak, and she found herself smiling at the wood instead of glaring at her desk.

chapters.title: Chapter 1913 Happiness
paragraphs: The study went quiet.
"???" Feng's grape missed her mouth entirely and bounced off the windowsill.
"The dwarves." Felicity gasped. "Overnight?! You walked in there and walked back out with a kingdom?!"
"They were weakened from recent events."
Feng stared at the wall. "You're still incomprehensible."
"So cool!!" the Queen of Vraven beamed, in the voice of a girl whose own morning had been about paperwork.
Then she pouted. "Wait, why didn't you bring me with you? I get that Feng is quite useless, but what about me?"
"Hey. What did you just say?"
As the two friends were about to enter a hissing contest, Quinlan stepped back, pulled a sphere of clean water out of the air, and walked through it.
He twisted the air into a wind that stripped the wet off him before it touched the carpet, and [Synchra] rippled from battle-plate into casual black.
"This, too, is a sight I'll never get used to..." Feng muttered, watching the used water fold itself out of existence.
Felicity applauded the performance.
"Where are Sera and Iris?" he asked.
The bounce went out of the young queen. "Still in the infirmary wing... Sera hasn't come out all night."
Quinlan nodded. On his way out he ruffled Felicity's hair, then Feng's.
"Hey... I'm not a little kid..." grumbled Feng, and leaned into it anyway.

The royal infirmary occupied the stillest wing of the palace. Tall windows ran its whole length, pouring morning light across white linen and polished floor, and the air held the clean bite of healer's herbs over the sugared smell of fresh salve.

Beds stood made and waiting down both sides, curtains tied back, basins filled for patients who had not arrived. Out past the far arch, a fountain in the recovery garden kept up a small, steady sound.
Only one bed at the end of the ward was occupied. Quinlan crossed all that hush to reach it.

Seraphiel stood where she had sat all night. Barefoot on the cold marble, golden hair dulled by exhaustion. Healing light gathered at her fingertips, sank into the girl under the blanket, and did nothing whatsoever. She was already gathering more.
Iris Ravenclaw lay small against the pillows, black hair spread, splinted arm resting over the covers, her eyes shut. Asleep, the Demon of Vengeance simply looked like a young woman.
Quinlan laid a hand on Sera's shoulder.
She jumped hard enough to rock back on her heels. "?!" Her head whipped around, and the relief on her face crumpled straight into frustration.

"I can't heal her." Her voice was frayed at both ends. "Her class takes everything I pour in and burns it as fuel instead of mending her. She had that spell, [Severance of Mercy], that similarly debilitated her. I think that just got upgraded alongside her class."

[Severance of Mercy] was a spell that transmuted a Child of Reckoning's pain into raw power instead of mending wounds. Healing Iris too early meant burning through the stockpile she'd been building with every hit.

Quinlan let out a breath and shook his head at the unfairness of the whole thing, then sat down on the edge of the bed. His fingers slid into the black strands spread across the pillow, slow and careful.

"You poor thing... When will you be able to catch a break?" His voice stayed low. "You went from Child of Agony to Child of Reckoning to the Demon of Vengeance. Your revenge is finally finished, and you already decided you won't rest until every innocent child is safe. It's as if you cursed yourself for the rest of your life."
Sera sighed, tender and bone-tired, and shifted around to sit close against him on the bed's edge. His free hand settled on her thigh. Her fingers joined his.
"She'll never fully heal from her childhood. I know that. I've accepted that." Her thumb traced a slow line at Iris's temple. "But at least... must she keep suffering in the present too?"

Light flared at her fingertips again, harder this time. She poured until her hands shook and the glow guttered out between them, and under the blanket the splinted arm stayed exactly as broken as before.
"Why can't I heal her?!"
Her voice broke apart on the last word, and the tears she had refused herself for hours finally spilled over.

Seraphiel had carried dying allies through an entire war and lost almost none of them. Now a broken arm and exhausted body had refused her all night, attempt after attempt. The helplessness sat in the healer's chest and would not move.
Quinlan took her shaking hands out of the air before they could gather any more light and folded them into his own, and he kept them there until they stopped trying.
"I'm afraid it has to be this way. She built herself around suffering. It has become more than a constant in her life. She now lives and breathes it, deriving immense power from it."
Sera lifted her head.
"The power her class carries would tear her mortal body apart. The pain that won't close is likely the balance holding everything together. Wash the cost away, and the class might take her instead."
Sera bit her lip.
"Maybe it eases as she levels," he added, hand returning to stroking Iris's hair.
"Stop petting me."
The growl arrived fully formed from the pillows. Red eyes opened.
"And stop pitying me. I'm fine."

"?!" Sera's spine snapped straight. "You! You kept your eyes closed the entire night, and the second Quin shows up, you're awake?! What are you, some sleeper agent who only activates when her dashing prince walks into the room?!"
Iris regarded the elf with flat, lethal calm. "I woke up because you two can't shut up."
Sera puffed her chest out in triumph. "That's not true. I was talking to you the whole night! Caught you!"
"..." Iris decided to ignore the elf.
"Don't ignore me!"
Then Iris looked at Quinlan, and the irritation went out of her face.
"My revenge is complete..." she said.
Quinlan nodded, smiling.
"Your mother and the little hero can rest easy now. The Ravenclaw name stands restored, and their beloved Iris didn't kill herself avenging them." He tilted his head at her. "They must be glad."
Iris didn't answer. The ward's hush stretched out between the three of them, and the morning light kept moving across the blanket.
"Quinlan." She was looking at the window now, not at him. "Your lover... I..."
His finger landed on her lips.
"Iris Ravenclaw." He was not amused. "You can't be serious. I help you achieve your revenge, and you think you're obligated to part your legs for me?"
She looked away, and her voice went thin.
"That's the only thing I can give you... You deserve so much more, but I can't... I have nothing else to give..."
The girl who had walked through an entire life of hell without once bending looked, right then, more fragile than any injury had ever made her.
So Quinlan pinched her cheek.
He took hold and pulled, and his expression was visibly, thoroughly irritated.
"I swear. You two are on exactly the same wavelength. You've both forced me into pinching your cheeks in a single morning."
"Wha-!" Iris's bewilderment fought the stretch of her own face. "Don't compare me to that flat board of a-"
Sera giggled, leaned in, and got two fingers on the cheek Quinlan hadn't taken. "How did you know who Quin was talking about?"

Iris refused to answer. Held by a cheek on either side, she aimed her glare at a fixed point on the far wall and pretended with her entire being that neither of them existed. She managed it with the outraged dignity of a cornered squirrel.

"Now listen well, you hopeless woman," Quinlan sighed, cheek firmly in custody. "I cherish you every bit as much as I cherish my lovers. In some ways, what you and I share runs even deeper. I want nothing more than to watch you smile one day with none of your past's weight left on you. A full, brilliant smile, radiant like the morning sun. That's what I want from you."
He nodded along with his own solemn words.

"I don't know what the future holds for us. I don't know what you need to get there. My heart is bottomless, there's always a room for you. And Quinlan Junior is a mighty warrior who has never once backed down from a challenge. He'd manage just fine."
Sera bit down on a laugh and lost.
Iris snarled at him, and the two sets of fingers on her face pulled every tooth out of it. "Stop your creepy bragging and get to the point...!!"
So he let go and leaned in, and the teasing left his voice entirely.
"Long story short. Whether as your good friend, whether as your fervent lover, whether as a distant observer... I don't care."
Then he leaned down and kissed her forehead.
"All I want is to see you happy."
Iris went rigid.

Her whole life, enemies had been for cutting and problems had been for punching, and grief had been beaten into a training wall until it behaved. Nothing in that arsenal applied to such sweet words and a forehead kiss, and the system failure crawled across her face in real time.
Her mouth opened, closed, and opened again with nothing loaded in it. Red climbed from her neck to the tips of her ears.
"Nn." Whatever that was, it was not a word.
Then her good hand shot up, fisted in his collar, and hauled him the rest of the way down.
Iris devoured his lips, hungry and graceless, all commitment and no technique, her eyes screwed shut like she was bracing for a blow.
She broke it just as suddenly, shoving him back to arm's length, upright in the bed now, scarlet to the hairline and breathing hard.
"Nothing happened," she informed the room.
"It very much did!!" Sera screeched. "You can't just erase-"
Then the bed creaked, and Iris was off it like a released spring.

Her good arm scooped Seraphiel clean off the mattress and folded the elf over her shoulder like a sack of potatoes. Sera went up with a squeak, her hair swinging down Iris's back, and Iris was already marching for the doors.
"Wha- Iris?! I spent the entire night healing you and now I'm being kidnapped?!"
The complaint bounced off without effect.
"I think I can be healed now. Get to work."
"Hah? Drop the attitude, young lady, or I'll teach you respect!"
"Go ahead."
"I'm getting mixed signals over here," Quinlan called after them. "Wait. Is this you asking to be friends with benefits? No strings attached?"
He shook his head. "I'm not the kind of guy who'd go for that, but for my beloved Iris..."
Without breaking stride, Iris raised her splinted arm just enough to show him one finger.
The middle one, to be specific.
He snickered. "And where are you two going?"
"Portal!" Iris demanded, without turning around. "Kill. Destroy. Level up."
The Primordial Villain's grin went wide, and his hand was already rising.
"Sounds like a plan."
It was time to move on.

Iris devoured his lips, hungry and graceless, all commitment and no technique, her eyes screwed shut like she was bracing for a blow.
She broke it just as suddenly, shoving him back to arm's length, upright in the bed now, scarlet to the hairline and breathing hard.
"Nothing happened," she informed the room.
"It very much did!!" Sera screeched.
"You can't just erase-"
Then the bed creaked, and Iris was off it like a released spring.
Her good arm scooped Seraphiel clean off the mattress and folded the elf over her shoulder like a sack of potatoes.
Sera went up with a squeak, her hair swinging down Iris's back, and Iris was already marching for the doors.
"Wha- Iris?!
I spent the entire night healing you and now I'm being kidnapped?!"
The complaint bounced off without effect.
"I think I can be healed now.
Get to work."
"Hah?
Drop the attitude, young lady, or I'll teach you respect!"
"Go ahead."
"I'm getting mixed signals over here," Quinlan called after them.
"Wait.
Is this you asking to be friends with benefits?
No strings attached?"
He shook his head.
"I'm not the kind of guy who'd go for that, but for my beloved Iris..."
Without breaking stride, Iris raised her splinted arm just enough to show him one finger.
The middle one, to be specific.
He snickered.
"And where are you two going?"
"Portal!" Iris demanded, without turning around.
"Kill.
Destroy.
Level up."
The Primordial Villain's grin went wide, and his hand was already rising.
"Sounds like a plan."
It was time to move on.

chapters.title: Chapter 1914 Aldoria's Labyrinth
paragraphs: "By royal proclamation!"

The crier had held the center of Aldoria's market square since dawn, and his voice was audibly paying for it. "King Alexios has passed the crown to his chosen heir! Long live Her Majesty, Queen Felicity Primrose Amabelle Valorian, sovereign of Vraven!"
"And by the Queen's own free word! Vraven kneels to the Primordial Villain! The kingdom, the crown, and every soul within now stand under his protection!"
Criers like him had been shouting the same words in every city of the kingdom since dawn.
Aldoria had already argued the news to death, and moved on to the practical questions, like how they'd put food on the table today. So the market simply flowed around the man and let him work.

The labyrinth gate of Aldoria opened at dawn, and the queue of adventurers formed by sunrise. Guardsman Hadric stood his post beside it the way he had stood it every day since the bounty sheets: sweating under his armor, flinching at every flash of light in the market square.
His three fellow gate knights found this endlessly entertaining.
"Oy, Hadric." The nearest one dug two bronze coins out of his pouch and held them up beside Hadric's helmet.
*Clink. Clink.*
"Stop that."
*Clink.*
"I'm warning you-"
"The Primordial Villain is coming for youuu~" the knight sang. "Conqueror of the elves. Liege lord of all Vraven. Surely his next great campaign is the gate knight who jingled forty bronze at him."
Down the wall, the other two were already wheezing.
Every knight on this rotation knew the story, because Hadric had told it white-faced to anyone who would listen.
Less than a year ago, a nobody with a shabby spear and a single silver to his name had paid the fee at this gate; Hadric had clinked the coins in his palm and smirked at the farmer behind his visor.
Then the bounty sheets started circulating. The rumors started circulating.
And Hadric became sure that the filthy peasant he mocked was the Villain himself, at the very start of his rise.
Nobody believed him. Or rather, the part where he'd come back for revenge.

"He rules half the continent, man," the second knight managed between wheezes. "He has elven queens and shrine maidens pouring his wine. I wouldn't be surprised if he added both Elf Queen Myrasyn and Princess- I mean Queen Felicity to his harem."
"Yeah, dude!" another laughed. "He is not coming back to take revenge."
The air over the market square split open.

A warp gate spun wide between the vendor stalls, taller than a man, and the morning crowd of Aldoria went quiet in a spreading ring around it, because there was exactly one man on the continent who tore doors into the air like that.
Iris Ravenclaw stepped out of his gate with an elf over her shoulder.
She stopped two paces from the gate and stared at the scene in front of her: a queue, a stone doorway, a sign listing an entrance fee.

The line ran long: farmhands with pitchforks and patched boots come to trade field work for a better life, a pair of teenage girls sharing one rusted sword between them, a boy nervously re-counting his coppers.
All of that hope for a better tomorrow was currently busy gawking at the hole in the world and the two women who had stepped out of it.
"Why are we at a labyrinth?" Iris said flatly, to nobody.
"Second question," Seraphiel offered from her shoulder, golden hair hanging toward the cobbles. "Why am I still being carried? Put me down already."
"You can focus on healing fully like this."
"I'm starting to understand why Ayame keeps butting heads with you, young miss!"
"Fine!" The elf abandoned dignity, and her hands found the splinted arm hanging free at Iris's side. Golden light sank into it. "Then you hold still, because I have questions for this arm."
The light took. Iris's red eyes were on the crowd, the crowd's eyes were on her, and her face committed to nothing at all.
"Unbelievable," Sera declared at rising volume. "All night this arm spat my healing out like poison. All night! And now it drinks every drop like fruit juice! Look at it knitting!"
The splint's straps loosened on their own, the whole thing clattered to the cobbles, and the arm underneath flexed whole.
"So..." The Dawnbringer's voice went from wounded to sharp. "Your class holds your wounds hostage, doesn't it? Pain is your fuel, so no healing mid-battle, and none right after either."
"First you overcome the worst yourself, sleep it out, and only then does my light get permission. That's the rule, isn't it-"
Iris's good hand released the elf's waist and arrived over her mouth instead.
"Mmph?!"
"You're too loud. At this rate I'm trading a broken arm for a splitting headache."
"Mmmmmmmmmmm!!!"
A certain bombshell of an elven healer wasn't quite happy at this very moment.
The elf came off Iris's shoulder and onto her own feet, mouth finally free.
Then Quinlan Elysiar walked out of his own gate in casual black, and the street stopped pretending it wasn't watching.
"It's him," someone whispered by the potion stall. "Goddess above, it's actually him."
"The Villain! The Primordial Villain is in Aldoria!"
"Why is he here?!"
Quinlan took in the gawking street, the fleeing pigeons, the hundred held breaths, and shrugged.

[Synchra] flared a brilliant red and rippled up his body, casual black flowing into dark battle-plate, crimson light bleeding through every seam. His eyes lit a terrible red, and the air over his shoulders warmed like a forge drawing breath.
The market of Aldoria received the sight of the Primordial Villain in full regalia, and lost its collective mind.
"Aaaah! He's come to conquer Aldoria!"
"We're already conquered, you idiot! Run anyway!"

A cabbage vendor fainted backward into his own produce. A carter threw himself off his bench and offered the entire cart to nobody in particular, horse included. Two veterans in the queue dropped flat on the cobbles, arms over their helmets.
"Take the cart! Take the whole cart!"
By the potion stall, a boy hid his coppers behind his back.
Quinlan watched all of it with deep, genuine enjoyment, then finally addressed the hysterical crowd.
"There's a line," he announced reasonably. "I'm merely waiting my turn."
Nobody heard a word of it. The screaming continued, a door slammed somewhere, then another, then an entire street of doors.
"...Okay." He sighed and started forward.
The queue came apart at his first step, labyrinth explorers and farmhands scattering out of his path, diving behind stalls, pressing themselves flat against the shopfronts.
When the dust settled, exactly one obstacle remained between the Primordial Villain and the labyrinth gate.
Two girls. One rusted sword, held between them in four shaking hands, its tip wobbling through an area the size of a barrel.
He stopped in front of them and said nothing at all.

"W-w-we..." The taller one had planted herself half a step in front of the smaller one, which would have been more impressive if her knees weren't knocking together audibly. "We hope to one day... to be like the Scarlet Lilies! Sir! My lord! Your Villainy!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1915 Stubborn Youngsters
paragraphs: "This is a public labyrinth!" the smaller one squeaked from behind her. "Everyone may enter! It's the law!"
"We've waited since dawn! If we don't make money today, we don't eat! So we can't let you cut in- no! We can't afford to skip- no, um-"
"What she means is we're very sorry and please don't kill us but we were here first!"
The excuses arrived as a bombardment, delivered with chins up and faces gray, two girls attempting mighty and landing somewhere near seasick.
Quinlan listened to every word of it, amusement plain on his face.
"The Scarlet Lilies, huh." The terrible red eyes considered them. "An admirable goal."
He nodded at the rusted sword.
"But with that equipment, chances are you'll die long before you get there."
The girls bit their lips in unison, and the chins came down.
"W-we know!" the taller one managed. "But getting to eat stale bread is already a good day for us. Equipment is..." She didn't finish it.
"Where are your parents?"
"Don't have any..." the smaller one said, too fast and too flat for it to be anything but old ground. "We ran from the orphanage."
The taller girl's hand found the smaller one's sleeve.
Iris stood by the warp gate with her arms crossed, red eyes fixed on the two of them: runaways, one planted in front of the other, guarding what little they had with a rusted blade.
Iris knew that arrangement on sight, and it put her straight back inside a cage she had grown up in. Her face gave the market nothing.
The hand tucked under her elbow curled closed, and stayed closed.
Iris knew that arrangement on sight, and it put her straight back inside a cage she had grown up in. Her face gave the market nothing.
The hand tucked under her elbow curled closed, and stayed closed.
"I see," said the Primordial Villain. "Then let me sponsor you."
The rusted sword's tip stopped wobbling out of sheer shock.
"S-s-sponsor?!"
"Why not?" He shrugged, dark plate whispering. "I'm curious what becomes of you two. I might as well."

His pocket ring flashed. Two spears slid out of the light and planted themselves upright in front of the girls, honest steel with a faint reinforcing glow along the hafts. After them came boots, padded jackets, waterskins, and a fat paper sack that smelled aggressively of fresh bread.
"A spear is how I started in this very labyrinth, as it happens. Swords look better on a poster, but a spear keeps you alive while you learn. Or so my teacher have told me."
The girls stared at the pile of gear with their mouths open, entirely unequipped for any of it.
By the warp gate, Seraphiel had laced her fingers together, watching her lover with a soft, glowing smile she didn't bother to hide.
"One more thing. [Awaken]."
Soulfire poured up out of the cobbles beside him and took shape: a tall knight of a woman in royal guard plate, spectral, blue-white fire rolling off her pauldrons.
The market found a brand-new register to scream in.
"Necromancy!"
"He's raising the dead in the street!"
"Cassandra." Quinlan tossed her a heavy coin pouch, and she caught it without looking. "Drill the basics into them, and make sure they eat something other than stale bread."
The dead squad captain of the royal guard pressed a fist to her breastplate and bowed to her summoner.
"Yes, Master."
The girls' heads went back and forth between the ghost and the Villain fast enough to endanger their necks.
Then the red eyes came back down to them, warm with amusement.
"Now then. May I pass?"
The girls looked at him. Then at the gate behind them. Then at themselves, standing in the exact middle of his path.
"Hie!"
They cleared it with a squeak and a burst of speed no stat sheet of theirs could explain, ending up three stalls away in a tangle of limbs and new equipment.
Both of them folded toward the Villain in bows so deep their foreheads nearly reached their knees.
"Thank you, Mister Villain!!"
"Thank you for the spears and the bread and-" The smaller one's inventory dissolved into tears halfway through, and the bow only went deeper.
Cassandra regarded the two of them, and a smile crossed the dead captain's face.
"If you want to thank him, grow strong."
The girls came up from their bows with wet eyes, gripping their new spears with both hands.
At the gate, three knights had been holding their salute to their sovereign since the moment the armor flared, arms trembling with the effort, and now he was finally walking their way.
The fourth had made a sound like a stepped-on dog when the red light first bled through those seams, and his spear had slid out of his numb grip.
*Clatter!*

That was all the movement Hadric's body had agreed to since. Every nightmare he'd sweated through since the bounty sheets had just spent ten minutes in the square sponsoring orphans, and was now strolling toward his gate.
'Run,' he told his legs. 'Run. Run!!'
His legs held their post, but loyalty to the crown wasn't on his mind at all.
"Morning, gentlemen." Quinlan arrived in front of four statues wearing armor. The one still holding the mocking coins was visibly considering eating them. "What's the entrance fee these days?"
"T-twenty," that knight managed. "Twenty bronze, my lord. Per... per head."
"Still twenty, huh? Fine, I'll pay for my whole party."

He didn't reach for his pouch. [Soul Reaper], still rippling with the remnants of Cassandra's summon, stopped hovering at his back and hung flat in the air at his waist, lying on its side like a serving tray.
Quinlan's coins rose from the pouch on threads of wind.
"Twenty for me."
*Clink.*
The first coin landed on the flat of the blade, and inside his helmet, Hadric stopped breathing. He knew that sound. He had made that sound once, slowly, into this same man's face.
Blue soulfire kindled along the saber's length to light the count.

"Twenty for the lovely lady glaring at me." *Clink.* "Twenty for the otherworldly elf beside her. Twenty for my adorable second-in-command. Twenty for the charismatic wife with the axe. Twenty for the tanned fire wife. Twenty for the loud fox. Twenty for the cutest pup. Twenty for the needy witch. Twenty for my tomboy smith, and twenty for my amazing alchemist."
Eleven stacks of twenty built themselves coin by coin with no hand anywhere near them, each clink unhurried, placed into the silence like a nail.

By the fourth stack, three of the knights were sweating freely inside their helmets. By the eighth, a thin, continuous whine had started somewhere inside the fourth's, like a kettle boiling three streets away.
The coin-holder's visor tilted toward Iris and Seraphiel, then back to the eleven stacks. "M-my lord... there are... three of you?"

"You know," Quinlan ignored the question and instead said conversationally, to nobody in particular, "I promised myself I'd remember the knight who clinked my coins at me that day. Smirked at me through his helmet and jingled my last bronze like a bell, as if the toll wasn't insult enough."
He gestured at the four of them. "But you all wear the same armor. I never could tell which one of you it was."
A thread of wind plucked the top coin off the nearest stack, raised it high, and let it drop.
*Clink.*
The fourth knight's whole body spasmed hard enough to rattle his pauldrons, and the faraway kettle arrived at a rolling boil.
"There he is," the Villain smiled.

chapters.title: Chapter 1916 The Masterplan
paragraphs: "There he is," the Villain smiled.

"AH- my lord- Your Majesty- sire-!" Hadric hit his knees in front of his sovereign, gauntlets coming up, words arriving in whatever order they escaped. "The coins- I wasn't- there's a counting protocol! Standard procedure! I count everyone's- I have a mother!"
Quinlan's crimson eyes flared bright. The Soul Reaper's flames intensified. Synchra's red veins raced.
Hadric made a noise no knight academy had ever trained a man for.
Then his nerve snapped outright.
"Mercyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy!!"
Hadric departed at a full sprint through the vendor row, screaming all the way.
"Hmm..." Quinlan mused, stroking his chin. Then, as if nothing had happened, he moved on.
"..." Iris looked at Seraphiel. Seraphiel looked at Iris.
One of the remaining knights began taking Quinlan's fee, coin by careful coin.
"That," Quinlan told him pleasantly, "was the last entrance fee this gate will ever collect."
He turned to the street.
"People of Aldoria! The Goddess raised the labyrinths for everyone, and for too long you've paid nobles for the privilege of risking your own lives inside them."
He swept a hand at the little stone doorway.
"From this day, in every land under my rule, every labyrinth gate stands open. Go get strong and make me proud."

As far as Quinlan was concerned, these labyrinths were the perfect training tools to get one started on their leveling journey. If he allowed people to train for free, he would have more superhumans down the line to bulk his nation up with quality citizenship.
If he wanted to make money, which he did, there were many better avenues to tax.
For one heartbeat the street held its breath.
"...Free?" The boy by the stall looked up from his coppers. "It's free?!"

He counted them again, the eleventh time since dawn, and for the first time all morning the number did not matter. Twenty bronze had been the entire distance between him and the rest of his life, and the Villain had erased it in one sentence.
"The Villain opened the labyrinths!"

The street came apart. Explorers and adventurers roared, the scattered queue poured back out of hiding as a mob of celebration, and a potion vendor bellowed, "Free samples!" going along with the sovereign's vibes.
Quinlan raised one hand, and a second warp gate opened beside him.
<We're beginning, ladies,> he sent over the family link. <Come on through.>
The family stepped out of the gate into the middle of a street festival that had not existed a minute ago.

Ayame came first, then Serika, Lucille, Vex, Kitsara, Blossom, Kaelira, and Aurora. Eight women took in the roaring adventurers, the weeping boy clutching his coppers, the three knights cradling two hundred twenty bronze, and their smug husband, in that order.
"It's the whole harem!"
"Don't stare at them! Don't stare at any of them, he'll take your eyes!"
A farmhand near the front of the queue dropped to one knee and started thanking a goddess. He was not particular about which one.
"Yay!!" Blossom's ears shot straight up, and she began cheering along with the crowd on pure enthusiasm. "Blossom doesn't know what we're celebrating, but it must be about Master!!"
The rest of the girls looked from the festivities to their man with extremely wry eyes.
"I left a half-built dwarven council for this," Ayame said, arriving at his shoulder. Her gaze swept the entrance sign, the queue, the little stone doorway. "Quin. What is this?"
"Our next campaign."
"A labyrinth." Flat as a blade. "I told you on your second day in this world that labyrinths pay worse than the wild."

"You did. Then we killed or befriended everything the wild had worth hunting." Quinlan gestured at the tiny doorway with real affection. "The deep floors are the only renewable hunting grounds left on this continent."
Ayame's eyes narrowed, because that was not the question that mattered, and both of them knew it.
"And the beastkin? You seriously intend to level up instead of running them down?"
"We could obliterate them. A week, two at most, and the Confederation kneels." He said it without a trace of doubt, and nobody present doubted it either. "But Vex once made a very good point."
Vex stopped mid-step.
"..." Her red eyes came around slowly. "That's right. I always make good points."
Then her head tilted. "Which one?"

"The Heavenly Restriction has stood over this continent for hundreds of thousands of years," Quinlan repeated her logic, while his witch glowed. "Whoever drew it never once came back to collect. The odds of that changing this week, or this month, are next to none. Which means..."
He spread his hands and let his family finish it.
"...there's no clock," Serika said slowly. The grin crept up her face as she said it.
"Chances are that past the Veil, we're small fish," Aurora added, arms crossed, mind already three steps down the road. "At least, that's the attitude we should operate with."
"The races need the time just as much as we do," Lucille chimed in warmly.

"I opened a kitchen under the dwarven mountain this morning," she continued. "The dwarves are darlings, and not one of them can ask a human to pass the salt without rehearsing it first, much less an elf. A few months of the races working side by side and it becomes natural. Force it, and it tears."

"So Iskaris settles into its new shape at its own pace, with nobody getting the new world shoved down their throat." Ayame took the thesis home, and her voice had gone thoughtful despite herself. "And we spend that time climbing, so that whatever waits beyond the Veil finds us as ready as this continent can make us."
She looked up at him, eyes narrowed with deep suspicion.
"You planned this. You, the man who fled a council hall this very morning."
"I run from nothing. I delegate."

The girls traded looks around the circle, and the same verdict settled over all of them at once. Their man could not sit through a single council meeting. He had never balanced a ledger in his life and clearly never would.
And every woman present was beaming at him anyway, because the job he actually held was leading his family to the best future in reach, and at that job, no being in this world could touch him.
"Enough talking." Iris rolled her freshly healed shoulder, red eyes already fixed on the doorway. "Let's go."
"You're right. Let us begin, sidekick," Ayame agreed sweetly.
Iris's eye twitched.
"Labyrinth time with Master!!" Blossom was vibrating in place.
Then Kitsara raised a finger, five tails swaying slower and slower.
"Sooo... question." The foxy's voice climbed carefully toward hope. "What about the beastkin. We just... leave them alone?"
"Leave them alone?" Quinlan repeated.
The Primordial Villain chuckled, low and rolling, and the sound alone made half the girls lean in.
"No, my beloved fox. The beastkin are about to face a crisis unlike anything in their long history."
He said nothing more.
His girls, warm-hearted women every one, looked at their chuckling man and grinned like a den of adorable little demonesses.
Together, they followed Quinlan through the labyrinth's stone doors.
