chapters.title: Chapter 1917 Rash Decision
paragraphs: The first floor of the Aldoria labyrinth had not changed in the months since Quinlan Elysiar walked into it with a shabby spear and a borrowed stance.

The same pale stone corridors ran ahead of the family, lit by the same veins of soft blue light, and the same first-floor trio still held them: Steel Carapace Beetles the size of hunting hounds, red-eyed Shadow Wisps trailing their tendrils, and thorn-plated Bramblebacks the shape of angry boars.
What had changed was the party.
A beetle charged the group from a side passage, mandibles wide, and Ayame cut it in half without looking at it, mid-sentence, her katana back in its sheath before the two halves finished falling.

"As I was saying." The petite samurai walked at Quinlan's right, arms folded, chin up. "I understand the sentiment, Quin. Truly. We were robbed at that gate once, and my petty primordial never forgets a perceived injustice done to him like that."
"Forty bronze," Quinlan agreed pleasantly. "I felt as if they sucker punched me."

"And that's precisely my problem." Her gaze narrowed up at him. "You avenged a forty-bronze grudge with altering national policy. The level 1 Commoner-class you with the spear could afford that grudge. The ruler you commanding three peoples and counting is spending a nation's future on it."
[You've Slain Steel Carapace Beetle (Level 1). You've Gained 0 XP]
The notification chimed at the edge of Quinlan's vision and he dismissed it without a glance.

The first Steel Carapace Beetle he ever killed on this floor had been worth three experience points. It had also cost him a great deal of shouted coaching from the samurai now walking at his right, who had twice deflected its mandibles off him before he found the joints himself.

"So think it through with me," Ayame pressed on. "Is it truly in this nation's interest to have crowds camping in front of every labyrinth door? You saw the queue outside, and that was with the entrance fee. If we take it away, it'll run down the hill, past the barracks, and out of sight."

Another beetle scuttled out of a nook toward Seraphiel's bare feet. Iris's hand snapped out sideways, caught it by the shell, and threw it into the walls, creating an ugly painting art. She didn't even seem to realize what she'd just done, moving on with zero emotion on her face.
"Nothing," she reported flatly. "It gave me nothing."
"We're passing through, not farming," Serika snickered. "Deep floors, remember?"
Ayame ignored the exchange entirely. Her arms stayed folded, chin up, and she was not finished.

"Farmers are already abandoning their fields to chase a better tomorrow, Quin. Now they heard 'free' and will drop all their plows. And most of them will get exactly what a level three farmhand gets on floor four."

Her voice stayed level, but it had weight in it now. "They'll die or get crippled, in the thousands first and then the hundreds of thousands. We'll lose millions of farmers due to this policy change."
The corridor forked, and the family flowed around a beetle that had planted itself in the middle of the junction, rattling its shell in challenge at the eleven people currently walking through it.
Lucille patted it on the carapace. It exploded into gore and loot a moment later. Lucille was already three paces past it.
"She's not wrong," Aurora noted from the back, a step behind Kaelira. "The gate fees were a filter. An ugly one, but a filter."
"They were," Quinlan agreed.
He walked on for a few paces, hands loose at his sides, the blue wall-light sliding over his casual black.

"You bring up good points, Ayame. There's going to be chaos. Crowds will camp the gates, people will brawl over corridor rights, and plenty of hopefuls will walk in and never walk back out. I'm not blind to any of it. I just think most of it solves itself with time."
"The crowds thin out on their own once the stories of the dead start coming home."
"And the dead?" Ayame pressed on.

"The dead were given a chance. That's all I care about." He said it without flinching. "A farmer who dies on floor four got to try for his potential. Under the old fees he'd have died anyway, just slower, at age fifty, with a crooked back and rotten teeth, having never once been given the chance to realize his potential."
"And if one doesn't die? If one in a thousand climbs?" Quinlan's eyes lit up.

"Then our nation just created a future cornerstone. Someone who'll reach heights where a human lifespan stretches into centuries. The strongest of them will still be building our country a thousand years from now, long after every fat noble who ever charged a gate fee is dust."
"One in a thousand," Ayame repeated. "And the other nine hundred and ninety-nine are gone."

"Their gear stays where they fall, though," Kaelira said slowly, working through it aloud. "A spearhead doesn't rot down here. Neither does a shield, or a decent set of greaves, or plate that only needs the blood scrubbed off it."
"The labyrinth preserves all of it," Quinlan confirmed.

Aurora caught up to the shape of it, and her fingers stopped their absent counting against her thigh. "So the next hopeful walks that same corridor and picks it all up. Every farmhand who dies down here arms the one who comes after them."
Silence held for a few steps, apart from the crunch of a Brambleback that had made the mistake of charging Blossom and met her gauntlet mid-charge, thorns and all.
Ayame walked several paces without saying anything, hunting for the hole she had been certain was in there somewhere.
Forty bronze had lit the fuse, but the reasoning underneath it was cold, and it had clearly been finished long before the gates ever opened.
"He's not stupid, just infuriatingly arrogant," Iris said, to nobody in particular. "Everyone always assumes he never thinks before he acts. Shouldn't a loving wife know differently?"
"...You did not just say that," Ayame's eyes narrowed.
"But I did."

"...I'll deal with you later." Ayame's chin came down a degree while looking at Quinlan. "I know you're not stupid, and I know you do think. But I also know that you can be emotional and impulsive. I just wanted to make sure."
"Much appreciated," Quinlan grinned. "This is the job of my adorable second in command. You're doing perfectly."
"...Hmph."
Two forks and a flight of stairs later, the beetle corridor gave way to a wider gallery, and Aurora decided the first problem had been settled long enough.
The alchemist had worked her way up the group to his left side, platinum hair catching the wall-light, already three moves down the road.
"Then solve the next one," she said.

"You've just drained the farms into the labyrinths. Millions will abandon their homes, most never to return. So now we will have less food produced. But then another of your directions is that healing should be more accessible to the common folk, which means that despite the mad rush of farmers to their deaths, overall fewer people will die young, which means more mouths to feed, not fewer."

She ticked it off on her fingers. "More mouths, fewer farmers. That's not chaos that time solves, Quin. That's a famine with a schedule. We need an answer before Iskaris starts eating its seed grain."
"Once again, that's right," Quinlan agreed.
His hand found her hair as they strolled, fingers sliding slowly through platinum, and Aurora leaned into it on pure reflex while her expression insisted that this was serious statecraft.
"Which is why it's time for the new era's cornerstones to shine," he continued. "Tell me, my gorgeous alchemist. Why does everyone assume alchemy means healing potions?"
"Because it is always applicable and pays well," she said instantly.
"Because war made it always applicable and pay well." A Shadow Wisp darted at them from a nook, red eyes glinting; a thread of his wind removed it from the conversation.
"But what if there's no constant war waged all across the continent?"
"...We'll need to adapt."

"Yeah. Adapt. How about some soil fertilizers, brewed by the vat? Soil transmutation, turning exhausted dirt into prime black loam. Growth elixirs that cut a harvest cycle in half. If an alchemist can rebuild a man's ruptured organs, why not a field's?"
Aurora stopped walking.
She had gone wide-eyed, and her mouth moved before her composure caught up with it.
"There were experiments," she muttered. "Verdanal's fertility tinctures. The Loamwright trials. Early prototypes, years ago, some of them actually worked..."
Her fingers came up, counting again, faster now.

"But they never spread. Rulers wanted every alchemist to mass brew potions for their endless wars, so it was efficient to focus on the few that assisted soldiers win their battles. And the nobles who owned the land had no reason to want bigger harvests. Overproduction crashes grain prices. Cheap grain shrinks their rents. And millions of tenant farmers suddenly out of work, wandering the roads..."
She looked up at him. "They buried farming alchemy precisely because it worked."
A beetle chose that exact moment to charge her flank. Kaelira's rune-etched backhand removed it from existence without anyone, including Kaelira, acknowledging the event.
"So the knowledge exists," Quinlan said. "It's just been sitting in a drawer, waiting for a ruler who profits from feeding people instead of sending them to war."
He spread his hands as they walked.
"What if the world opens up to us? The Restriction won't stand forever. What if my portals and Iskaris's fields could move grain to nations facing famine, anywhere, in an afternoon?"
His primordial eyes flashed with the light his girls knew well, the one that redrew maps.

"Or what if we conquer a new continent, and its farmlands burn in the fighting? We could make our newest citizens' first experience of my rule a full granary instead of an empty one. Nobody rebels against the man feeding their children."
His girls were smiling now, slow and wide, one after another down the line.
"And I have other ideas too," he went on.

If an alchemist can rebuild a man's ruptured organs, why not a field's?"
Aurora stopped walking.
She had gone wide-eyed, and her mouth moved before her composure caught up with it.
"There were experiments," she muttered.
"Verdanal's fertility tinctures.
The Loamwright trials.
Early prototypes, years ago, some of them actually worked..."
Her fingers came up, counting again, faster now.
"But they never spread.
Rulers wanted every alchemist to mass brew potions for their endless wars, so it was efficient to focus on the few that assisted soldiers win their battles.
And the nobles who owned the land had no reason to want bigger harvests.
Overproduction crashes grain prices.
Cheap grain shrinks their rents.
And millions of tenant farmers suddenly out of work, wandering the roads..."
She looked up at him.
"They buried farming alchemy precisely because it worked."
A beetle chose that exact moment to charge her flank.
Kaelira's rune-etched backhand removed it from existence without anyone, including Kaelira, acknowledging the event.
"So the knowledge exists," Quinlan said.
"It's just been sitting in a drawer, waiting for a ruler who profits from feeding people instead of sending them to war."
He spread his hands as they walked.
"What if the world opens up to us?
The Restriction won't stand forever.
What if my portals and Iskaris's fields could move grain to nations facing famine, anywhere, in an afternoon?"
His primordial eyes flashed with the light his girls knew well, the one that redrew maps.
"Or what if we conquer a new continent, and its farmlands burn in the fighting?
We could make our newest citizens' first experience of my rule a full granary instead of an empty one.
Nobody rebels against the man feeding their children."
His girls were smiling now, slow and wide, one after another down the line.
"And I have other ideas too," he went on.

chapters.title: Chapter 1918 Plans for the Future
paragraphs: "I'm no expert, but I did read about a few farming methods in my textbooks, back in my old world. Crop rotation. Selective breeding. Things nobody here ever needed to invent, because magic was always the answer to everything."
"Wait!! Master!!" Blossom's head came around, and the entire discussion visibly rearranged itself inside her skull. "Blossom has an idea! What if Master involved more than just alchemists?"
It was the gorgeous dogkin's turn to get her head petted, which she enjoyed by the most joyous of squeals.

"My Pupcake is on the same wavelength, I see," Quinlan chuckled. "I'm thinking we leverage the dwarves for the tools, have them create enchanted steel plows and seed drills instead of the shoddy sticks used by the masses today."

Sera wasn't one to let dwarves outshine elves, so, proudly, she pitched her own people. "The elves have an unnatural affinity with nature, so we could sense how a crop is doing before blight ever shows, ensure a healthy growth, and listen to whatever complaints the crops make."
"Won't they throw a massive hissy fit if their beloved greens get harvested on repeat?" Lucille asked, almost purring, eagerly awaiting a response.
The blonde elf's lips trembled wryly. Then she straightened her spine. "It has to be Quinlan who asks for volunteers. If it's the Holy Son, those crazies would do whatever he says."
"I see~"

"Humans can do the busy work, as there are too few elves to conduct this at scale and their fragile bodies and bitchy attitudes aren't great for the hard labor part. Potentially even the beastkin's noses could be of use, though we'll have to run some tests on that," Aurora continued, already deep in thought.
"And conquer them," Vex added, grinning.
"And conquer them. Yep," Quinlan chuckled.
Back at the foot of the entry stairs, two girls with brand-new spears stood frozen in place.

They had spent the entire morning of their yesterday on the first Steel Carapace Beetle, circling, jabbing, screaming advice at each other, prying at the shell seams while the thing rattled and lunged.

On the forty-somethingth try, the taller one had finally driven her spearpoint into the soft joint behind its head. Both of them had collapsed against the wall afterward, shaking, bleeding from three scrapes apiece, grinning like they'd slain a dragon.

Now, the gallery ran straight for two hundred paces before the first fork, which was why they could still see clear to the far end of it, where the Villain's family was disappearing down a corridor, chatting about farming.

Beetles, wisps, and bramblebacks charged that group from every nook, and died mid-lunge to a katana that never seemed to leave its sheath, a bare hand, a gauntlet, an elbow, a stray breeze. The family kept walking and kept talking, and not one of them turned to look.
"They're not even trying," the smaller one whispered. "That one killed it with her hair. I saw it. Her hair!!!"
"That was a knife," the taller one said. "I never saw her draw it."
"It took us all morning," the smaller one said, renegotiating her entire understanding of the world out loud. "One beetle. All morning."
"Correct," said Cassandra.
The spectral captain of the royal guard stood behind them in her plate, blue-white soulfire rolling quietly off her pauldrons, arms crossed, entirely unmoved by the view.

"I'd say Quinlan Elysiar is at least at the level of Lilith Ravenshade, if not stronger already, while his wives could each at least hold their own against a member of the Lilies. That's the distance you're looking at," she said, and reached over to shove the taller twin's grip further up the shaft without turning her head. "Higher. Hold it down there and you'll lose fingers."
She nodded down the gallery at the family. "Every explorer who ever lived started at the end you are standing on, including the man who now owns this kingdom."
The twins looked down at their new spears the way acolytes look at relics.
Cassandra's gaze swept the empty corridor ahead.
"Wait for the monsters to respawn," she said. "Then we begin."
A few corridors ahead, Quinlan slowed his stride.
"I need a few minutes. You ladies go on ahead."
He got a look from Ayame, and a longer look from Vex. Then ten women continued down the corridor, reading in his tone exactly how much of an answer they were going to get.
A warp gate spun open, and the Primordial Villain stepped out of his labyrinth and into the sky.

Wind took his weight. The world fell away in tiers of cloud, and the peak of the dwarven mountain rose ahead of him, white and silent. It stood so far above the gates of the vertical city that the hymns and hammering below arrived as less than a rumor.
Black Fang sat alone at the summit.
She sat cross-legged on bare wind-scoured stone with her serpent-patterned blade across her knees, back straight, lids down, frost dusting her shoulders and her hair.
She had been meditating, to all appearances, since the family left the mountain that morning without her.
Quinlan landed without a sound ten paces away.

He looked at her for a moment, and then, grinning, he crossed the distance, sat down directly opposite her, folded his legs into a mirror of hers, straightened his back into a mirror of hers, and closed his eyes.
The wind moved over the peak and frost gathered on them both, and neither of them moved for a long stretch of nothing.
"Why are you here."
Her voice came out flat, and her lids did not lift.
"Hm? I'm meditating. It's very peaceful up here."
"You should be taking your partners leveling."
"Oh?" He opened one eye, delighted. "And how do you know what I'm taking my girls to do today?"
Silence.
She did not bother responding.
Quinlan chuckled, low and warm, and let the wind have the peak again for a while.
Black Fang sat across from him, radiating, to anyone who didn't know this unique woman, serene indifference.
Quinlan knew her very well.
"Are you sulking, Black Fang?" he grinned.
She had been left behind twice now. Once at the dwarven war's opening, by an oversight she had muttered about, and once this morning, on purpose, by the man sitting in front of her.

Had he asked her to come along and level, she would have run the numbers in her head and refused before he finished the sentence, so he had not asked at all. He had left her up here instead, with nothing to do all morning except notice that he had taken everyone else with him.
And, truthfully, he just wanted to be a bit playful with this amazing creature.
By the looks of things, his sulking question was ignored as well.
"Come with us," he asked. "I'd love to spend more time with you."
"...Pointless. I'd only be stealing resources."

At level 74, Black Fang only gained a single point of experience at a time, and only the strongest of prey yielded even that. At the current rate, her next level would arrive in several billion years.
It was best to let the others slay the labyrinth monsters.
Quinlan made no particular effort to stop what rose in his chest.
This creature.

She had taught herself everything, because the world had offered her nothing. At some point she had decided that tenderness was a fiction told to children and grief a waste of a morning. Nobody had ever handed her a reason to think otherwise.

He loved her in a way he had never once been permitted to say out loud, on her strict and standing terms. Watching her refuse to admit any part of what was happening on this mountain filled him with extreme fondness.
She was perfect.
"You're right," he admitted. "You can't level up. Your presence would be an active hindrance to the progression of my family."
Black Fang said nothing.
Quinlan's grin deepened. "Good thing I'd like you there for something else entirely."
"If you expect me to follow you around so you can flirt-"

"You're the most lethal killer on this continent," he interjected. "Your experience, honed instincts, and demonstrated ability to raise disciplines to the level you already had... Your presence could prove even more beneficial to our future than the levels themselves."
Black Fang finally opened one eye, looking at him silently, observing, studying.

"On my first visit to the labyrinth," Quinlan went on, softer, "back when I was a nobody with a shabby spear, a wonderful samurai girl walked me through these same corridors and taught me how not to die. Everything I have grew out of what she planted in me back then."
He extended his hand across the space between them, palm open.
"Now I'd like to ask her big sister to teach all of us."
Her other eye opened as well, unblinking, on him and on his open palm.
"Will you prepare the women I love for the vast outside world for me, Black Fang?"
The peak held still around the question. She looked at his hand for a long moment, expression at absolute zero.
Silence ruled supreme for a few seconds, poker faced terror staring at the tenderly smiling villain.
Then her hand came off her blade and closed around his.
"Okay."
A warp gate opened in a blue-lit corridor of the Aldoria labyrinth, and the Primordial Villain stepped through with the Venomborne Terror at his side, walking with her head held high.
Ten women turned.
"Sis!" Ayame lit up first.
"Oh?" Serika's grin spread. "Welcome to the party."
Vex said nothing.
The Hexwitch only smiled, small and private, at her mentor arriving at her husband's side like it meant nothing.
Black Fang swept the gathered family once, head to toe, ten of the strongest women alive standing in a comfortable, chattering cluster in a monster corridor.
"First lesson."
And just like that, minutes turned into hours, and hours into days.
But while Quinlan and the gang were farming experience, the rest of Iskaris were experiencing a rapid shift.
A shift that would shake up the rest of the world.

chapters.title: Chapter 1919 Incoming!
paragraphs: Skarn of the wolfkin rounded the western palisade for the fourth time that night, and the sentries posted along it had learned to stop breathing when he passed.
Below the wall, the heartlands of the Beastman Confederation were digging.
The deep drums had run nightly since the war-lodge council: sharpen, stockpile, drill.
Then, days ago, a blood-run relay had carried the word over the border passes: the dwarven mountain had fallen. Not besieged for a season, not starved out. Fallen, in a single night, to the Villain.
The same relay carried the rest of it. The Villain granted the dwarven king a warrior's death in front of his whole city, and the city swore hammer oaths to their conqueror. They chose him.
The drums were joined by shovels within the hour.

The digging was days old and looked it. Palisade stakes still wept sap. Boarkin crews cut trench lines by torchlight. Runners crossed between the lodges with stores manifests nobody had finished tallying.
On the near field, a row of cubs drilled with wooden claws strapped to their paws, each tiny war-cry arriving a breath behind its swipe.
Invasion was coming, the Confederation had decided, and it intended to be found awake.

"You have walked that wall all night," Rajah observed from beside the great fire, sprawled along a bench that had seated four soldiers before he arrived. Amber eyes tracked the wolfkin lord with lazy patience. "Walk it a few more times. Perhaps it grows taller."
"Someone on this council should be awake."
"We are all awake." The tigerkin's tail swayed once.

Across the fire, Gorruk worked through a stack of border slates, twice the height of the soldier who kept bringing them, reading each report to its end before setting it down. "Passes are watched," he rumbled. "Dens report at the moon. Stores fill before the cots do." The last slate went down. "The Confederation prepares as one."

Vargis Ironfang sat where he had sat since the council, giant blade across his knees, whetstone circling the edge in slow, even strokes. His proposal, to send for the Villain and ask what terms would fit both sides, still lay on that fire where he had set it down.
Not tonight, the fire had ruled, and no night since had been the night either.
Then the deep scouts began coming home.

They were the pairs that had been living inside the Villain's lands since the mobilization began, and they came in through the gray morning, spaced out along the ridges, each pair leaving the fire circle quieter than they found it.

The first pair brought the labyrinth gates. "He has thrown them open, great lords. Labyrinth gate after labyrinth gate across his lands stands free of charge, by his own decree. Farmhands are walking in with spears, and the queues run out past the city walls."
"What is he, retarded?" Skarn scoffed. "Such an imbecile..."
The next pair had seen the camps, and the older of the two kept his eyes on the flames while he gave it.

"The three races train together now on the old border between Vraven and Elvardia. They're trying different formations, making use of each race's advantages while wearing armor our forges could not match on our best day." He swallowed.

"They drill against the Villain's dead legions, the Vesper Consortium's forces, the Scarlet Lilies, summons of an alleged wife of the Villain, and a few of their own powerhouses who act as hostile. Even retired King Alexios partook. The armies had to keep their own commanders alive while he and Morgana Ravenshade hunted them."
The fire cracked into the silence that followed.

The four of them had survived a combined span of years measured in a lot more than a single millennium, and the instincts that had carried them through those years were howling the same warning at once.
That sense had never once lied to any of them.
"Days ago the dwarves were a nation," Rajah said. "Now they sharpen his spears and sing while they do it."
"Us versus the world." Skarn's growl stayed low. His tail did not move at all.
The last pair came in at dusk, from the western road, and they came in running.

"A column has left the mountain, great lords!" The scout got his breath under control on the second try. "It came out of the east mountain gate and it's following the pass road toward our border. We counted a long train of wagons under guard, driven by dwarven crews. At their pace they'll reach us within two days."

Nobody slept that night either. The walls gained a third watch, the reserve dens stayed woken, and every eye the Confederation owned pointed west, waiting to learn what the Villain sent a conquered nation's wagons to do.
The horn came at midday, and it hit the war-lodge like a thrown spear.
One long note came off the western pass, and a second climbed over the top of it.

The fire circle emptied between one heartbeat and the next. Skarn crossed the compound as a gray blur and hit the palisade with his claws already out, hackles standing the length of his spine, snarling at a column he could not see yet.

Rajah arrived a blink later at a speed nobody's eyes could confirm. The tigerkin lord had never once hurried anywhere in front of witnesses, and he spent his first breath on that wall gripping the timber hard enough to print his claws into it.
Below them the camp detonated. Trench crews came up out of their own trenches with shovels held like axes. Kennel-masters bellowed over each other.
The cubs' drill instructor herded her entire class behind a woodpile with her body, and three different horns answered from three different walls in an order no signal-book contained.
"It's them!" The runner was screaming it before he cleared the gate, voice cracking through two octaves. "The column, on the western pass!! Banners! Wagons! They're here!!"
"Form lines!" Skarn's roar flattened the compound. "Archers to the wall! Wake the reserve dens!!"
A tigerkin quartermaster sprinted past the great fire armed with the ladle she had been counting rations with. Somebody loosed a signal arrow that meant flood, or possibly fire, or possibly both.
On the wall, a hundred claws came out with a sound like a forest icing over.
The column crested the western pass, slowed, and stopped in plain view of the entire western wall.
Then, politely, it raised its banners.

The banners were white. Trade-white, parley-white, on each wagon of a long mule train. The train had arranged itself into neat rows on the pass road, where dwarven crews in town clothes were now sitting down on their own crates to wait.
A single figure detached from the column and walked up to the gate under the aim of a hundred arrows, unhurried, consulting a ledger as he came. A dwarf, gray-bearded, dressed for market day.
He stopped before the gate timber, looked up at the wall of drawn claws above him, and knocked. Twice.
"Reparations delivery for the honored Beastman Confederation!" he called up. "Requesting entry and a flat place to unload, if it pleases the great lords!"
The wall gave him nothing.
The herald consulted his ledger again. "We are also instructed to ask whether the honored Confederation would prefer the crates under roofs," he added. "It is snowing."

The four of them had survived a combined span of years measured in a lot more than a single millennium, and the instincts that had carried them through those years were howling the same warning at once.
That sense had never once lied to any of them.
"Days ago the dwarves were a nation," Rajah said.
"Now they sharpen his spears and sing while they do it."
"Us versus the world." Skarn's growl stayed low.
His tail did not move at all.
The last pair came in at dusk, from the western road, and they came in running.
"A column has left the mountain, great lords!" The scout got his breath under control on the second try.
"It came out of the east mountain gate and it's following the pass road toward our border.
We counted a long train of wagons under guard, driven by dwarven crews.
At their pace they'll reach us within two days."
Nobody slept that night either.
The walls gained a third watch, the reserve dens stayed woken, and every eye the Confederation owned pointed west, waiting to learn what the Villain sent a conquered nation's wagons to do.
The horn came at midday, and it hit the war-lodge like a thrown spear.
One long note came off the western pass, and a second climbed over the top of it.
The fire circle emptied between one heartbeat and the next.
Skarn crossed the compound as a gray blur and hit the palisade with his claws already out, hackles standing the length of his spine, snarling at a column he could not see yet.
Rajah arrived a blink later at a speed nobody's eyes could confirm.
The tigerkin lord had never once hurried anywhere in front of witnesses, and he spent his first breath on that wall gripping the timber hard enough to print his claws into it.
Below them the camp detonated.
Trench crews came up out of their own trenches with shovels held like axes.
Kennel-masters bellowed over each other.
The cubs' drill instructor herded her entire class behind a woodpile with her body, and three different horns answered from three different walls in an order no signal-book contained.
"It's them!" The runner was screaming it before he cleared the gate, voice cracking through two octaves.
"The column, on the western pass!!
Banners!
Wagons!
They're here!!"
"Form lines!" Skarn's roar flattened the compound.
"Archers to the wall!
Wake the reserve dens!!"
A tigerkin quartermaster sprinted past the great fire armed with the ladle she had been counting rations with.
Somebody loosed a signal arrow that meant flood, or possibly fire, or possibly both.
On the wall, a hundred claws came out with a sound like a forest icing over.
The column crested the western pass, slowed, and stopped in plain view of the entire western wall.
Then, politely, it raised its banners.
The banners were white.
Trade-white, parley-white, on each wagon of a long mule train.
The train had arranged itself into neat rows on the pass road, where dwarven crews in town clothes were now sitting down on their own crates to wait.
A single figure detached from the column and walked up to the gate under the aim of a hundred arrows, unhurried, consulting a ledger as he came.
A dwarf, gray-bearded, dressed for market day.
He stopped before the gate timber, looked up at the wall of drawn claws above him, and knocked.
Twice.
"Reparations delivery for the honored Beastman Confederation!" he called up.
"Requesting entry and a flat place to unload, if it pleases the great lords!"
The wall gave him nothing.
The herald consulted his ledger again.
"We are also instructed to ask whether the honored Confederation would prefer the crates under roofs," he added.
"It is snowing."

chapters.title: Chapter 1920 Emperor
paragraphs: On the palisade, Skarn stared down with his claws still out. "You are requesting entry."
"Yes, my lord," the herald said, with dignity. "The deal between the Beastman Confederation and His Majesty-"
"I know the damn deal!" Skarn snapped. "Let them in."
What followed was, by the account of the soldiers on that wall, the strangest hour of the mobilization.
The gates opened. The mule train came in under a guard that outnumbered it twenty to one.
Dwarven crews unloaded crate after crate with parade precision, stacking them in rows and checking the seals twice. They plainly hoped an enemy would open one and judge it.

The tigerkin quartermaster, ladle abandoned, pried the first crate open, lifted out a sword blank, and went still. She bent the blade against her knee, read its flex, and dragged one claw down the length of it.
"This is excellent quality," she said. "They're showing off."
The nearest dwarf did not look up from his stacking. "That's the standard run, ma'am."
"Standard."
"Export grade." He smoothed the crate seal down, and there was no mistaking the pride in it. "Mind the edges, please. We don't want the emperor's steel to hurt his respected neighbors."
Rajah took the manifest from a quartermaster who had carried the page across the compound like a live coal, held it between two claws, and read it aloud in a voice stripped of all its play.
"'By declaration of Emperor Quinlan Elysiar. The reparations owed the Beastman Confederation for its part in the late war: first installment, paid in full.'"
He read it a second time. The page said the same thing again.
He had spoken the test himself, at this same fire: the Villain had promised to reach out, and if he did, the Confederation would learn what his word was worth.
The answer had now walked over the pass under white banners, mere days after Quinlan had conquered a nation, priced in steel their own forges could not follow.

"He offered us these reparations at the war's end, and this council deferred him," Gorruk noted. "He gave me his word he would raise the matter again." The rumble settled over the fire. "He's doing it."
"Emperor Quinlan Elysiar is a man who keeps his promises," the herald said proudly.
"Emperor." Skarn spat the word into the flames. "There is no such throne. There has never been such a throne on Iskaris. He is a king with extra provinces, and his clerks flatter him on paper."
Grumbles of agreement ran the circle, from soldiers grateful to be handed a thing they were allowed to agree with.
"The elves dissolved their own crown for him, becoming a theocracy," Gorruk said.
The grumbling died.
"The human queen holds her throne at his pleasure and calls it an honor. The mountain swore itself to him, singing." Gorruk's rumble stayed level the whole way through.
"Three peoples on the Confederation's scale kneel to him. What is he if not more than king?"
"Careful, bear." Rajah's drawl slid back on, and it fit badly.
Skarn's hackles lifted. Across the fire, Vargis's whetstone never changed its stroke.
The delegation did not leave.
When the last crate stood stacked, the herald opened his ledger to a second page, and for the first time all day he looked apologetic about what was written on it.

"There is a further matter, great lords. The steel is only the first half of the installment. The second half is labor." He turned the ledger around, as if the lords across the fire could read it from there.

"His Majesty instructs that the villages destroyed in the old war, the ones overrun by the lionkin and by the necromancer's horde, are to be rebuilt at our cost. The wagons behind the steel carry timber and tools."

He closed the ledger. "We would ask the lords' leave to travel to the ruins and begin, if it pleases the Confederation. We are instructed to build to dwarven standard while ensuring the result will please its future inhabitants."
Nobody at the fire had an answer ready for him.
The ruins of the old war had stood black and empty since the burning. No tribe had found the hands or the coin to raise them again. Mourning them had been cheaper.
Skarn watched the herald fold his ledger shut, and his hackles did not come down.
"The walls go higher," he said at last. "The watch doubles. The reserve dens stay woken. And those crews do not draw one breath on our ground unwatched."
"Our best eyes go with them, to every ruin, every camp they pitch, every hour they stand on Confederation soil. If the Villain hides a knife inside his gifts, we will be prepared when it comes out."
The drums took up again at dark: sharpen, stockpile, drill. On the near field the cubs returned to their forms, wooden claws rising and falling in the torchlight.
Beyond them, the first dwarven wagons rolled out toward the dead villages of the old war, under an escort of the Confederation's finest killers, sent to guard their people from carpenters.
No soul on that field let itself look at both sights at once.
Quinlan Elysiar flew his family up out of the labyrinth and held them in the air over Aldoria, watching the streets from high above.

The snow that had lain clean in banks along the shopfronts when the family went down was gray at the edges now, rotten under the awnings, packed to ice across the square where the explorer queues had trampled it.
Around him, his family blinked against the daylight, hair full of dungeon dust.
"Sunlight," Serika groaned, stretching until her spine crackled. "I'd almost forgotten what it tastes like."
"You basically produce sunlight at will," Lucille grinned.
"That doesn't count!" the tanned redhead laughed.
The rhythm had set itself in the first days of the grind and had not changed since: dive until they were properly exhausted, surface, and spend the rest day however each of them desired.
All of them spent it moving.
Quinlan landed his family on the nearest hill, raised a hand, and a warp gate opened on the slope in front of them.
"Do try to actually rest," he said, without any hope.

His girls scattered through the gates he summoned one after the other in the space of ten heartbeats, each toward her own idea of an afternoon rest. Vex went last, and not alone. She hooked her arm through Black Fang's on the way past, cheerful as a thief taking a purse.
The gate swallowed them both mid-objection.
Quinlan looked at the one woman remaining. Kitsara smiled up at him, five tails swaying, wearing the expression of a fox with plans.
"Quinnie, my rest day involves you, a hot bath, and no witnesses. Well, no witnesses who judge me for what I'll make you do to me."
"We're going back down the stairs."
"Oooh~ Kinky labyrinth seggs!!"
The river town on Vraven's southern trade road had a dockside cellar its own town watch had learned not to ask about.

Iris Ravenclaw stood across the street from it in the thin winter light, arms crossed, listening to a nervous man in a ledger-keeper's coat. Blossom crouched at the corner beside her with her nose up, reading the air off the cellar grate.

chapters.title: Chapter 1921 Afternoon Activities
paragraphs: "Debt-pens in the cellar," the Vesper man said, tapping his list. "Children in the debt-pens. The buyers rotate through on market days." He glanced up at her face and back down at his list. "You are early."

The Vesper Consortium had been many things down the centuries, and lawful was never one of them. Then they had bled beside the Villain's armies through the war and been granted legitimacy for it, and these days they audited their own streets with the zeal of the freshly converted. Scum running rackets beside their business offended them professionally.
Iris had made her oath.
Every innocent left in this world, safe from cruel hands.
After each dive, instead of resting, she'd work until it was time to go back down.
"Openings," she said.
"Two doors, one grate."
"Blossom."

"Blossom found all three already!" The dogkin's ears lay flat with disgust, tail low and still. "Blossom smelled the cellar from the bridge. It smells like chains, scared kids, and bad people." Her voice dropped into the flat register that meant the pup had left the conversation entirely. "Very bad people."
Ayame came off the alley wall behind them with her scabbard already in her hand.
"Let's knock," Iris said.
She crossed the street and removed the cellar door along with its frame.
"INTRUDERS! GET-"
The first slaver's warning ended there, because Iris's fist arrived where the rest of his sentence was going.
The cellar boiled. A knife-man lunged out of the dark at her flank and met Ayame's scabbard across both wrists, then her palm across his ear, both blows bored and exact.
A crossbow clicked at the top of the stairs, aimed down at Ayame's back. It never fired.
Golden light took the shooter off his feet and folded him into the ceiling beams, and Seraphiel came down the steps after her handiwork, barefoot on the freezing stone, radiating disapproval.
"Why are there so many of you scum?"
A second crossbowman rose from behind the wine racks. Sera's spear of light took him through the shoulder and pinned him to the wall like a note on a corkboard.
The cellar's owner made his choice at the grate exit, where Blossom was sitting. Just sitting, blue eyes gone empty.
"Blossom counted nine kids in the pens." Static crawled up her gauntlets. "Blossom wants to see you suffer."
"Ahh! Mercy! I have a wife and children!" He turned and ran the other way, which was Iris.
Afterward, the chains came off the children with more care than anything in that cellar had been touched in years.
Iris crouched to the smallest girl's height while Sera's warm light moved from child to child behind her.
"You're out. It's over." She built each word by hand. "Eat first. Cry after. That's the order that works."
The girl nodded at her, solemn, and Iris nodded back like the two of them had signed something.
By the stairs, the Vesper man was already chalking a mark on his list. "That clears this street, my lady. Two more towns flagged along the river."
Iris rolled her shoulder and stood.
"Next."

The townhouse had belonged to a count who had chosen the wrong side of human decency, so it now belonged to the crown. Then the crown's liege lord's family came asking, and by the end of that same conversation it belonged to them.
It had forty rooms, a walled courtyard, and a kitchen built for banquets no one would miss.

Lucille walked the main hall with her sleeves already rolled, pointing at things while a small storm of carpenters trailed her. "Dormitories along the upper floor. That parlor becomes a classroom. The ballroom stays a ballroom; children need somewhere to be loud."

Jasmine ticked columns in her ledger without looking up. "Beds, linens, three cooks, winter coal. I priced it out this morning." Her blue eyes flashed coin-gold for one satisfied blink. "We could run a hundred of these before the realm's books cleared their throat. My love conquers faster than his family can spend."
"That sounded like a challenge."
"Just an acute observation," Jasmine grinned.

Through the tall windows, the courtyard was already loud. The children had arrived that morning, gathered ward by ward across the capital, some orphaned, some not. They had discovered two things in short order: the ballroom floor was perfect for sliding on in socks, and the red-haired lady was climbable.
Serika stood in the middle of the courtyard with one child on each shoulder, a third on her back, and a fourth hanging determinedly off her flexed arm like laundry.
"You're all brown," the one on her arm marveled.
"Sun-forged," Serika said solemnly.
"Sun? Does the hair burn?"
"Sure it does~" Serika mused and activated her powers, her red locks turning molten orange.
The children screamed with delight.
Many girls found their idol that day, while the boys...
The stock value of confident, tanned, athletic women with red hair would rise exponentially by the time these boys came of age.
Vex went by the hall doors at a trot with a rolled floor plan under one arm and a carpenter jogging to keep up with her.
"No lock and no bolt goes on the outside of any door a child sleeps behind," she decreed, to the corridor at large. "A child in this house can always open her own door and walk out."
"Nobody will ever be locked in anything again. And I will be checking every door myself, so do save us all the trouble~"
She was three rooms away before the carpenter finished writing it down.
"It still needs a name," Jasmine said, arriving at Lucille's side with the ledger closed. "The crown's clerks won't register 'that thing the Villain's family is doing with the townhouse.'"
"We are not calling it an orphanage," Lucille said. "Kids in orphanages get a bad reputation."
"The Elysiar Youth Program." Jasmine tried it out loud, nodded once, and wrote it down in the same motion.
"Let's open enrollment to any child, orphan or not," Lucille said. "In the first years they'll start with letters and numbers. Enough of both that nobody can ever lie to them on paper."
"Love it," Jasmine nodded. "And then?"
"Then we stop with the mandatory lectures. That is where Quin says the rot appears in his old world, and I think he is right about it. A farm girl does not need three years of mathematical theory."
Jasmine was on the same wavelength.

"Right. She needs the ability to read and understand what the dwarves published about drainage this spring, and the ability to calculate whether a second field pays for itself," the Tyrant of Commerce listed. "Give her that and she is the best farmer in her province."
"Sit her in a hall reciting theory she will never touch and she quits at fourteen and rushes into a labyrinth to escape the madness."

"After the basic stuff, we show it all to them," Lucille continued, envisioning it all. "We walk them through the smithies. The farms. The market on market days. The army yards. Any enterprise that will open its doors to a line of children."
"My warehouses will," Jasmine said. "And the Lorien laboratory, on days when nothing inside it is on fire."
"So, never."
"On the quiet days," Jasmine amended.

"And the Lorien laboratory, on days when nothing inside it is on fire."
"So, never."
"On the quiet days," Jasmine amended.

chapters.title: Chapter 1922 Unique Interview Method
paragraphs: "On the quiet days," Jasmine amended.

"And when one of them plants herself in front of a forge and won't leave," Lucille said, and her smile went slow and warm, "or takes a market ledger apart for fun, then we know what she is. And we feed it. Special education from there."
"But we have to be careful," Jasmine was already searching for vulnerabilities. "We shouldn't force a kid to become a farmer for life just because he liked how a cow sounds at age ten."
"Right, right," Lucille nodded along.
"When Quin hears of this, he's going to be smug for a week," Serika called from under her pile of children.
"He will be smug about it forever," Jasmine corrected fondly, "and fund it without reading a single page."
"And pamper us all with his overwhelming love afterward..." Lucille muttered, eyes dreamy.
"...Correct," the Villain's dutiful governor smirked, gaze hungry for the reward she knew she deserved.
The line at the townhouse's side entrance had formed before noon the next day, and it was quiet in a way market lines never were.
Word had gone out through the wards with the previous morning's bread carts: the Villain's family wanted matrons, cooks, cleaners, and minders for the count's old townhouse.
War widows first. Paid in coin. Children of employees enrolled free.
The capital did not lack for war widows, and each woman in that line had spent the winter learning exactly what the city offered her.
Nothing.
If they didn't want to see their children starve, their options ran like this:
Sell the furniture, then the roof, then themselves, and when that ran out, the children.
That was the whole market.
Now there was a fourth thing on it that was none of those, and a table standing between them and it.
The table had two women behind it, and the line could not decide which of the two frightened it more.
The screening had been Black Fang's, proposed over breakfast in the voice she used for casualty counts.
"Put a slave collar on every applicant," she had said. "Then ask her whether she wants to molest children."
Lucille had objected that they were hiring grieving mothers, not prisoners.
"An honest answer costs an honest woman nothing but a minute of her freedom," the Venomborne Terror reasoned.
Vex had voted yes twice, for emphasis.
"Name?" Vex asked brightly, quill poised, red eyes shining with civic enthusiasm.

"M-Mara, my lady. Mara Wint. I have two boys. I kept a tavern kitchen before the war took... before." Her hands strangled each other at her waist. "I can cook for a hundred. I swear I can cook. Just give me the opportunity."
"Wonderful~! One small formality." Vex turned the smile up a notch. "Master? She's ready."
The woman beside Vex had not smiled all morning, or, by most accounts, ever.
Black Fang set the collar on the table between them: plain slave iron, rune-cut, the same pattern that rode her throat back in Elvardian captivity.
Locked shut, it took refusal away. Asked a question by the hand that closed it, the woman inside answered, and the runes burned if what came out of her was not the truth.
"Absolutely standard hiring practice," Vex chirped. "Put it on, answer one question, and you're hired. Oh, and the collar will of course come off, too."
Mara looked at the collar for a long moment, then lifted her chin and held herself still while Black Fang closed it around her throat. The runes woke, faint and orange.
"State your intentions toward the children who will be in your care without holding a single detail back," Black Fang said.
"I... want to feed them?" Mara looked between the two women, terrified of getting the truth wrong.

"Mine first, if I'm honest. But I kept the neighbor's girls fed all autumn too, and I don't hit children, and I want... that sounds like begging. I'm sorry. I want a wage. I want to stop being afraid of the thaw."
Her voice cracked on nothing at all. "That's everything that's in me, my ladies. I swear it."
The runes stayed quiet. Black Fang opened the collar.
"Acceptable."
"You passed~!" Vex translated, delighted, stamping the contract. "Kitchen wing, morning shift. Your boys will be educated while you work. Sign here~"
Mara stared at the contract, then at the wage line on it, and her knees quit.
She went down onto the boards on both of them and stayed there, one hand fisted in the hem of Black Fang's coat, forehead pressed to her own knuckles, saying thank you over and over into the floor.
She had walked into that house an hour ago expecting to be turned away at the door.
She wept into her fists, tried twice to apologize for it, and failed both times.
Night came down softly over the Program.

Lamps went out wing by wing. In the dormitories, the capital's newest students slept in real beds under new linen, several still wearing the socks they had refused to surrender. In the kitchen wing, dough rose for a breakfast someone was being paid to cook.
A matron on her first shift walked the halls twice as often as her rounds required, checking on sleeping children nobody was coming to take.
Vex stood at the corridor window at the end of the dormitory wing, where the lamplight didn't quite reach.

She had been there a while. The courtyard below sat empty, blue with snow-light. The glass held her reflection: white hair, red eyes, the mark of the man she loved warm and hidden beneath her clothes.
Some of the small sleepers behind her had no one at all. Vex kept her eyes on the glass, held her own elbows, and said nothing.
Black Fang walked down the corridor past midnight, on her way to nowhere she would ever explain, and stopped at the window beside her disciple.
"I'm so happy right now..." Vex whispered. "My chest just wants to burst with joy."
"..." Black Fang watched her own expression in the reflection.
She didn't seem happy.
"I could've done this long before. I had the means." Her eyes flashed bright purple. "Instead, I killed and sold drugs."
Vex's eyes widened. She reached out and hugged her mother-figure by the waist.
"Master, that's just not true! You raised us while you were hunted by the whole world. You were dealt a hand worse than anyone, yet look at what you became."
Red eyes flared, crimson and violet staring at each other in the reflection.
Vex's arms tightened as she smiled. "Just today, you helped us protect the innocence of hundreds of children with your idea, while sending pedo scum to hell."
"If you keep sulking, I'll get mad!" Vex finally stomped, hissing low enough not to wake anyone.
"...I don't sulk."
"..." Vex's eyes turned wry. "Liar."
"No."
"Yes."
As the two women argued back and forth, the night's first snow began to fall on the Elysiar Youth Program.

chapters.title: Chapter 1923 Rapid Climb
paragraphs: Forty-five floors beneath Aldoria's market square, a chamber the size of a cathedral was trying to kill two of the Primordial Villain's women, and Black Fang was taking notes.
She waited on a shelf of black rock above the killing floor, one thigh crossed over the other.
Below her, forty-five monsters poured out of the tunnel mouths in waves. Ashmaw Orcs led the charge, tusked and plate-muscled, crude cleavers hammering off Kaelira's raised shield.

Behind them, Cragspit Tortoises squatted at the chamber's edges, spitting fists of rock in flat arcs over their own line. Gloomhide Prowlers slid along the walls, hunting a path around the shield to the caster behind it.
*RRAAGH!*

The Venomborne Terror had split the family into pairs of her own design, shield and curse in this case. The rule she had given them was one sentence long: your chamber is yours alone, and nobody comes to save you.
The pace they were setting would've floored any professional dungeon explorer.
Behind the labyrinth's little stone doorway, buried countries unfolded, one per floor, corridor systems feeding chamber after chamber, and all of it stocked full of monsters.
"Left tunnel," Kaelira reported from behind her tower shield, runes flaring along its rim as tortoise shot and cleavers hammered it in turns. "Eight more incoming."
"I see them~" Vex sang from atop a dead orc, one hand weaving, and a wave of grey rot rolled across the chamber floor like spilled water.
Green flesh withered. Six charging orcs folded mid-stride, muscle rotting off the bone, and Vex hopped down to open the nearest one's throat with her sword, as an afterthought.
A Gloomhide Prowler dropped from the wall at her back before her boots touched the floor. Two dancing steps took her out from under its claws, and the third put her blade up through its jaw.
"Four minutes," Black Fang said from above.
"Yesterday it was six!" Kaelira called back, and drove her shield edge down through a crippled orc with a *CRUNCH*.
"Kaelira, you're powerful. But you keep acting as though your worth was only your shield." The verdict came down flat.
"...But I'm-"
"A tanker whose job is to protect others," Black Fang finished for her. "The best way to protect those behind you is to kill what's in front of you."
Without wasting a breath, she moved on. "Vex. You spent mana on six when only four would breach the wave."
"Master watched me kill six at once?" Vex tipped her head back at the shelf, red eyes shining hopefully through the gore.
"I saw you waste mana on two." Black Fang let that sit. "The footwork was acceptable."
Vex beamed like she'd been handed a medal.
On the western border of the Beastman Confederation, snow lay knee-deep on the watch-ridges, and the wolfkin posted there could no longer feel their own faces.

They were the best eyes the Confederation owned, sent by Skarn's standing order to watch every wagon the Villain's lands dared roll their way. The schedule taken down from the first delivery said the second installment would cross the pass in eight days.
The horn blew on the fifth.
"Count again," the senior watcher growled.
"I've counted three times!" The younger one's ears were flat against his skull. "Same banners, twice the wagons. They're early. Who is early with a mule train through mountain passes in deep winter?"
Below their ridge, the column crested the pass road unhurried, trade-white banners bright against the snow, and the escort riding its flanks was so thin it read as decoration.
On the fiftieth floor, Quinlan Elysiar stood at the mouth of a chamber built for an army and flooded it.

One hand lifted, magma answered, and a burning tide rolled wall to wall in a single breath, climbing the tunnel mouths, swallowing fifty war-howls before they could finish leaving fifty throats. Heat washed back over him like a furnace door opening.

Duskhorn Minotaurs went under mid-charge beside Gravehide Trolls, and with them a whole rank of Ashmaw Orcs, five levels heavier than their kin upstairs. The labyrinth reshuffled the previous floors' monsters into its deeper stock now and then, raised to the local level, and today the orcs had drawn the short straw twice.
[You've Slain Duskhorn Minotaur (Level 50). You've Gained 12,400 XP.]
[You've Slain Ashmaw Orc (Level 50). You've Gained 12,000 XP.]
[You've Slain Gravehide Troll (Level 50). You've Gained 12,150 XP.]
The kill notifications climbed the edge of his vision faster than he could dismiss them, a waterfall of blue script with no end in sight.
"Cheater," Ayame observed from the corridor behind him, arms folded, entirely unbothered by the heat rolling past her.
"It's called skill," he corrected pleasantly.
"Saber only next chamber," came the flat voice from the corridor mouth. Black Fang had arrived without sound, as always, and her violet eyes gave the cooling lake of stone exactly zero appreciation.
"Yes!" Ayame grinned, already victorious.
"...Yes, teach," the Primordial Villain sighed.
The next room he took with the Soul Reaper alone, and the Venomborne Terror's corrections fell on him the entire time, precise as thrown knives.
Your left hip opens before your cut. You gave that cleaver your shoulder for free. Stop killing them in the order they arrive, kill them in the order that costs least.
Ayame hugged her scabbard and committed every second of it to memory while her big sister dismantled her lover's swordsmanship layer by layer.
Quinlan was already a great user of the blade, even if not on her level. But the fact that her sister found so many tiny gaps to voice...
Ayame sported a brilliant smile.
The convoy reached the Confederation's western gate at midday, and the watchers above it got their first clear look at the crews.
Dwarves drove the lead wagons. That much was expected.
Then came the second rank, and it was human.
Then the outriders dismounted, and they were elves.
"Elves," the senior watcher said, as though saying it plainly might unmake it. "Riding escort. For dwarven wagons. Carrying human cargo hands."
This wasn't like the first delegation that arrived. Something had clearly changed.
His partner had stopped hearing him. The gear had all of him.
The humans wore interlocking plate that moved with them like cloth and shed the cold like a hearth, dwarven make in every line of it, fitted to human frames.
Scaled mail rippled on the elven outriders, forge-runes glowing faint at the collar seams.
No kingdom's army had ever fielded armor like it. These were cargo guards, and they were equipped beyond the Confederation's finest champions.
And the strangest part wasn't the steel.

The elves passed crates down to the dwarves at arm's reach, close enough to smell beard and sweat, and stayed there. The dwarves griped about the cold, the mules, the crate count, about everything except the elves.

"Even Elvardia never looked like that," the senior watcher muttered. The old alliance had put elves and dwarves under one banner, and they had still salted every shared road with contempt. "What did he do to them?"
Nobody answered him.
"You saw it," the senior said at last. "You write it."
"I am not writing that. The great lords will have the messenger skinned."
"I outrank you."
"Then you write it."
"...Fuck."

chapters.title: Chapter 1924 Passive Income
paragraphs: On a rest day between dives, Kaelira walked the joint halls under the dwarven mountain, where three races now worked one forge floor at her direction.

Half the benches were turning out enchanted plows and seed drills for the spring planting, the emperor's farming project made steel. The other half fitted dwarven plate to human and elven frames for the joint army.
A human journeyman and a dwarven smith were about to come to blows over a quenching trough on the plow row, and neither of them noticed the elf until she was already between them.

"You pulled the blade at the wrong color," Kaelira said to the human, taking the tongs out of his hand without asking. She turned to the dwarf. "And you let him, to prove a point. The steel paid for your pride."
The dwarf's beard bristled. "Girl, I've worked this floor six hundred years."
"Then you know I'm right."
Silence sat between them for a moment.
Then the dwarf grunted, and it came out closer to a laugh than he would have admitted, and the human ducked his head at her in apology.
The Runeweaver Titan was already gone down the aisle, sleeves rolled, calling corrections at a rack of half-finished plow blades.
At a forge, nobody ever remembered she was shy.

The report reached the war-lodge fire at dusk, and Gorruk read it through twice before passing it into the circle, which had become his habit lately. The page said the same impossible things both times.

"They put armor our forges can't make on cargo guards," Rajah said from his bench, and there was no drawl left in it at all. "Three races riding one column, and they came in early, as though the winter roads meant nothing."
"The escort was twelve riders," Gorruk rumbled. "Twelve. For wealth that could ransom a county."
Skarn had not sat down since the horn. "Because nothing on those roads dares touch it. Double the watch on every pass. I want eyes on that column every hour it breathes our air."
"You doubled the watch after the first delivery," Rajah observed.
"Then I'll double it again!"
Across the fire, Vargis Ironfang said nothing at all, merely shook his head.
The circle had stopped asking his opinion. His silence had begun to sound like one.
The family surfaced in the last light of afternoon three days later, and winter had moved without them.

Outside Aldoria's labyrinth gate the drifts reached the knee where they had been ankle-deep at the dive's start, and the gate knights' braziers burned twice as tall. The city had pulled its shoulders in under the snow, chimney smoke standing straight up in the windless cold.
Quinlan gated his women home, and the evening ran the way home evenings ran: a dinner loud enough to rattle the windows, and a long stretch afterward that was considerably less clothed.
Then, the pile.

He slept buried in the middle of his family, sensual breathing all around him, soft bodies clinging to his skin from every side. Kitsara's tails had claimed his arm, Seraphiel's lips rested warm against his shoulder, and the whole tangle of them rose and fell in one slow, contented rhythm.
*Ding!*
His eyes opened at dawn to a soft chime and a line of blue script hanging in the dark.
His last swing had been hours ago, deep in the labyrinth.

Every night, while his family slept, his thousand-plus Elite Souls filed down into the labyrinths of Iskaris and hunted until morning, and every point their kills earned flowed to the Necromancer who held their souls.
The wives ground by day, the dead ground by night, and their emperor leveled around the clock.
"Good morning to me," he murmured into Aurora's hair, and dismissed the window.
At breakfast, Lucille eyed him suspiciously over her tea. "What are you smirking at, baby?"
"An oiled machine," Quinlan grinned.
In the burned lands of the old war, on Confederation soil, the first rebuilt village raised its walls before the deepest snows could stop it.
The crews were dwarven, sent north under the labor half of the reparations bill.
They worked the timber and stone to dwarven standard, which meant the granary went up square, sealed, and warmer than anything the village had owned before it burned.
Around the site, in a wide and watchful ring, stood the finest killers the Confederation owned, breath steaming through their guard rotations.
The carpenters they guarded waved at them at shift change. None of the killers had yet decided what to do about that.
The Elysiar Youth Program, in the capital of Vraven, had discovered ice.
The courtyard fountain had frozen solid, and the children had learned that the ballroom's sock-sliding records translated poorly to the real thing.
Serika Vael turned in the middle of it with a child riding her shoulders, one hanging off each arm, and a fourth locked around her waist, all four shrieking as she spun.
"Faster, Miss Serika!!"
"Faster? You'll fall off-"
"FASTER!!"
She went faster. The Solar Fist's laughter carried over the wall and down the street, chased by four smaller ones.

The third installment from the human-elf-dwarf budding nation without a proper name crossed the pass before the moon turned, weeks ahead of any schedule the ledgers implied, and the watchers on the ridge saw why before they saw the wagons.

The empire's half of the pass road had changed since their last rotation. Living root ran beside the roadbed the whole way down the valley, thick as a rampart, and the wagons rolled along its back at a pace no mule train had any right to hold.
"The road," the senior watcher said slowly. "The road is alive."
"The road is helping them," his partner whispered. "Since when do roads take sides?"

The root was Rosie Elysiar's doing. The Princess of the Eternal Tree had ridden the empire's half of the pass with her palm flat to the roadbed, and the Tree had come down the valley after her. It had not stopped growing since.
High above the cargo, elven rangers rode the bare winter canopy, watching the land.
"Her Highness Rosie Elysiar is watching us. Make no mistakes," their leader ordered.

On Confederation ground the deliveries stopped pretending to be deliveries. The column split at the burned crossroads into a crew for every dead village of the old war at once, and within days the ruins wore scaffolds, well-cranes, and granary frames.
And the crews had brought children.

Human and dwarf kids in half-sized work coats came down off the wagons, the first apprentice cohort of the Elysiar Youth Program, sent out by the governor's own decree: a few children of the realm, old enough and set on learning architecture, picked to ride along and learn from the masters on the job.

So the escorts of the war-lodge, hand-picked killers every one, held their posts around a rebuild site and listened to a gray-bearded dwarven master walk a fourteen-year-old down a roof beam, broad hands over the boy's on the hammer.
"Feel that? The beam talks when the nail sits wrong."
"It's not talking, Master Dolgrin, it's creaking-"
"That's talking. Learn its language."
*Tok. Tok. Tok.*
"It went quiet!" The boy's whole face lit up under his oversized cap.

sentences.text: On a rest day between dives, Kaelira walked the joint halls under the dwarven mountain, where three races now worked one forge floor at her direction.
Half the benches were turning out enchanted plows and seed drills for the spring planting, the emperor's farming project made steel.
The other half fitted dwarven plate to human and elven frames for the joint army.
A human journeyman and a dwarven smith were about to come to blows over a quenching trough on the plow row, and neither of them noticed the elf until she was already between them.
"You pulled the blade at the wrong color," Kaelira said to the human, taking the tongs out of his hand without asking.
She turned to the dwarf.
"And you let him, to prove a point.
The steel paid for your pride."
The dwarf's beard bristled.
"Girl, I've worked this floor six hundred years."
"Then you know I'm right."
Silence sat between them for a moment.
Then the dwarf grunted, and it came out closer to a laugh than he would have admitted, and the human ducked his head at her in apology.
The Runeweaver Titan was already gone down the aisle, sleeves rolled, calling corrections at a rack of half-finished plow blades.
At a forge, nobody ever remembered she was shy.

The page said the same impossible things both times.

"Three races riding one column, and they came in early, as though the winter roads meant nothing."
"The escort was twelve riders," Gorruk rumbled.
"Twelve.
For wealth that could ransom a county."

"Because nothing on those roads dares touch it.
Double the watch on every pass.
I want eyes on that column every hour it breathes our air."
"You doubled the watch after the first delivery," Rajah observed.
"Then I'll double it again!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1925 No Creativity Allowed
paragraphs: "It went right," the dwarf corrected, and his beard could not quite hide the grin. "Water break. Then you do the next ten alone."
Farther down the scaffold, a dwarf girl with charcoal on her nose complained about smith-school homework to an elven ranger.
The ranger looked down her long nose at the child, informed her that pages were wasted on smiths, and held the practice slate steady for her anyway.
The wolfkin escort captain counted the children twice. Then she counted their guards.
There were none. The empire had sent its pups onto Confederation soil, into ruins the old war had made, with an escort of carpenters and a handful of elves.
"It's almost like they're baiting us..." the escort captain muttered.
"They're taunting us!" her soldier hissed. "That long-eared slut is looking at me like I was a filthy dog!"
"Those bitches always have a condescending expression. Ignore it," the captain sighed.
At the western gate, a herald left a sealed letter on his way through: the joint domain would welcome a Confederation delegation, any size, any season, to see the works with their own eyes.
The scouts wrote all of it down. Then they spent an hour arguing over who would read it aloud at the fire.

On the beastkin side, the cubs' class ran evening forms in the torchlight, out on the drill field behind the Confederation's western wall. Every den owed the muster its young. That was the toll the war-lodge had set, and the dens had paid it.

Wooden claws rose and fell in ragged lines, small feet stamping the packed snow, and each tiny war-cry arrived a breath behind its swipe, as it had for weeks now. Their instructor walked the rows, straightening elbows, tightening straps against the cold.
Halfway through the forms, a cub with frost on her whiskers raised her wooden claw.
"Instructor... Is it true the human cubs over the border get hammers and letters instead of drills? I don't want to become a soldier... I also want to create-"
"Silence. The Confederation needs you strong, not creative."
The torches burned down. The forms went on.
Fifty-three floors beneath Aldoria, Iris Ravenclaw fought alone, and finally, the labyrinth was paying its debts.
She had asked the Venomborne Terror for her chambers solo, and got them without issue.
Black Fang understood the desire to stand tall alone.
Down here the monsters hit hard enough to matter, hard enough to feed the pain-forged furnace of her class.

A Bonehide Ogre's club caught her shoulder and opened it to the bone, its roar rattling the chamber. The pain went white and enormous behind her eyes, then folded down into her palm as power she could spend.
She drove it back out through the ogre's skull, bonehide caving under a blow that had not existed a second earlier.
She straightened, breathing hard, red eyes bright in the blue gloom.
"I'm becoming strong," she realized with a perfectly flat tone.

The deep scouts came home to the war-lodge fire after three days inside the Villain's borderlands, and the older of the two faced the great lords with the report gripped in both hands, visibly wishing it belonged to someone else.
"Speak," Gorruk rumbled.

"Great lords. The joint army trains on the old Vraven-Elvardia border, as reported before. We watched the war games for three days." He stopped. He started again. "I cannot tell you who the enemy was."
Skarn's growl rose. "You watched three days and cannot name the enemy?"

"Nobody can, great lord! The first day, the summons held a fortress and all three races stormed it together. The second day, the dwarves held a valley beside the elves, against the humans and the summons, the same legions everyone had stormed together the day before."
His grip tightened on the report until the page buckled.

"The third day they played escort, a queen's carriage crossing open ground, and by dawn the sides had shuffled again. They are not training against an enemy, great lords. They are training against... against all of it. Every war at once, while strictly documenting the strengths and weaknesses of each setup."
The fire cracked.
The fortress had not existed at sunrise.
Quinlan Elysiar had walked out onto the frozen plain of the old border with his hands in his pockets, and the ground had simply obeyed him.

Stone groaned up out of the earth in ring after ring, ramparts shouldering aside the snow, towers rising like things grown, magma veins glowing along the wall seams before cooling into black iron-hard mortar.
By noon, assisted by the deployment of dwarven reinforcing artifacts, a fortress worthy of a hundred-year siege stood on the plain, steaming in the cold.
By early afternoon, half the joint army was inside it, and the other half had been ordered to take it from them.
*BOOM!*
Dwarven siege engines opened first. The lead boulder came in short and burst a stretch of the outer rampart into gravel. The third took the roof off a tower, and most of the tower after it.

Human assault columns ran the killing ground under tower-shield roofs. Where one of those boulders came down on a roof, the roof folded, and the column that was left stepped over the rest and kept running.

Elven volleys arced overhead, hundreds of light-arrows blazing against the winter sky and coming down inside the walls like falling stars. Where they landed the parapet went bright, and Elite Souls came apart mid-swing, blue-white fire scattering across the rampart.
The mixed garrison of all three races and a thousand Elite Souls answered with everything they had.

Ballistae punched clean through the shield roofs below. Oil came over the parapet in sheets and left the storming ladders steaming, and the dead worked the defense as tirelessly as they had stormed positions of their own on the other days.
"Ladders on the west wall!!" a human general bellowed from the command rise. "Where is my second wave?!"
"Your second wave is dying in my trench!" a dwarven general roared back, delighted. "Whose idea was the trench?! Say it louder!"
"The trench was the elf's idea!"
"Of course it was an elf's idea," an elven marshal said proudly, chin held high.
Nobody was in overall command.
Three nations' generals screamed at each other all afternoon, and doctrines collided like weather fronts.
The roaring machine worked anyway, simply because every soldier on that field knew whose idea the field itself was, and no one wanted to oppose their new tyrant.

High above the bombardment, the Primordial Villain stood in the air with his hands back in his pockets, watching his fortress get stormed, delighted that his sandcastle had started a war and that his soldiers were already showing promising signs of cooperating together properly.
At dusk the horns called it. The attackers owned the outer ring, the garrison owned the keep, and both sides claimed victory at increasing volume across the wreckage.
The fallen souls came apart into blue-white fire and drifted home to their master's saber, already reforming, ready to be dealt onto whichever side tomorrow's shuffle required.
Skarn walked the western wall alone that night.
Below him the drums kept their rhythm.
Sharpen, stockpile, drill.
Out on the pass road, the convoy's lanterns crawled away into the dark, one small light at a time, in no hurry at all.
His claws were printed deep in the palisade timber before he noticed he had gripped it.

The wolfkin lord stood there long after the last lantern was gone, hackles risen against an enemy the night refused to show him, and the only sounds were the drums, the wind, and his own people, watching.
The afternoon's dive ended with a warp gate opening on the cleared chamber floor and the family filing through it home, trading tallies of their XP gains.
Black Fang went last.
At the gate's edge she stopped and looked back down the corridor, toward the stairs that led deeper, a moment longer than any count required.
Then she stepped through, and the gate closed behind her.
