chapters.title: Chapter 1926 Princess Defense
paragraphs: Four weeks after the dwarven mountain fell, winter still owned the old Vraven-Elvardia border, and the fortress Quinlan Elysiar had pulled out of the frozen plain in a single day had stopped being a wonder and become a schedule.
Today's entry on that schedule was an escort.

A dwarven marshal read the rules out at dawn in a voice like a rockslide. The armies would move one person from the east gate to the western ridge by dusk, against the hunters already waiting on the field: the retired king, Morgana Ravenshade, and the Scarlet Lilies, hired for the afternoon.
If any hunter touched the person being escorted, every general on the escort had to analyze and submit a report on what went wrong and how they proposed to improve the current setup.
The person being escorted was Rosie Elysiar, sole living Princess of the budding empire, who was having the best day of her winter.

"Rosie thinks everyone looks very cool today! Almost one percent as cool as Rosie's Papa!" she told the human vanguard from the middle of a moving fortress of tower shields, waving at soldiers as though the formation were a parade organized slightly in her honor.
"...Princess, please keep your head down," a general begged.
"Okay! Rosie's head is down!"
It was not down.
The hunters started at noon.
Alexios Valorian came up out of a drainage ditch inside the escort's left flank and did not slow down.
"CONTACT LEFT!! IT'S THE KING!!"
A dwarven anchor squad locked a shield ring across his path. He walked through it without changing stride, and the ring came apart into dwarves.
"HE'S THROUGH!! SECOND WALL!! SECOND WALL!!"
It was too late.
Forty paces on, the ground opened under him. The dwarves had dug a pit across the lane that morning and roofed it over with dirt. They knocked the props out as he crossed.
Alexios landed on a falling rubble midair and used it to jump out before properly landing in the trap.
"A nice attempt," he told them.
Then he killed all of them.
"Why is everyone lying down?!" Rosie asked her general, up on tiptoe to see behind the column.
"They got killed."
"Oh, no!!" Rosie yelped.
"...In game."
Obviously, the war games didn't go until death. Those who were 'killed' were to stop resisting and wait for the turn to be over.
"Phew!" Rosie wiped her brow.
Morgana came over from the far side, and the far side had been waiting for her. The Elemental Sovereign shouted a name and opened the first shield wall like a curtain.
The elven counter-volley arrived before she could shout a second, hundreds of light-arrows on a flat arc, and her staff came up to answer them instead of the road ahead.
While she burned the sky clean, a human flex company rotated a fresh wall into the gap she had just made, and dwarven crews re-staked the lane behind it.
She made three walls into kindling and got no closer to the princess than the length of a market street.
"You cannot win," Morgana informed the fourth wall.
"We know, my lady!" a voice called back from inside it, muffled and cheerful. "But we only have to slow you down!"
The Scarlet Lilies attacked as a unit, on the theory that four centuries of teamwork beat any doctrine a committee had invented.
They were nearly right. Bronnya went through the first wall laughing and wore half of the second as a collar. "BAHAHA! Boss! They've stopped breaking!!"
"I noticed!!" Lilith was carving through her third shield rotation with what sounded suspiciously like joy. "Void! VOID! Do your thing!"

Void, asleep on Bronnya's back through the entire charge, opened her eyes. She took in the four fresh walls standing between the squad and the princess, the two ballista crews tracking her specifically, and the sliver of sun left on the ridge.
"No," Void murmured, and went back to sleep where she hung.
"What do you mean no?!"
"I don't want to be against Scar ever again... I don't like this game..."
The horns called it at dusk.
Rosie crossed the western ridge untouched, then went back down the line and thanked her escort personally, which took until full dark, because she meant it literally.
The generals' argument started before the horn echoes died.
"The dwarven line held them longest! Write that down!"
"Your line held because our volleys kept closing your gaps!"
"And who filled every hole they tore? Humans! With their bodies!"

Alexios worked a dent out of his vambrace in the falling dark, grinning. He might've found his new overlord infuriating on a personal level, but being given the task of acting as a high-level hostile against the armies was a role he played with a joyous heart.
Both he and Quinlan wanted an army that could do more than just face the enemy's fodder.
The portals opened at full dark, one to a province, and the armies went home through them in the order they had marched out.
The dead went last, because the living kept stopping them to say things.
"Same wall tomorrow, yeah?"
"Same wall."
They stepped through to New Whisperfield.
The lamps were coming on and the streets were warm underfoot, because Jasmine Argentis had her towns piped full of the earth's own deep heat and considered frozen cobblestones a personal insult.
Marlen walked home through the lamplight with the exercise's dust still on his boots.
He was a human spearman of middling height and unremarkable face, and he had died on Whisperfield's wall, killed by the man who now held his soul.
These days a faint blue-white light came off him at the edges, like breath in the cold. The neighbors had stopped noticing it.
"Marlen!" Petyr leaned out of the tavern doorway across the lane and flipped a coin at him. "Here's a silver."
Marlen caught it. "Three silver left."
"...You really could've forgiven my debts after your rebirth. Shouldn't they have died with you?"
"Nope," Marlen grinned and received an onslaught of grumbling.
The door of the third house on the lane banged open before he touched the latch, and his daughter hit him at the knees.
"Daddy!"
"Father! You're back!"
His son arrived a breath later at a full sprint and got an arm around his neck, and Marlen carried them both inside at once, wearing children instead of armor.
"You're late," Wenna said from the stove, in the tone that meant the opposite.

"The retired king walked through our entire shield line like weather," Marlen said, setting the little one on a chair. "Twice. We drilled the counter-form after. I'll show you, Tam, hand me the broom."
Dinner was loud. The broom became a spear, the spear became a lesson, the lesson collapsed when the little one commandeered the broom and declared herself the retired king.
Wenna laughed until she had to sit down, and the stew nearly burned. Nobody in that kitchen would have traded the noise for a quiet house in paradise.
Marlen sat back and watched them, and the light at his edges dimmed to nothing.
He had died at the wall in the rain, and most men who die get one ending and keep it.

What he had instead was the stew and the shrieking, a friend paying down four silver one coin a year out of pure stubbornness, a wife who had buried him and then answered a knock one evening to find the burial canceled.
His boy was taller than the last mark on the doorframe. He would be there to cut the next mark too.
"You're staring again," Wenna said softly.
"I'm counting what I get to keep," Marlen said. "The count keeps going up."
She kissed the top of his head on her way past. Her eyes were wet.
Neither of them mentioned it.
When the children were asleep he stood at their door a while, then kissed his wife at the threshold.

All along the lane, in the hour after the lamps went out, the dead of New Whisperfield left their houses quietly and walked toward the muster square together, where the Necromancer would arrive and portal them to the labyrinths.
That was, in every way that mattered, exactly what it was: a night shift.
Six weeks after the mountain fell, the snow on the Confederation's watch-ridges had gone rotten underfoot, and the war-lodge fire had a problem it could not burn.

sentences.text: Four weeks after the dwarven mountain fell, winter still owned the old Vraven-Elvardia border, and the fortress Quinlan Elysiar had pulled out of the frozen plain in a single day had stopped being a wonder and become a schedule.
Today's entry on that schedule was an escort.
A dwarven marshal read the rules out at dawn in a voice like a rockslide.

The armies would move one person from the east gate to the western ridge by dusk, against the hunters already waiting on the field: the retired king, Morgana Ravenshade, and the Scarlet Lilies, hired for the afternoon.
If any hunter touched the person being escorted, every general on the escort had to analyze and submit a report on what went wrong and how they proposed to improve the current setup.
The person being escorted was Rosie Elysiar, sole living Princess of the budding empire, who was having the best day of her winter.
"Rosie thinks everyone looks very cool today!

Almost one percent as cool as Rosie's Papa!" she told the human vanguard from the middle of a moving fortress of tower shields, waving at soldiers as though the formation were a parade organized slightly in her honor.
"...Princess, please keep your head down," a general begged.
"Okay!
Rosie's head is down!"
It was not down.
The hunters started at noon.
Alexios Valorian came up out of a drainage ditch inside the escort's left flank and did not slow down.
"CONTACT LEFT!!
IT'S THE KING!!"
A dwarven anchor squad locked a shield ring across his path.
He walked through it without changing stride, and the ring came apart into dwarves.
"HE'S THROUGH!!
SECOND WALL!!
SECOND WALL!!"
It was too late.
Forty paces on, the ground opened under him.
The dwarves had dug a pit across the lane that morning and roofed it over with dirt.
They knocked the props out as he crossed.
Alexios landed on a falling rubble midair and used it to jump out before properly landing in the trap.
"A nice attempt," he told them.
Then he killed all of them.
"Why is everyone lying down?!" Rosie asked her general, up on tiptoe to see behind the column.
"They got killed."
"Oh, no!!" Rosie yelped.
"...In game."
Obviously, the war games didn't go until death.
Those who were 'killed' were to stop resisting and wait for the turn to be over.
"Phew!" Rosie wiped her brow.
Morgana came over from the far side, and the far side had been waiting for her.
The Elemental Sovereign shouted a name and opened the first shield wall like a curtain.
The elven counter-volley arrived before she could shout a second, hundreds of light-arrows on a flat arc, and her staff came up to answer them instead of the road ahead.
While she burned the sky clean, a human flex company rotated a fresh wall into the gap she had just made, and dwarven crews re-staked the lane behind it.
She made three walls into kindling and got no closer to the princess than the length of a market street.
"You cannot win," Morgana informed the fourth wall.
"We know, my lady!" a voice called back from inside it, muffled and cheerful.
"But we only have to slow you down!"
The Scarlet Lilies attacked as a unit, on the theory that four centuries of teamwork beat any doctrine a committee had invented.
They were nearly right.
Bronnya went through the first wall laughing and wore half of the second as a collar.
"BAHAHA!
Boss!
They've stopped breaking!!"
"I noticed!!" Lilith was carving through her third shield rotation with what sounded suspiciously like joy.
"Void!
VOID!
Do your thing!"
Void, asleep on Bronnya's back through the entire charge, opened her eyes.
She took in the four fresh walls standing between the squad and the princess, the two ballista crews tracking her specifically, and the sliver of sun left on the ridge.
"No," Void murmured, and went back to sleep where she hung.
"What do you mean no?!"
"I don't want to be against Scar ever again...
I don't like this game..."
The horns called it at dusk.
Rosie crossed the western ridge untouched, then went back down the line and thanked her escort personally, which took until full dark, because she meant it literally.
The generals' argument started before the horn echoes died.
"The dwarven line held them longest!
Write that down!"
"Your line held because our volleys kept closing your gaps!"
"And who filled every hole they tore?
Humans!
With their bodies!"
Alexios worked a dent out of his vambrace in the falling dark, grinning.
He might've found his new overlord infuriating on a personal level, but being given the task of acting as a high-level hostile against the armies was a role he played with a joyous heart.
Both he and Quinlan wanted an army that could do more than just face the enemy's fodder.
The portals opened at full dark, one to a province, and the armies went home through them in the order they had marched out.
The dead went last, because the living kept stopping them to say things.
"Same wall tomorrow, yeah?"
"Same wall."
They stepped through to New Whisperfield.
The lamps were coming on and the streets were warm underfoot, because Jasmine Argentis had her towns piped full of the earth's own deep heat and considered frozen cobblestones a personal insult.
Marlen walked home through the lamplight with the exercise's dust still on his boots.
He was a human spearman of middling height and unremarkable face, and he had died on Whisperfield's wall, killed by the man who now held his soul.
These days a faint blue-white light came off him at the edges, like breath in the cold.
The neighbors had stopped noticing it.
"Marlen!" Petyr leaned out of the tavern doorway across the lane and flipped a coin at him.
"Here's a silver."
Marlen caught it.
"Three silver left."
"...You really could've forgiven my debts after your rebirth.
Shouldn't they have died with you?"
"Nope," Marlen grinned and received an onslaught of grumbling.

chapters.title: Chapter 1927 Iskaris Agricultural Development Program
paragraphs: The problem was a letter.

The old invitation the dwarven herald had left at the western gate weeks ago still sat on the stones of the fire circle where Skarn had thrown it, unopened, unburned, read by every soul who passed close enough to see the wax.
That morning, the same herald had knocked at the same gate and left a second one, and the second one had a date on it.

"By grace of the peoples of Iskaris," Vargis recited from his bench, the new letter open in his hands. "We invite the honored Beastman Confederation to the unveiling of the Iskaris Agricultural Development Program, a development we believe will shape the future of our continent."
He read the rest to himself, then aloud. "A delegation of any size. Three days hence, on the old border." He lowered the page and took up his whetstone. "It carries the seals of three rulers."
"It's bait," Skarn growled from the palisade stairs. "You do not walk into a predator's den because the predator holds the door open for you."
"We are predators too," Rajah murmured.
Under the argument, steady as rain, ran the sound that had run under every council since the mobilization began: Vargis Ironfang's whetstone, circling the edge of his great war axe.
The whetstone stopped.
Heads turned at the silence before they turned toward the sound of the dogkin lord standing up. Vargis folded the invitation and put it inside his coat.
"I have sharpened this axe enough. Before I swing it, I will see what it is meant to cut. I invite you three to do the same."
Nobody spoke. Outside the palisade, the drums went on keeping their rhythm for a war nobody in that circle had named in weeks.
"The letter says any size," Vargis added, already turning. "I am merely one man."
"...Then I am two." Gorruk, lord of the bearkin, set down his slates and rose to his full mountain of height beside him. "Four eyes read a den better than a written report."
"Ah, damn it all." Rajah poured himself off his bench and stretched until his spine crackled. "Someone must count their soldiers while you two count granaries."
Skarn dropped off the stairs with his hackles up. "Have you all gone mad?! The council of the Confederation does not deliver itself to the enemy in one basket!"
"Then stay," Gorruk said.
"Hold the walls, mighty wolf," Rajah purred.
The wolfkin lord held rigid, and everyone at that fire watched the two things he could not survive fight it out on his face: walking onto the Villain's ground, and letting other eyes see it first.
"I trust no eyes but my own," Skarn snarled at last. "The watch doubles while we are gone. Every den stays woken."
"And each den sends at least one of its young with us," Gorruk added, "so the Confederation cannot call four old men liars when we return."

On the appointed morning the four great lords of the Beastman Confederation walked the western pass together, a dozen young of the dens at their backs, and the drums kept their rhythm behind them until the border took the sound away.
On the empire's side of the pass, the road was waiting for them.

Rosie Elysiar's living root ran beside the pass road all the way down the valley, thick as a rampart, and when the delegation stepped onto the trade path the root's back rose gently under their boots and began to move.
"The enemy is carrying us," Skarn said through his teeth, standing absolutely still on wood that would not stop being helpful.
"Try to enjoy it," Rajah murmured, already sprawled across the moving timber like furniture. "Your dignity can only take so much."
The young of the dens listened to the tiger lord and abandoned dignity inside the first mile. By the second they were racing each other up and down the root's spine.
At midday the road dropped out of the pass, and the letter's promise stood waiting in a valley the scouts' reports had described and entirely failed to convey.
The empire had chosen its ground with intent.

These were the dead fields of the old Vraven-Elvardia border, land an older war's battle-magic had salted gray three centuries ago, so famously ruined that both kingdoms had simply drawn their maps around it.
Nothing had grown here since.

Today, across the nearest of those dead fields, rose a platform hung with the banners of three peoples, and around it a crowd big enough to garrison a fortress: farmers in their thousands, smiths, white-robed elven maidens, noble delegations under every seal in Vraven, and children everywhere underfoot.
And at the very back of the crowd, where nobody important stands, Skarn found the Villain.
Quinlan Elysiar stood among ordinary farming families, his women around him, his arms lazily crossed around two thin waists, watching the platform like any other spectator.
He had brought no throne, no honor guard, and no stage.

Skarn's hackles rose and stayed risen. The most dangerous creature alive was thirty paces away, unarmored, and paying the four great lords of the Beastman Confederation no attention whatsoever, because today, apparently, belonged to a plow.

Jasmine Argentis waited on the platform in governor's white, with the rulers of three peoples filling the row beside her: Queen Felicity of Vraven, chin high, taking the occasion very seriously; her father the retired king one step behind her; Governor Myrasyn of Elysaria, who had signed the empire's grain pledge that morning.

At the row's far end waited Isveth, at the head of her white-robed maidens, with Brokk of the Royal Smithy beside her in the only formal coat she owned, counting the minutes until she could take it off.
When Jasmine raised one hand, the crowd noise fell away.

"Three races built what you are about to see, so it carries all their names at once: the Iskaris Agricultural Development Program." The Tyrant of Commerce let the name settle over the valley. "Dwarven runecraft. Elven growth-song. Human alchemy and hands. Today they go into one harness for the first time, and here is what it means for you."
She counted it off the way she counted coin, one finger at a time.

"Your soil grows richer every season instead of poorer. Your harvest stops being a hostage of the weather. One field feeds what two fed before, and the surplus sells at a fair price, because the royal granary pledges to buy it all."
The farmers' side of the crowd had gone very quiet, in the manner of people afraid to believe something out loud.

"And while the fields learn to need fewer backs," Jasmine went on, "the Youth Program teaches your children letters, numbers, and craft. Your daughter will work a field because she chose it, if she chose it. That is the Program."
"Letters?!" a man repeated to the person beside him, checking that he had heard it right. "That's a noble's privilege..."
"Girls too?"
"For everyone's," his neighbor said. "She said everyone's."
She did not open it alone. A charter board came up onto the platform on the shoulders of four apprentices, and the rulers put their marks on it one after another in front of the whole valley.

Felicity signed with her entire arm. Myrasyn added the elven seal beneath hers, and Isveth pressed her palm into the wax rather than take a pen to it. Brokk cut her hammer-mark into the board with a knife and handed the knife back, unrepentant.
"Now then," Jasmine smiled. "Miss Alchemist."

Aurora Lorien knelt at the edge of a strip of field that had been dead for three hundred years. Her parents flanked her, and between the three of them stood a row of casks that had taken the House of Lorien six weeks of very loud joy to brew.
"Soil restoration tincture," the alchemist told the valley. She had tested it two hundred times. "One cask wakes forty paces of dead earth. We can brew thousands."
She broke the first cask's seal and poured, working down the strip.
Where the tincture soaked in, the frost line retreated and the gray dirt darkened, until the strip of murdered field lay black and rich, steaming gently in the winter air.
The valley went silent.
"That ground's been dead since my grandfather's grandfather," a voice said somewhere in the press, unsteady. "That's cursed ground. Everyone knows it's cursed ground."
An old human farmer ducked the rope line before anyone could stop him, knelt at the strip's edge, and worked the new loam through his fists.
"It's warm," he called back, and his voice cracked through the middle of it. "The dirt's warm! It smells like planting week!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1928 The Gap Widens
paragraphs: The roar started at the rope line and rolled the whole length of the valley.

"Note the color!" Gideon Lorien lectured the front row, which contained a queen. "Verdanal chased this seven thousand years ago and got mud! My daughter got soil you could grow a ship's mast in! Of course, she was already brilliant at six, there was the time she transmuted my-"
"Dad!"
"Dear," Naomi smiled and planted an elbow in her husband's side.
"Ah. Got carried away," Gideon wheezed through gritted teeth.
Down on the new loam, Kaelira had the plow teams lined up, and there was no shy elf anywhere in her.
"First team, walk it in," the Runeweaver Titan called down the row, sleeves rolled in the cold.
The enchanted plow parted half-frozen earth like a keel through still water, and the furrow it left glowed faintly along its edges before the glow sank in and faded.
"No oxen," a farmwife at the rope said, to nobody, to everybody. "It's cutting frozen ground and there's no oxen."
"What does one cost?!" a man shouted toward the platform, and the crowd laughed, then hushed itself, because it wanted the answer too.

"The state will fund every registered farmland with one over the coming months," Jasmine called back without missing a beat. "And if you desire to buy more, they will cost less than a season of ox-feed."
Multiple seasoned farmers could be seen falling unconscious, only to be caught by their teary wives and children.
The men who went down were thinking the same thing: a nation that had finally treated them better than the lowest rung of society, a nation already investing in their future.
Although Quinlan said nothing the entire time, dozens of gazes aimed at him with overwhelming gratitude.
Half the teams on that strip were dwarves, who had come down out of the mountain to watch the thing work and pushed it themselves inside an hour, sleeves rolled like Kaelira's.

When a rune stuttered on the third plow, Kaelira was in the dirt at the coulter before anyone called for her, redrawing the line freehand with one finger, apologizing for the delay the whole time she did it. "It's still a work-in-progress prototype!!" she promised the audience.
Behind the plows came Isveth's maidens, palms open over the turned earth, singing the growth blessing.
"The Holy Son wills a garden of this world," one of them whispered under her breath.
And in the middle of all of it, unguarded and unescorted, stood the four great lords of the Beastman Confederation.
Gorruk was running sums under his breath, slow and thorough: paces of dead field to casks, casks to seasons, seasons to grain in a storehouse.
He reached a total, stopped, and started the count over, because the total could not be right.
It came out the same.
"Say it," Rajah murmured.
"Their worst valley will out-yield our best land by first harvest," the bearkin lord rumbled, quiet enough that only the lords heard it. "And they will have a hundred valleys."

Rajah looked down the white trade road toward the pass, at the wagon queues already forming to carry the Program to provinces that were not his, and for once the tigerkin lord found nothing playful to lay on top of anything.
Skarn hunted the crowd one more time for the trap.
He counted soldiers and found vendors. He counted watchers and found none, because nobody in that valley was tracking the enemy council standing in the open on imperial ground.
He found farmers weeping over dirt instead, and a villain at the back of his own festival, laughing about something with his girls, letting his people hold the stage.
The first furrow reached the strip's end. The crowd's roar hit the ridge lines and came back down like a landslide.

"The Program is officially open! Register your farms at your local administrative hubs and you will join the waiting list," Jasmine called over it, grinning, and threw her arm toward the field's edge, where trestle tables ran longer than the furrow itself.
"Now, then. Three nations cooked for their farmers today. Eat well, dance, and go home ready for the greatest spring of your lives!"
The crowd did not need telling twice.
Somewhere between the platform and the tables, farmers who had never spoken to a dwarf in their lives were toasting the mountain.
An old man kept telling anyone who would listen that the dirt was warm, that his grandson would read, and that he had lived to see both.
They were given no minders, so the lords went four separate ways into the festival.
Gorruk walked the model farmstead the Program had raised beside the field: granary, stables, workers' quarters. He read the frames like border slates, joint by joint, to the end.
Behind them stood a children's house for the farmhands' families, first of its kind outside the capital. He went in and counted the beds twice.

Rajah found a skewer stall. He ordered by pointing, paid double out of pure suspicion, and ate the best thing he had tasted all winter standing up, furious about every bite. He went back for a second one.
"Cold out, my lord?" the human vendor asked the tigerkin lord of the Beastman Confederation, conversationally, entirely unafraid. "The dwarves built the braziers. Stand closer if you like."
Vargis leaned on the fence of the children's row, watching dwarven masters walk human children down a beam on miniature scaffolds, when the crowd behind him produced his daughter.
Kitsara arrived already mid-hug, five tails everywhere, cheek against his chest plate.
"You came!!"
"Daughter." The dogkin closed one arm around the foxkin and held on, and his war-council face lasted less than a breath.
"You look fed," he managed.
"I look radiant," she corrected into his chest. "Right?"
"Radiantly well fed."

She leaned back to inspect him, eyes bright. "That's right! Quinnie feeds- wait, no, allow me to change topic," the white-haired beauty realized it was best to keep her protein-rich diet hidden from her father. "Stubborn wolf let you come?"
"Nobody lets me do anything, girl." He glanced past her at the festival, at the children, at the plows, and took his time about the next one. "Are you happy?"

"Good."

"No."
"Eh?" Kitsara's eyes widened, taken aback.
"That's a close second. But the best decision was taking in a little foxkin all those decades ago."
"F-father!!" Kitsara laughed, hug tightening even further.

"Mister wolf. Are your ears soft like Miss Blossom's?"
Skarn bared his teeth on pure reflex, the display that made veteran soldiers step backward.
"Do it again!!" the girl demanded, delighted.

The young were louder.

The crews unloaded, stacked, checked every seal twice, bowed to the gate wardens, and rolled home into the dusk.
Then the road went empty.
No column crossed the next day.
None crossed the day after that.

"The bill is paid," the younger watcher said on the third empty evening. "This was supposed to bleed him, sir. A generation, they told us, that's what the council said, a whole generation of him paying us and he-" He lost the sentence and found a worse one. "He paid it early. And now he's stopped coming."
"He has."

The road is empty.

"What does one cost?!" a man shouted toward the platform, and the crowd laughed, then hushed itself, because it wanted the answer too.
"The state will fund every registered farmland with one over the coming months," Jasmine called back without missing a beat.

Multiple seasoned farmers could be seen falling unconscious, only to be caught by their teary wives and children.

Half the teams on that strip were dwarves, who had come down out of the mountain to watch the thing work and pushed it themselves inside an hour, sleeves rolled like Kaelira's.

chapters.title: Chapter 1929 Silent Conquest
paragraphs: Gorruk said them.
"I walked his granaries. I counted the beds in his children's house. I stood a day and a night in the open on his ground, the lord of an enemy nation, and no one so much as set a watcher on me."
The bearkin lord set the ridge report down on the stack with all the others.
"I have read enemies the whole of my long life. There is no war in that valley, and nothing in it that needs us beaten."

"And there is a market in it," Vargis sighed. "All the other peoples on this continent are already trading with each other under his watch. We are the only ones out here with our arms crossed, being proud at a wall nobody is coming to."
"We hold the walls," Skarn snarled, pacing the fire's edge. "We double the watch. We drill the dens, we stockpile, we..."
He heard himself.
The pacing stopped.

In front of the whole circle, in front of the soldiers along the palisade, the wolfkin lord ran out of sentence, and the drums outside filled the quiet where the rest of his argument should have been.
"...This is a mistake," Skarn said at last, without heat, which no one at that fire had ever heard from him.
"Name the better one," Gorruk rumbled.
Silence answered for everyone.
Then Skarn stood still in front of his own soldiers, and when he spoke again his voice came out level. The circle went stiller than any snarl had ever made it.
"Hear the shape of what was done to us."
He looked around the fire, lord to lord.
"He swore never to raise a claw against our people, and he kept it to the letter. He put schools where we put drills. He armored wagon drivers past our champions."
"He rebuilt our dead villages with his own coin, let our best eyes watch every hour of the work, and when there was nothing left to show us, he paid his bill and closed the road."
His claws flexed once against nothing.
"There was no siege, no ultimatum, and no enemy for a single horn to call. We mobilized our people, mounting a defense against invasion, but we hadn't realized that he was already attacking us."
"A conquest of politics," Rajah exhaled.
"There was no siege, no ultimatum, and no enemy for a single horn to call. We mobilized our people, mounting a defense against invasion, but we hadn't realized that he was already attacking us."
"A conquest of politics," Rajah exhaled.
They all knew what the Villain was: a cold-hearted killer just like them, a man driven by his selfish goals.
They assumed he was sending the reparations so diligently because he had to.
But he was showing off, telling them what they would miss should they resist him any longer, in a language only rulers understood.
"Kindness or conquest, it doesn't matter. The end result is the same. All that remains to decide is whether our pride keeps our children out of the world," Gorruk rumbled.
Vargis Ironfang had not touched his whetstone since the delegation returned. Now he looked into the fire and offered the council the only counsel he had given since the drums began.
"For the future of our people, I choose the cubs."
The fire cracked, and the sentence stood where he had put it.
"Then it is said." Gorruk rose to his feet, and the circle rose with him. "Send for him."
Quinlan Elysiar came on the first true morning of spring, with the pass streams running loud and the forests on the empire's side of the border already waking green.
He walked the pass road alone, hands at his sides, taking his time.

Halfway up, without breaking stride, Quinlan took a small crystal from his pocket: the Consortium's age-artifact, the same one that had read a certain nobody at seven weeks old back at the Phenom Trials.
He turned it over his knuckles once and let it taste his palm. The runes woke, circled, and settled on their answer.
[Age: 365 days]
'One year old finally, huh?'
Quinlan smiled at the crystal, pocketed it, and kept walking.
One horn note lifted off the western pass at midday.
The sentries had a call for a column and a call for danger, and the horn blew neither. It blew the single note that meant one traveler, walking.
Every claw the Confederation owned packed the western wall to watch him come. He nodded up at them as he climbed, to no one in particular, and the wall did not know what to do with it.
Skarn waited over the gate, looking down at him.
"Open the gate," Skarn said.

They received him at the fire circle, the four great lords on their own ground. Behind them the heartlands had emptied themselves into the compound: den upon den, ring upon ring, every soul the Confederation could gather standing silent in the spring dusk.
For the first time since the mountain fell, no drums were beating anywhere in the heartlands.
Gorruk spoke for the council, and the council had weighed every word.

"Quinlan Elysiar. The Beastman Confederation wishes to end the non-aggression pact and make an offer." The bearkin lord's rumble reached the last ring of the assembly. "We would enter your empire as its fourth people. Equal in standing to the humans, the dwarves, and the elves."
"Our dens keep their lands and their customs. Our young enter your programs. Our goods ride your roads."
"And we ask one oath in return," Vargis said from beside him. "That a beastkin cub in your empire stands wherever any other child stands. Swear that, and the Confederation is yours."
Quinlan stood at their fire and let the last free nation of Iskaris finish offering itself to him.

"I, Quinlan Elysiar, swear it on my life and all those I cherish. The beastkin people shall be equal to all other races inside the realm I govern, and any internal hand that treats yours as less shall answer for it. Any outside hand raised against your people will be treated as an attack on my person. This I promise."
Then Skarn came forward, the last argument the Confederation had ever owned, and stopped across the fire from the Villain.
"Before my people kneel to you, I will have one honesty." His hackles stood the length of his spine, and he made no attempt to smooth them.
"Say it plainly, Villain. Here, in front of my people. Give the thing that was done to us its true name."
The compound did not breathe.
Ring upon ring, cubs, mothers, and soldiers, an entire people waited on one man's answer.
The Primordial Villain smiled.
"Conquest."
The word went over the rings the way cold goes through wet fur.
Then Vargis Ironfang came forward.
The dogkin lord unslung the great war axe, looked down its edge once, and laid it flat on the bare trampled earth between himself and the Primordial Villain.
"The dogkin kneel to Quinlan Elysiar," he said, and went down on one knee, and a winter of carrying went out of his shoulders as he did.
Gorruk followed him down, mountain joints cracking, head bowed to the man across the fire.
"The bearkin kneel to Quinlan Elysiar."

"Ah, well." Rajah flowed onto one knee beside them, with a theatrical grace that fooled no one present. "The tigerkin kneel to Quinlan Elysiar. My people have always enjoyed a winning side. I have simply never stood on one this large."
Skarn stood alone, looking at the man who had answered him honestly.
The howl that had ridden his spine since the Villain's first step onto beastkin soil went still at last, as though it had never wanted anything else.
In the dens' oldest law, the law that sits under all the others, no wolf is shamed by lowering its head to the apex.
Pretending otherwise is what shames a predator, and Skarn was done pretending.
"The wolfkin kneel to Quinlan Elysiar," he said, and knelt to the Villain, last of the four, and his hackles, risen since the mobilization's first horn, finally lay down.
Ring by ring, the Beastman Confederation went down after its lords, to the man standing at their fire.
The sound that moved through the rings was the sound of a den after a storm passes over it.
The last free people of Iskaris had been conquered with granaries, schools, and one silent road, and not a single drop of their blood had paid for it.
"The pact between the Beastman Confederation and Quinlan Elysiar ends today," Gorruk said from his knee, formally, before all the dens. "By our own word. With no clause of it broken."

He felt it before he finished reading it.
The packed earth under his boots stopped being mere earth.
It was his now. He could tell it on an instinctual level.

The compound, the pass road behind him, the rebuilt villages of the old war with their square dwarven granaries, the fortress on the border plain, the labyrinth gates standing open in every city he owned, all of it arrived at once, pressing up through the soles of his feet like the floor of his own house.
Roads ran through him like veins. Cities sat in him like warmth. He could feel where his land ended at the coasts and the far passes.
And threaded through every mile of it, under the roads, the fields, and this very compound, ran his daughter.
Ever since her birth, Rosie had been busy expanding under all her cutesy behavior. Just like her father, she, too, was a conqueror.
Her roots lay under the whole continent now, a living lattice from coast to coast, and where they ran thickest the land felt awake in a way the rest of it did not.
'Someone has been quite the diligent little lady,' the Primordial Villain grinned inwardly.
The window was not finished with him.
[A prior claim exists over this land.]
[The prior claim has been contested and defeated.]
[Domain Protection: 24:00:00]
The last two digits rolled over to 59 while he watched.
[Once Domain Protection ends, more information will be relayed and the Suppression will end.]
'Okay,' Quinlan thought. 'Things just got serious.'
He knew as much about the prior claim as anyone alive did, which was close to nothing.
Archduke Vasilen had called it the Suppression as well. He had watched it cripple almost everyone above the seventy-fourth level on the day it first came down.
Chizuru's clan had spent numerous generations trying to bring it down, and the old woman was still afraid of whatever waited on its far side.
Every soul on Iskaris knew it as the Heavenly Restriction, the ceiling nobody had ever climbed past, and nobody in living memory had known who laid it or why.
The window had just called it a claim. Somebody's claim.
The worries came in order, because that was how his mind worked.

Would the far side feel it go, be notified by the system itself, or would the barrier come down quietly? If it went loud, whoever laid it would know within the hour that a land on their map had stopped answering.
He remembered the look the Archduke had given him, the one reserved for mud tracked into a clean parlor. That had been an outsider's honest opinion of Iskaris's strongest.

If whoever laid that barrier sent an army through the hole tomorrow, level two hundreds if such a thing existed on the far side of it, then the fortress, the Program, the mountain, the roads, all of it got left behind.
He would gate his family out of a burning continent with whatever they could carry, and their hard work would be destroyed.
Twenty-three hours and fifty-nine minutes.
The four great lords were watching him.
Skarn had come up off his knee first, because of course he had. The wolfkin lord stood with his hackles half-risen, staring at the Villain's face while the Villain stared at empty air.
"Something changed-" the wolf lord began, but was interrupted because, from one moment to the next, the sky lit up.
Heat rolled over the palisade on a wind that had blown from the north all day and now came from the west. The fire circle leaned away from it as one body.
Beneath his skin the whole continent pulled toward one point like a tide going out, every road and every field of it dragging the same way, and he knew the point before he turned.
The target was his stronghold, his home.
It was exclusively her.
Far to the west, past the border plain and every mile of empire between, a pillar of white-green light stood up off the horizon and climbed.
The tree in his garden had woken the moment the land became his, and this was what that looked like from a thousand miles away.

It rose straight, clean, and impossibly wide, taller than the mountains between them. The underside of every cloud from the north to the south, east to west of the continent, turned the color of new leaves.
Every pair of eyes the continent owned turned to look at it.
"What is that?!"
Skarn's roar cracked across the compound, and for once there was nothing in it but the thing he had spent his life refusing to admit to. The unknown was standing on his horizon.
Rajah was on his feet with his claws out.
Gorruk had risen to his full height without a word and stood with one palm spread flat against the nearest palisade post, as if the timber might tell him what his eyes could not.
Along the palisade soldiers had their weapons half-drawn against a light no blade could reach.
Only Vargis Ironfang stayed on one knee, and the dogkin lord was looking at the Villain's face instead of the sky.
"My daughter is showing off," Quinlan grinned.

Through the land under his boots he felt every branch of Rosie's crown lift at once, as if the tree had drawn a breath, and they were still lifting, bending upward past the angle wood could bend, feeling along the empty sky like a hundred thousand green tentacles on the hunt.
They touched it.
There was nothing up there.

There had never been anything up there that any eye could see, only the ceiling every child on Iskaris learned about before it learned to count, the invisible wall that forbade them from ever leaving the continent.
Rosie's branches found it.
Where each tip pressed upward, the air dimpled like water taking a fingertip, and held.
Ten thousand dimples.
A hundred thousand.

chapters.title: Chapter 1931 The Eternal Tree's Declaration
paragraphs: The empty sky over the estate puckered in a vast slow field of ripples, one for every branch, and the branches pushed through.
At the beastkin fire, a thousand miles east, the clouds over the compound rippled in the same rhythm.
"The sky," a cub's voice said somewhere behind the woodpile. "Instructor, the sky is moving."
His daughter began to drink.

The pillar on the horizon went from white-green to white. Heat rolled over the palisade a second time, hard enough to flatten the war-lodge fire sideways and send sparks streaming east across the compound.
Under Quinlan's boots the ground began to hum, a note too low to hear that came up through his heels and sat in his teeth.
Blue script bloomed beside the counter.
[The Eternal Tree is draining the local reserve.]
Whatever held that counter up was drawn from the same well she had her mouth on, and every swallow she took came out of his day.
The counter was moving.
[Domain Protection: 21:40:12]
'...' Quinlan had a wry smile on his face as he watched.

He trusted his daughter greatly. But that counter was the only thing standing between his continent and whatever had laid the ceiling. Watching her drink it out from under him turned his stomach over.

For perhaps thirty heartbeats he had held the counter in the corner of his eye, and it had lost two hours. While he watched, the minutes began to fall faster than minutes should, the tens digit ticking down like seconds.
'Fine... If you're so hungry, Daughter...'
'Then take it all. Consume to your heart's content.'
On the horizon, the light climbed.

It had been a pillar. Now it had a shape at the top, a spreading darkness inside the glare that widened as he watched, and he understood that he was looking at a crown of branches from all these miles away.
The tide he had felt at the first flare never turned back.

It became a current he could follow with his eyes, mana coming off the whole sky in long bright ribbons, bending down out of empty air toward one point on the horizon and going into it the way water goes down a drain with no bottom.
Where a ribbon passed low enough to catch the ground, the grass under it silvered and stood up.

The top of his daughter's tree cleared the mountains between them. It kept going. He watched the crown put on a mile the way an ordinary tree puts on a season, and then another mile, branches unrolling out of the glare faster than his eye could hold them, until the shadow of it walked east across the border plain.

By the time the counter read ten hours, the tree stood higher than the mountain the dwarves lived inside. By the time it read six, its shadow lay across three provinces, and the sun had gone green over half his empire.
Gorruk's voice crossed the fire like a rockfall. "Villain. What is your daughter doing to the sky?"
"That's a very good question," Quinlan said.

Under his boots the humming stopped. For one held breath the compound stood still, the fire straight again, the wind dead, a hundred thousand beastkin holding their claws and their tongues under a green sun.
Then every root under the continent flexed at once.
The drill field behind the western wall heaved like a blanket being shaken out, and the cubs' class went down in a heap of wooden claws.

The palisade timber, a thousand years dead and sun-bleached gray, put out leaves along its whole length in the space of a heartbeat, and the soldiers standing on it grabbed for a rail that was suddenly in bud.
Spring hit the compound hard enough to make eyes water: wet earth, green sap, and blossom together, a season arriving in one breath.
West, the root road down the pass valley flowered from end to end.
Her voice came up out of the ground.

It came out of the ground under the beastkin fire and out of the ground under Aldoria's market square. It came out of the mountain's forge floor, the capital's cobbles, and the dead fields of the old border that had learned to be soil again.
Every road on Iskaris spoke in the same clear child's voice, solemn as a proclamation, and every soul heard it in the same moment.
"The Eternal Tree claims the Continent of Iskaris, and the Eternal Tree bows to the Primordial Villain."
The cubs on the drill field lifted their heads out of the heap.
"The Eternal Tree thus solemnly vows her eternal loyalty to Quinlan Elysiar."
The tree's light on the western horizon flared once, so bright that every claw on the palisade threw its shadow the length of the compound, and held.
Then, her girlish tone returning, "That's all!!"
[Domain Protection: 00:00:00]
[The prior claim over Iskaris has dissolved.]
[Ding!]
[The Eternal Tree has blessed your domain.]

[Blessing of the Eternal Tree: the Suppression stands until the sovereign wills it broken. He may shatter it at will within the next 24 hours. Once he does, or the time runs out, the Eternal Tree will raise a barrier of her own in its place, ensuring that the prior claimant perceives its claim intact.]
He read it to the end.
Then he read the last line again, and the smile that spread across the Primordial Villain's face was the one his enemies had learned to dread and his women had learned to adore.
The wall would come down when he said so, and the world would not know.
"Daughter... you're far too amazing," he spoke under his breath, and from beneath his feet, soft giggling sounded.
"Hehe! Come home, Papa. Everyone's waiting!"
Quinlan settled things with the beastkin lords in short order and stepped through his portal.
Grass came up under his boots, and Quinlan Elysiar walked out of the gate into the shadow of a mountain.

chapters.title: Chapter 1932 Embarrassed Girl
paragraphs: The tree that had shaded half the grounds by winter was gone. In its place stood a trunk wider than the main house, silver-green bark rising out of the garden without a single branch for what looked like a mile, and a canopy above that was weather.
The green cast that had ridden the daylight while she drank was already fading, and under a crown standing miles above the roofline, ordinary warm sunlight came down on the garden as it always had.
On the terrace the maids stood in a line with their faces turned up, each of them still holding whatever she had been carrying when the light came.
At the trunk, five of the household's elves were moving around frantically, awed but concerned, checking if their little lady was still as healthy as before she decided to grow a few miles in height.
"Jasmine is waiting for you!" Rosie's voice came again, though the little lady herself was nowhere to be seen.
Jasmine Argentis had asked for the Bloodfather ribbon yesterday, and she had asked him to conquer the continent for her by the time she awoke.
She wanted their nation to finally have a name, which she knew he'd only give once all four races were his, so she decided to go unconscious until he did so.
He had grinned at his woman's audacity, and he had seen straight through it.
The bravery was a facade. She did not want him sitting on his thumbs watching her, afraid she would take far longer than the other girls, because she still thought herself the weakest of them.
Knowing all of it, he had bled for her as he had bled for his other women on the moss before.

The ribbon had struck her sternum, and she had gone down on the boards with her ponytail still in its working knot. Since then the restructuring had held her under, carving the mark through her one line at a time.
As tasked, he had left her in it with his girls staying by her side.
He stepped into a room that housed all his women, sitting or standing around the bed in which Jasmine lay.
But before he could take a proper look, a timid little voice sounded.
"...Papa."
The voice was hers, but smaller than he had ever heard it.
Blossom sat on the floor by the bed, and behind the dogkin, mostly hidden, a girl was peeking out at him with one eye.
"Rosie has nothing to fear!!" Blossom decreed.
"B-but Blossom Mommy...!" Rosie whined. "Rosie is different now... She changed..."
"Let me see," Quinlan asked.
The big eyes aimed at him widened and blinked. Then, after a deep breath, the little lady steeled her heart.
She came out one careful step at a time, fingers knotted in the hem of her dress.
This morning his daughter had ridden on shoulders, a small green thing with tiny legs and a voice too big for her.
The girl standing there was eight years old, long-legged, the baby roundness gone from her face and a princess left in it, her skin deepened from spring green to the green of a leaf in full summer.
"Rosie grew," she told the floor. "Rosie isn't little and cute anymore. Is Papa... mad?"
Quinlan crossed the room and picked his daughter up the same as he always had, and she had weight now, real weight, legs wrapping his ribs instead of his arm.
"Mad?" He looked her over once, slow, so she could see him do it. "My daughter conquered the sky before my very eyes. I have never been prouder in my life."
"...Really?"
"And you're still the cutest thing on this continent."
"!!" Rosie's face went through three expressions and landed on radiant.
"Rosie can still call Papa Daddy?"
"Even if you grow into a woman ten times my size, you'll still be my adorable little princess," Quinlan announced.
"Daddy!!!!!!!!!!" Rosie squealed and buried her face in his neck. The arms that squeezed him were long now, and strong.
Then the room turned to the bed.
"It started before dawn! It's been so slow, like a scribe copying..."
Gina Argentis spoke, a small woman with her daughter's blue eyes.
Jasmine lay on top of the covers in a thin shift with her hair down around her, damp at the temples, her lips parted.

Below her navel, where the shift lay flat, dark crimson script moved under her skin like ink poured into still water, line writing over line, sigil folding into sigil, faster than an eye could follow.
Seraphiel sat on the edge of the bed with one hand on the governor's brow, radiating irritation.
"Nothing to heal..." the healer said, before he could ask. "Rather, if I heal her, she'll fail."
"Hmm... she's taking her time, but it's not like she's been in a coma for days," Quinlan reasoned, seeing the worry in so many gazes aimed at him.
Then, as if Jasmine herself heard her family's worry, Quinlan felt it arrive abruptly.
Under his own skin the crimson lattice of the Bloodfather class had lit along his left arm and shoulder, pulsing toward the bed, the same visible pull it gave whenever one of his bonded drew on him.
"Speak of the devil. Here she comes," Quinlan smiled and gave as much as she needed.
"Jasmine, you can do it!" The cheerleading began, by none other than Vex. "Suck Hubby dry, I give you full permission. He's all yours today!"
"Fight, daughter!!" Gina joined, ignoring the Hexwitch's crude language. "Suck your man dry! He can take it!"
Or not.
"Go, Jas, go!" Serika joined, tanned muscles flexing in excitement.
"The Tyrant of Commerce is about to collect her dues..." Aurora grinned.
"Quin, brace yourself," Ayame purred. "She might present herself humble and innocent, but this girl might just be the greediest of us all~"
The pull on the lattice climbed until his whole forearm glowed through the sleeve, and Quinlan stood there and let his newest bonded take everything she reached for.
Then the drawing eased, gentle as a hand letting go, and the room hushed on its own.
The script under Jasmine's skin ran to the end of itself.
It stopped. The moving lines fixed all at once into a single sigil, crimson and clean, a coin's-edge circle full of interlocking script, and lay on her womb like a seal pressed into wax.
Jasmine opened her eyes.
They were blue. Then, for one blink, they were the bright unnatural gold of freshly minted coins, and then blue again, looking at her mother.

It's been so slow, like a scribe copying..."
Gina Argentis spoke, a small woman with her daughter's blue eyes.
Jasmine lay on top of the covers in a thin shift with her hair down around her, damp at the temples, her lips parted.

Below her navel, where the shift lay flat, dark crimson script moved under her skin like ink poured into still water, line writing over line, sigil folding into sigil, faster than an eye could follow.
Seraphiel sat on the edge of the bed with one hand on the governor's brow, radiating irritation.
"Nothing to heal..." the healer said, before he could ask.
"Rather, if I heal her, she'll fail."
"Hmm... she's taking her time, but it's not like she's been in a coma for days," Quinlan reasoned, seeing the worry in so many gazes aimed at him.
Then, as if Jasmine herself heard her family's worry, Quinlan felt it arrive abruptly.
Under his own skin the crimson lattice of the Bloodfather class had lit along his left arm and shoulder, pulsing toward the bed, the same visible pull it gave whenever one of his bonded drew on him.
"Speak of the devil.
Here she comes," Quinlan smiled and gave as much as she needed.
"Jasmine, you can do it!" The cheerleading began, by none other than Vex.
"Suck Hubby dry, I give you full permission.
He's all yours today!"
"Fight, daughter!!" Gina joined, ignoring the Hexwitch's crude language.
"Suck your man dry!
He can take it!"
Or not.
"Go, Jas, go!" Serika joined, tanned muscles flexing in excitement.
"The Tyrant of Commerce is about to collect her dues..." Aurora grinned.
"Quin, brace yourself," Ayame purred.
"She might present herself humble and innocent, but this girl might just be the greediest of us all~"
The pull on the lattice climbed until his whole forearm glowed through the sleeve, and Quinlan stood there and let his newest bonded take everything she reached for.
Then the drawing eased, gentle as a hand letting go, and the room hushed on its own.
The script under Jasmine's skin ran to the end of itself.
It stopped.
The moving lines fixed all at once into a single sigil, crimson and clean, a coin's-edge circle full of interlocking script, and lay on her womb like a seal pressed into wax.
Jasmine opened her eyes.
They were blue.
Then, for one blink, they were the bright unnatural gold of freshly minted coins, and then blue again, looking at her mother.

chapters.title: Chapter 1933 First Kneel
paragraphs: "...How long," the governor said. Her voice was hoarse.
"About sixteen hours, sweetheart." Gina's hand was on her cheek.
"Where's Quin?" She looked around, frantic. Then her eyes found the love of her life, and her worries eased. A brilliant, radiant expression welcomed his eyes.
"I did it!"
"You did," Quinlan spoke softly, and caressed her cheeks tenderly. "Are you feeling okay?"
"Yeah!" She grinned. Then her eyes narrowed. "What about your homework?"
"You may grade it."
"!!" Jasmine's eyes softened. "I will... but, for now..." Her arms opened toward him, expectant. "Just hug me!"
He did. Tightly, lovingly, for a good minute.
Then he spoke what was on all their minds. "Tell us."
Jasmine's hand went to the mark, softly caressing her womb.
Her eyes went unfocused for the length of a breath while the window opened in front of her.

"Bloodfather's mark, confirmed." She stopped, then went on, flat, the voice she kept for cargo manifests. "Class augmentation. Within the Bloodfather's domain, the realm's roads, records, and borders answer to your seal."
Nobody in the room said anything.
"That's it?" Kitsara asked. "That's the whole line?"
"That's the whole line," Jasmine agreed. Then the window scrolled under her eyes, and the governor's eyebrows climbed. "Oh. There's a second page~"
She read the second page in the same voice, and it thinned halfway through.

"The realm is the steward's labyrinth. The wealth and prosperity of the nation feed its steward. As the realm grows..." Her thumb stopped on the seal. "...so do I. I can enhance my summons, their variety, their numbers..."
Nobody said anything to that either.
"So you need to govern well and you're going to be bombarded with rewards..." Aurora mused at last. "You can grow strong at your desk."
"Guess so!" Jasmine beamed. "This ability fits me perfectly. I love it."
Then she went still, and this time it was not a window she was reading.
"...There are a couple heavy men on my road," she said slowly. "On the pass road, coming toward us."
Quinlan's mouth twitched. "The beastkin lords. I invited them over to Miri Town."
"You invited apex predators to my town," Jasmine said, "without informing me."
"You were asleep."
"That is not an excuse, my love."
She was reading it again, and her hand had found her mother's on the coverlet and closed around it without her noticing.
"I can feel the roads. The granaries. The whole realm, laid out like a page." Her mouth thinned. "The toll house on the Greenvale east road is skimming its own count."
Her focus came back, and it came back gold.
"Somebody find my seal," said the Tyrant of Commerce, from her sickbed, with her hair down. "I'll make an example out of those sons of bitches. No one gets away with robbing my family."
The silence that followed had a different quality than the one before it.
"...Damn. This girl is a badass," Lucille giggled.
"You're not a mere governor anymore," Vex whispered, thrilled.
"She became a magic landlord," Iris said flatly, from the wall.
"A tyrannical magic landlord~" Ayame corrected with a purr.
Serika's laugh came first and loudest. Lucille crossed to the bed and gathered the governor into her arms, and Jasmine let herself be gathered.
Over the Bloodmonger's shoulder she caught Quinlan's eye and mouthed "I love you."
Quinlan watched her for a good moment, full of affection.
Then he looked at them.
All of them. Every woman he had ever chosen, in one room, the last of them awake at last and already threatening a toll house.
Vex bouncing on her heels. Ayame at the bedpost with her chin up, eyes shining, and no intention of admitting it.
Kaelira was wedged in the doorway behind Serika with her sleeves still rolled from the forge.
Blossom sat on the floor by the bed with Rosie back in her lap and her tail going, Aurora leaned on the far bedpost with her result confirmed, and Lucille had her cheek on Jasmine's hair.
Iris had the wall.
They were all so happy.
The room was full to the walls with it.
And it was in this moment that Quinlan decided.
'Father... Mothers... It's time. Grant your son strength not to fumble his next words.'
"You've all knelt before me a lot," Quinlan began.
Everyone stopped.
Every woman in the room turned to look at him wearing the same expression, and Kitsara's tails, which had been waving, went entirely rigid.
"...Quinnie, what are you saying?" the foxkin shook her head, gravely disappointed. "Jas's mother is in the room."
"Don't mind little old me," said Gina Argentis, without looking up from her daughter's hand.
Quinlan's eyes never left his women. "You've all knelt before me a lot. But now, it's my turn."
The Primordial Villain stepped back from the bed, unhurried, until every woman who had chosen him stood in front of him at once. Then, before all of them, he went down on one knee.
The wry looks died.
"Wait," Serika said. "Wait, wait, wait-"
Vex's hands flew to her mouth. Sera grabbed Kaelira's arm without looking, and got grabbed right back. On the floor, Rosie went completely still, both eyes enormous.
Jasmine sat up off her pillows, hair down, lips parted, the freshly woken governor suddenly wide awake.
"In the world I came from," Quinlan said, "a man kneels once in his life, and only to the woman he means to keep forever."
He let that sit exactly one breath.
"I've knelt to no one in this world. I was saving it."
Somewhere by the pillow, someone made a sound like a kettle taken off the fire.
"I have thought of every one of you as my wife since the day you chose me."
"We are your wives, you dummy," Lucille said, laughing and wet-eyed in the same breath.
"No."
Ayame's voice came out level, and the room turned to her. The second-in-command stood parade-even to the last word. "We're not. We've only been his girlfriends."
"That's right," Quinlan smiled, remembering his samurai's words from long ago. Until he asked for her hand properly, she would not consider herself his wife.
It was time to correct what was wrong in this world.
"You're my partners for life. Our bond goes far beyond that of a traditional husband and his wives. But we're still making it official. The world's most precious existences deserve a ceremony."
He looked from face to face, taking his time with each of them, and when he spoke again, the grin was gone and what was under it had no armor at all.
"So I'm asking you properly." His eyes found Jasmine's, then Ayame's, then all of them.
"Will you become my empresses?"

chapters.title: Chapter 1934 Proposed
paragraphs: Quinlan Elysiar stayed on one knee on the boards of Jasmine's sickroom, and the question he had just asked hung over ten women.
Will you become my empresses?
For one full breath, the only sound in the room was Gina Argentis, who squealed into her daughter's hair.
Then Ayame stepped forward.
She came off the bedpost with eyes wide, body shaking.
"You asked properly," the samurai whispered in disbelief. "You actually asked. I thought you'd chicken out and just keep saying we were already your wives."
She crossed the last step between them, and both her hands came up.

Ayame drew his head against her womb, against the mark he had given her, and held it there. Her fingers slid into his hair and began to stroke, slow and gentle, as if he were the one who needed steadying.
She looked down at him with the tenderest smile he had ever seen on her face.
"I accept."
He closed his eyes against her and breathed out, and for a moment the Primordial Villain was only a man being held by the first woman who had ever chosen him.
Then the rest of the room went off at once.
"Hubbyyy!!" Vex was losing it.
All of them were.
"YES!!!!" A thumbs-up from Serika, green eyes wet.

"Blossom accepts!!" Blossom's tail was moving with such speed she nearly took off like a helicopter. Then she went down. Rosie caught her by the back of her dress, propped her against the bedframe, and stayed there until the dogkin's eyes opened again.
"Rosie can be an empress too?!"
"You're the princess," Quinlan told his daughter.
"...Rosie will allow it."

"I can already hear my new nickname... Slutty Empress..." Kitsara complained, all the while wiping her tears. Then she began pondering. "No, wait, is it Slutty Empress Foxy? I'm not the only slut in the gang, but I'm the only foxkin... Hmm..."
"Y-yes," Kaelira said to the doorframe, and went scarlet to the ears.
"Yes." Aurora paused, then began crying. "...Yes."
"I gotta tell Mom!!" yelped Seraphiel. Then her eyes narrowed. "I can't believe you started your proposal with a sex joke! Quin!!"
Lucille said nothing at all for a moment, touching her heart with both hands, and then laughed. "I was wrong. I do want a proper ceremony."
Jasmine came last, sitting up off her pillows with her hair down and her eyes still flickering between blue and gold.
"Yes, my love," said the Tyrant of Commerce. "Please treat me well!"
Quinlan rose to his feet, and the whole room rose with him.
"Then it's decided. The ceremony is tomorrow."
"Tomorrow?!"
Eleven voices. Gina's head came up out of her daughter's hair.
"Before Rosie's clock runs out," the Primordial Villain said, meaning the twenty-four hours left on his daughter's blessing.
Once the barrier was down, and it was possible to leave Iskaris, none of them would ever be this idle again. He knew the mood wouldn't be the same.
"It has to be now," he confirmed with a nod.
The panic began with Serika, which nobody would have predicted, least of all Serika.
"What does a bride wear?!"
She said it to the ceiling, both hands in her red hair, and the question went through the sickroom like a thrown chair.
"What does a bride do?" Kitsara demanded of the room in general. "Besides the obvious. I have the obvious covered."
"Is there a rite? Sera, is there an elven rite?!"
"Of course there's an elven rite! There's an elven rite for almost anything! But I never cared for them!!" Seraphiel had come off the bed with her hands up. "MOOOOOOOOOM! Help!!"
"Ah, she's a lost cause," Aurora decided. "Then who-"
Every head turned at once, and every head turned in the same direction.
Lucille had been a wife once. An innkeeper's, maybe, but it made her the only woman among the girls who had ever been anyone's wife at all.
"Why are you all looking at me?"
"You were married!"
"To an innkeeper! What I know is how to marry an innkeeper! Which is to sign the papers and be done with it!"
The Bloodmonger was mobbed regardless, and went down under Serika, Kitsara, and Vex in a heap on the rug, still explaining that she had never owned a dress worth the word.
Between them, the women in that room had been heirs, fugitives, slaves, and sovereigns.
Every one of those jobs had skipped the wedding. They had knelt kings and ended a dwarven throne, and, one innkeeper aside, none of them had ever once been asked to walk down anything.
"We need a list," Jasmine decreed, getting out of bed.
She counted on her fingers, and her voice got thinner with every finger. "Dress. Rings. Vows. Venue. Witnesses. Food. Music. Some kind of... officiant? We have none of those."
"We have food," Lucille said from under Kitsara.
"Rosie will grow flowers!!" Rosie had climbed onto the bed to be heard.
"Blossom will...!!" Blossom thought for a long second. "Blossom will look pretty in her dress!"
"There is no dress!"
"Blossom will look pretty in the absence of the dress!!"
"Use your head, dummy! Without a pretty dress we're just horny bitches in heat!" Kitsara screamed.
"Ahh!!" Blossom gasped. "Blossom needs a dress!"
Jasmine had gold already bleeding back into her eyes. Her mother took her by the shoulder and returned her to the pillows with the ease of long practice.
"Governor, you've been awake for a quarter of an hour."
"Mother, there are four apex predators on my road and a wedding in twenty-four hours and I have no quartermaster-"
"And no slippers."
"Hubby!" Vex surfaced from the pile on the rug. "Aren't you going to do something?!"
Quinlan stood at the foot of the bed, nonchalant, while the most dangerous women on the continent lost their minds over hemlines.
Then he grinned.
"I did do something."

Before the Hexwitch could ask what he meant, Black Fang stepped through the sickroom door and took the corner. The noise had carried the length of the house, and she had come to see what was breaking.

The Venomborne Terror stood with her back to the wall and her arms folded, violet eyes moving once across the wreckage of the room: the pile on the rug, the governor being held down by her mother, the dogkin and foxkin having a meltdown while a certain century-old woman cried for her mother.
Her gaze reached Quinlan last.
He looked back at her across the noise, and the look asked her the same thing he had just asked the rest of them.
'Wanna join the fun?'
"No," said Black Fang.
The grin that spread across the Primordial Villain's face was the same one he had worn reading the last line of his daughter's blessing.
"Challenge accepted. You may escape your fate today, but I'll put a ring on that finger of yours."
Black Fang gave that no answer.

But her eyes went down to her own left hand where it rested against her arm. They stayed there long enough that Ayame, watching from the edge of the pile, quit moving to watch her sister look at her fingers.
"I have my doubts," the Venomborne Terror finally replied, and took her eyes off her hand.
Quinlan's grin only got wider.
"Master!!"
Vex hit Black Fang at full speed.

paragraphs: The Hexwitch came out of the heap on the rug like a thrown blade, crossed the floor in two steps, and slammed into her mentor's chest hard enough to move anyone who was not Black Fang.

"You have to help me! Hubby just proposed to me!" the Hexwitch was about to explode with worry. "I must be perfect for him! What should I wear to bring out my best features, how should I behave to appear as ladylike as possible, is there a-"

"I have never attended a marriage..." Black Fang whispered, taken off guard by her disciple's expressiveness. Then, for correctness, the Venomborne Terror added, "Not without being there to kill someone."
Vex stopped. Then her whole face lit up.
"Perfect! Then you have experience!"
"...I can offer my opinion," Black Fang finally relented.
"!!!!!!!!" Vex beamed like the happiest woman ever.
Because that was exactly who she was in this moment.
"Will you walk me to the altar?" Vex decided to push her luck.
"..." Black Fang looked uncomfortable with the question. This was not her world one bit.
But staring at the woman's pleading gaze she had known since she was a ten-year-old farmer girl, she nodded. "Yes."
Vex hugged her so tight Black Fang felt proper strain in her bones. But she did not tell her to stop.
The estate came apart in the coming minutes, and the noise went with it.

Serika ran the east stair three times shouting a measurement she kept getting wrong. Rosie had flowers coming up through the floorboards of two corridors and a stairwell, already practicing her job as the flower girl.
Aurora had a sheet of paper, a working quill, and the only actual plan in the building.

"Okay girls, listen to me. We're doing fittings one at a time," she announced to the corridor. "Rosie stops growing things in the stairwell. Nobody asks Lucille another question until she has eaten something. And we will do it all efficiently, there's no time-"
The house ran past her in both directions.
Blossom had rushed to her mother as soon as she realized she was in deep trouble, and was taking emergency lessons about the upcoming event so she didn't embarrass her Master.
"Blossom must say yes before it's her turn!!" Blossom recited from the kitchen table. "Blossom must not kiss Master too long!! Blossom must not- what was it again?"

Kitsara was using her tails to become copies of herself, and frantically tried a hundred dress combinations on them all, using them as props. Several maids were dragged in to help her and offer their opinion.
"Higher," said Anna.
"Lower," said Beatrice, the quieter of their twin maids.
"Stop messing with me you damned brats!" shouted three Kitsaras at once, in three slightly different octaves, and received Anna's loud laughter and Beatrice's sly smirk.
Then the others realized how useful their foxy was, and Kitsara spent the next hour standing in as every bride's mirror, model, and second opinion.
Iris made it as far as the east corridor before the second-in-command caught her.
"Iris."
"No."
"You haven't heard the question." Ayame fell into step beside her.
"You want me to marry him?" Iris asked, suspicious.
Ayame's eyes widened.
"So I can hear you hiss at me even in the bedroom?" she smirked. "Goddess, no."
"..." Iris's eyes narrowed. "You want to know what a bride does. I'm the only one in this house not screaming, so you think that means I know something." Iris kept walking. "I know nothing, midget."

Ayame's smugness increased to dangerous levels. "Of course you know nothing. For all intents and purposes, you have been a homeless vagrant for most of your adult life before we adopted you like a puppy, barely getting by on stale bread. I was raised as a noble duchess, I know a lot more about this. Why would I ever ask your opinion?"
Iris formed a fist and lunged, ready to shatter a certain snob cunt's skull into a thousand pieces. "Die!"
"Will you walk me to the altar?" Ayame asked just before Iris hit her. "That's what I wanted to ask."
The Demon of Vengeance stopped.
"Hah?"

Downstairs, with the house still screaming over their heads, Vex had her mentor by the wrist and was towing her through the main hall. Black Fang was allowing herself to be towed, which was its own kind of answer.
"White or red?"
"White with red accents."
"Do I wear the horns?"
"No."
"Why not???"
"You'll appear as though you're desperate to outshine the other women."
"But I am desperate to outshine the other women!!"
"You can't be obvious about it or you'll fail."
"Ohh!!" Vex's eyes brightened. "Master, you're so helpful! Thank you... I would be lost without you."
"...There's nothing to thank me for."
"Master, did you just smile? I saw a faint movement at the edge of your lips!"
"No."
"Yes!"
"...I'll leave."
"Aww!! There she is, using blackmail to get her way!" Vex pouted, then gave up.
If she had kept watching for a second longer, she would've seen a much bigger curve on her master's lips.
Serika gave up on the east stair and came back to the sickroom. It was the Solar Fist, planted in the middle of the rug, who asked the question that actually mattered.
"Where do we even hold it?!"
"Miri Town," Quinlan said, from the foot of the bed.
Serika opened her mouth to ask the next question, and never got to it, because Jasmine had gone completely still.
The governor sat against her pillows with one hand flat on the seal below her navel. Her eyes had gone gold, the bright unnatural gold of new coin, and they were not looking at anything in the room.
They were reading the realm, every road, record, and border of it laid out under her palm like a page.
"There is a building on my square," said the Tyrant of Commerce.
"Is there?"
"There is a building on my square that was not there when I went under." Her gold eyes narrowed. "It is very large. It has dwarven foundations. And why are there so many elves?! Quin, explain!"
The room had stopped panicking to listen.
That was the something he had done.
"I asked Myra and Isveth, Felicity and Alexios, and the dwarves last night, after I started your trial and before I walked the beastkin pass. They've been busy organizing the event ever since."
Jasmine was still reading. Her mouth had begun to thin, as it did over a fraudulent ledger.
"Twice," she said. "Beastkin lords on my road and a hall on my square. Twice in one day, you did something to my town while I was unconscious."
"I might've made a little mess in your absence," Quinlan grinned, entirely unapologetic. "That much I'll admit."
"How big."
"Big enough."
"How big, Quin."
"The dwarves were told 'make it perfect.'"
Jasmine sat there with her hair down and her hand on her seal, and somewhere in the middle of looking at the man at the foot of her bed the Tyrant of Commerce began, very slowly, to smile.
"...Somebody find my signet. And a quartermaster. And my slippers."
"Slippers first," said her mother.
